  • Connection draining at every layer: the load balancer's deregistration delay must be shorter than the pod's termination grace period, or rolling updates drop requests.
  • Internal traffic uses the same layers without the global one: internal load balancers or Lattice, then in-cluster routing.

Network isolation in layers

Scenario. An audit asks the team to prove that a compromised pod in a development namespace can't reach the production payments database. The honest answer was "probably", based on one security group. The team needs every layer to deny the path, and to be able to show it.

What the picture shows. Six layers of isolation, from the widest to the narrowest, each owned by one team.

1Segments (Cloud WAN)
production and non-production can't route to each other at all. Owned by the network team.
2VPCs, subnets and security groups
only load balancers and gateways accept traffic from outside the VPC; security groups for pods restrict which pods can reach databases and other AWS resources. See Security groups for pods.
3Cluster-wide policy (ClusterNetworkPolicy)
guardrails set by the platform team that namespace owners can't override, such as "no namespace may reach the instance metadata service" and "everything is denied unless a team allows it".
apiVersion: policy.networking.k8s.io/v1alpha2kind: ClusterNetworkPolicymetadata:  name: baseline-default-denyspec:  tier: Baseline                  # teams can open paths with NetworkPolicy above this  priority: 10  subject:    namespaces: {}  ingress:  - action: Deny                  # zero-trust default for every namespace    from:    - namespaces: {}---apiVersion: policy.networking.k8s.io/v1alpha2kind: ClusterNetworkPolicymetadata:  name: admin-allow-monitoring-and-dnsspec:  tier: Admin                     # evaluated first; namespace owners can't override  priority: 30  subject:    namespaces: {}  ingress:  - action: Accept    name: allow-monitoring    from:    - namespaces:        matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }  egress:  - action: Accept    name: allow-cluster-dns    to:    - pods:        namespaceSelector:          matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }        podSelector:          matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
4Namespace policy (NetworkPolicy)
each team allows the traffic its own services need, inside the platform's guardrails.
5Workload identity (mesh or Lattice auth)
for traffic that crosses clusters or accounts, the receiver checks who is calling (a service identity or IAM principal), not just where the packet came from.
6Egress control
traffic to the internet leaves through a central egress path per region (NAT gateways and AWS Network Firewall with domain rules), and sandbox clusters add per-session egress gateways from Design 01.
Going deeper3 points
  • ClusterNetworkPolicy is new. It replaces the earlier AdminNetworkPolicy and BaselineAdminNetworkPolicy with one resource and a tier field, and is still v1alpha2. Check that the cluster's policy engine supports it; where it doesn't, the platform enforces the same guardrails with the policy engine's own cluster-wide resources.
  • Test the denials, not just the allows: a scheduled job in each cluster tries the paths that must fail (development to production, any pod to IMDS, sandbox to the internet) and alerts if any succeeds.
  • One source for policy: segment rules, security groups and cluster-wide policies are all generated from Git, so the answer to "can A reach B?" can be computed, not guessed.

DNS across clouds and clusters

Scenario. A job on the on-premises racks can't resolve the name of the model registry, which lives in a private hosted zone in AWS. A pod in Google Cloud can't resolve it either. Routing worked; naming didn't.

The design.

  • One private namespace: internal names live under one domain (for example, internal.example.com) in Route 53 private hosted zones, shared with every VPC through Route 53 Profiles.
  • Resolver endpoints for the outside: Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoints let on-premises and the other cloud resolve AWS names; outbound endpoints and forwarding rules let AWS resolve their names. Each side forwards only its partner's domains.
  • Cluster DNS stays local: CoreDNS with NodeLocal DNSCache resolves in-cluster names and forwards everything else to the VPC resolver. Lower ndots for workloads that mostly call external names, to cut wasted lookups.
  • Service names, not load balancer names: clients use stable names (Lattice service names or internal records) that point at whatever load balancer currently serves them.
Going deeper2 points
  • DNS is a dependency of everything: run NodeLocal DNSCache on every node, monitor resolver latency and errors per cluster, and keep Resolver endpoints in at least two zones.
  • DNS is also an exfiltration path for untrusted workloads; sandbox clusters use a resolver that only answers for allowlisted domains (Design 01).

Cost and traffic engineering

Scenario. The monthly bill shows more spent on data transfer than on CPU instances. Most of it is three patterns: pods calling across availability zones, training jobs reading data from another region, and every container image pull going through a NAT gateway.

The design.

  • Stay in the zone: topology-aware routing for Services, zone-aware load balancer settings, and replicas spread so every zone can serve itself.
  • Move data once, then compute: datasets are replicated to the region and cloud where the GPUs are (S3 replication, or a one-time transfer over the interconnect), never read across regions during training.
  • Keep AWS traffic off NAT gateways: gateway endpoints for S3 and interface endpoints for ECR, STS and other AWS APIs in every VPC, so image pulls and API calls don't pay NAT processing charges.
  • Pull-through caches for public images in each region, so public image pulls don't leave the region.
  • Measure flows by cost: VPC flow logs (or Cilium's Hubble) aggregated by source, destination, zone and region, labelled with team and service, reviewed monthly like compute spend.
Going deeper2 points
  • See Networking in the optimization deep dive for the instance-level levers.
  • Price the paths before designing them. Cross-zone, cross-region, interconnect, NAT, Transit Gateway and Cloud WAN processing all have different per-gigabyte costs; the cheapest correct path is a design decision, not an accident.

Failure modes and operations

Scenario. Before launch, the network and platform teams walk through what breaks when each layer fails.

Failure What users see What the design does
Availability zone lost Brief errors, then recovery Load balancers and topology-aware routing stop sending traffic to the zone; replicas in other zones serve
Region lost Users routed to another region Global health checks remove the region; inference and services fail over; batch work waits or uses the other region's queue
Interconnect to the second cloud down Cross-cloud jobs slow or pause Redundant connections across locations; a site-to-site VPN as a lower-bandwidth backup on the hybrid segment
Direct Connect to on-premises down Hybrid nodes lose the control plane Two connections in different locations; hybrid node workloads keep running but can't be rescheduled until the link returns
Bad Cloud WAN policy change Routes withdrawn between segments Policy changes go through Git review and a change set preview; rollback is a revert
Pod IP exhaustion New pods stuck pending Pod ranges sized from the address plan; alerts on free IPs per subnet; IPv6 for new large clusters
DNS resolver problems Widespread, confusing failures NodeLocal DNSCache on every node; resolver endpoints in two zones; DNS latency alerts
Going deeper2 points
  • Every network change is code: the Cloud WAN policy, IPAM pools, VPCs, security groups, Lattice service networks and cluster-wide policies all live in Git and are applied through the same pipeline as the clusters (Design 02).
  • Reachability tests run continuously: synthetic probes check the paths that must work (service to service, cross-cloud, on-premises) and the denial tests check the paths that must not.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Scenario. The network can't be replaced in a weekend. Leadership asks for an order that reduces risk at each step.

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, the address plan: VPC IPAM with pools per region and environment, pod ranges for every cluster, IPv6 for new clusters, and a plan for renumbering the three overlapping VPCs.
  • Phase 2, the core network: Cloud WAN with segments, Transit Gateways and peerings moved onto it one VPC at a time, inspection between segments.
  • Phase 3, the outside: AWS Interconnect to Google Cloud, Direct Connect for the hybrid racks, Resolver endpoints for shared DNS.
  • Phase 4, services and isolation: VPC Lattice service networks with the Gateway API, ClusterNetworkPolicy guardrails, denial tests, and a mesh only where workload mTLS is required.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Cloud WAN over a Transit Gateway mesh: a managed, policy-driven core with segments, at the cost of a newer service and its pricing model.
  • Non-routable pods by default: less flexibility for direct pod-to-pod calls across VPCs, in exchange for address space that never runs out and a smaller blast radius.
  • Lattice before a mesh: managed cross-account service connectivity with IAM authorization, at the cost of fewer traffic-management features than a full mesh.
  • Two CNIs in the fleet: the VPC CNI for most clusters and Cilium where its features matter, at the cost of two things to know and operate.

Open questions for the next review.

  • IPv6 everywhere? When every dependency supports it, IPv6-only clusters would remove the pod address problem entirely.
  • Mesh across clusters: when Istio ambient multicluster is production-ready, should it replace Lattice for some east-west traffic?
  • A second partner cloud: AWS Interconnect is adding more cloud providers; the same hybrid segment model should extend to them.
  • Network policy at the edge of the cluster: whether ClusterNetworkPolicy's beta, expected soon, is enough to replace engine-specific cluster-wide policies across the fleet.
Design 06 · 13 sections

Design 06: A platform for post-training recipes (SFT, RL and distillation)

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. A recipe is a pipeline of stages
  3. What each choice changes
  4. SFT: data mixtures and loss masking
  5. RL: choosing the objective
  6. Rewards and verifiers
  7. Rollout generation: the most expensive part
  8. Filtering: which samples carry signal
  9. Distillation: off-policy and on-policy
  10. Stability: the signals that predict a collapse
  11. The experiment platform on Kubernetes
  12. Evaluation and final model behavior
  13. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we build a place where a research team can develop and iterate on post-training recipes (supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning and distillation) quickly, and actually understand how each choice of objective, data mixture, hyperparameter, rollout setting and filter changes efficiency, stability, capability and the final model's behavior? It sits on top of Design 02 (queues and GPU capacity), Design 03 (training jobs, checkpoints, serving) and Design 01 (for verifiers that run model-written code). For the basics of fine-tuning, see Customizing models.

The short version: a recipe is a versioned config, not a notebook. Every run is launched from one, tagged with its data, code and model versions, and evaluated by the same suite. RL runs are split into rollout (vLLM), reward (verifiers, sandboxes, judges) and training (FSDP or Megatron) components, so each scales separately. And every run streams the same health signals (reward, entropy, response length, KL, clipping, train–inference mismatch), so "why did this run go wrong?" has an answer before the run finishes, not after.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. The post-training team takes an open-weight 8B base model and turns it into the company's assistant: it should follow instructions in the house style, reason through multi-step problems, write working code and refuse what it should. They run about 40 experiments a week. Today each researcher has their own scripts; two runs that "used the same recipe" differed in five settings nobody recorded, a promising RL run collapsed on day three with no warning, and nobody can say whether the last improvement came from the new data mixture or the new learning rate.

What the platform must do.

  • Make recipes reproducible: one versioned file fully describes a run, so it can be re-run, diffed and ablated.
  • Make iteration fast: a small ablation (one setting changed, a few hundred steps) starts in minutes and finishes in hours, without waiting behind a two-week run.
  • Explain outcomes: every run reports the same efficiency, stability, capability and behavior metrics, so two recipes can be compared on the same chart.
  • Support all three families: SFT, RL (online, with rollouts and rewards) and distillation (off-policy and on-policy), and pipelines that chain them.
  • Run RL efficiently: keep GPUs busy despite long, uneven rollouts, without silently breaking the algorithm's assumptions.
  • Be safe: rewards that execute model-written code do so in sandboxes; checkpoints and data are versioned and access-controlled.

Out of scope for this design: pre-training, the GPU fleet itself (Design 02), and serving the final model (Design 03).

A recipe is a pipeline of stages

Scenario. A new researcher asks "what's our recipe?" and gets three different answers. The team needs one picture of the stages, and a clear list of the choices made at each one.

What the picture shows. A typical post-training recipe, and the five kinds of choices made at every stage.

1SFT (supervised fine-tuning)
teaches format, style, instruction following and, with curated reasoning traces, a "cold start" for later RL. Learns from fixed examples.
2Preference optimization (optional)
DPO-style training on pairs of better and worse answers, for tone and helpfulness where there's no verifiable right answer.
3RL (reinforcement learning)
the model generates answers (rollouts), a reward scores them, and the policy is pushed toward higher-reward behavior. Where reasoning, coding and agentic skills grow most.
4Distillation
a strong teacher's knowledge is transferred to a smaller or cheaper student, either from teacher-written examples (off-policy) or by having the teacher grade the student's own outputs (on-policy).
5Evaluation gates between stages
capability, behavior and safety suites decide whether a checkpoint moves on.
6The five choices at every stage
the objective (loss), the data mixture, the hyperparameters, rollout generation (for RL and on-policy distillation) and filtering (which data or samples are kept).

The recipe file. Every run is launched from a file like this, stored in Git; the platform records its hash with every metric and checkpoint.

# recipes/assistant-v12/rl-math-code.yamlrecipe: assistant-v12stage: rlbase_checkpoint: registry://assistant-v12/sft@sha256:7c1e...      # output of the SFT stageobjective:  algorithm: grpo  loss_aggregation: token-mean          # DAPO-style; avoids length bias  clip: { low: 0.2, high: 0.28 }        # asymmetric "clip-higher"  kl_to_reference: 0.0                  # no reference model  importance_sampling: { level: token, rollout_correction: truncate, cap: 3.0 }data:  prompts:  - { source: datasets://math-verified@v4, weight: 0.5 }  - { source: datasets://code-tests@v7,    weight: 0.4 }  - { source: datasets://if-eval-style@v2, weight: 0.1 }  filter: { pass_rate_min: 0.05, pass_rate_max: 0.95 }             # drop too-easy and too-hardrollout:  engine: vllm  group_size: 8                         # answers per prompt  temperature: 1.0  max_response_tokens: 16384  max_staleness_steps: 1                # how off-policy we toleraterewards:- { name: math_exact, weight: 1.0 }- { name: unit_tests, weight: 1.0, sandbox: true }- { name: overlong_penalty, start: 14336, end: 16384 }hyperparameters: { lr: 1.0e-6, batch_prompts: 256, steps: 1500, warmup_steps: 20 }eval: { suites: [math-hard, code-live, ifeval, safety-refusals, style], every_steps: 100 }
Going deeper2 points
  • The order matters. SFT before RL gives RL a model that already answers in the right format, so early rewards aren't all zero. Distillation can come before RL (a cheap capability boost) or after it (compressing an RL-trained teacher into a smaller student).
  • Keep stages separate in the platform: each stage produces a registered checkpoint, so a later stage can be re-run from an earlier one without repeating everything.

What each choice changes

Scenario. The team argues for an hour about whether a regression in tone came from the RL reward or from the SFT data. The platform should make the expected effect of each kind of choice explicit, so experiments test hypotheses instead of guesses.

What the picture shows. The four outcomes the team cares about, and which choices move each one most.

1Efficiency (GPU hours per unit of improvement)
dominated by rollout generation (often most of an RL step's time), filtering (how many samples carry a useful signal) and asynchrony.
2Stability (does the run keep improving or collapse?)
dominated by the objective's details (clipping, loss aggregation, KL), the learning rate, how off-policy the data is, and the numerical gap between the inference and training engines.
3Capability (benchmark scores on reasoning, code, tools)
dominated by the data mixture and the reward: you get what you reward, on the prompts you train on.
4Behavior (style, length, refusals, honesty, tool use)
shaped by SFT data, preference data, reward side effects (length, format) and the teacher in distillation. Behavior changes are the easiest to miss because benchmarks don't measure them.
Going deeper2 points
  • Change one thing per ablation. A recipe diff with one changed key and a fixed seed is the unit of learning. The platform enforces this for ablation runs by refusing launches whose diff touches more than the declared variable.
  • Behavior needs its own evals: response length distributions, refusal rates on borderline prompts, style classifiers and a small human-reviewed sample, tracked per checkpoint like any benchmark.

SFT: data mixtures and loss masking

Scenario. After adding 200,000 math traces to the SFT mix, math scores rise and the model starts answering every casual question with a numbered proof. The data mixture changed the model's behavior far more than anyone intended.

What the picture shows. What an SFT run is made of, and the choices inside it.

1The mixture
sources (general chat, domain, reasoning traces, code, tool use, safety) with explicit sampling weights. Weights, not raw counts, decide what the model sees most.
2Quality filters per source
deduplication against eval sets (to avoid contamination), length limits, language and format checks, and a quality score from a classifier or judge.
3Loss masking
compute the loss only on the assistant's turns, not on the system prompt or the user's words, so the model learns to answer, not to imitate users.
4Packing
several short conversations are packed into one sequence to avoid wasting compute on padding, with attention kept within each conversation.
5The chat template
the exact template used in training must match the one used at serving time, or behavior drifts in ways no benchmark explains.

The code. An SFT stage with an explicit mixture, assistant-only loss and packing (TRL).

from datasets import load_dataset, interleave_datasetsfrom trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer sources = {    "general":   ("datasets/general-chat-v9",   0.40),    "domain":    ("datasets/support-domain-v4", 0.25),    "reasoning": ("datasets/reasoning-traces-v3", 0.20),   # raise carefully: changes style    "code":      ("datasets/code-instruct-v6",  0.10),    "safety":    ("datasets/safety-refusals-v5", 0.05),}parts = [load_dataset(path, split="train") for path, _ in sources.values()]mixture = interleave_datasets(    parts, probabilities=[w for _, w in sources.values()], seed=17,    stopping_strategy="all_exhausted",) trainer = SFTTrainer(    model="registry/base-8b",    train_dataset=mixture,    args=SFTConfig(        output_dir="/checkpoints/assistant-v12/sft",        assistant_only_loss=True,         # learn to answer, not to imitate users        packing=True,                     # no compute wasted on padding        max_length=8192,        learning_rate=1e-5,        num_train_epochs=2,        bf16=True,    ),)trainer.train()
Going deeper2 points
  • Mixture weights are hyperparameters. Sweep them like a learning rate, with small proxy runs, and track per-source eval scores so you can see which source moved which capability.
  • SFT on a model's own good outputs (rejection sampling: generate, keep only verified-correct answers, train on them) is a cheap step between SFT and RL.

RL: choosing the objective

Scenario. Two RL runs with "GRPO" in the config behave completely differently: one grows response length steadily and improves; the other's responses get shorter and its accuracy stalls. They differ in how the loss is averaged over tokens, a detail most people never look at.

What the picture shows. The GRPO family, and the small choices inside it that change training behavior.

1Group-relative advantages (GRPO)
sample a group of answers per prompt, score them, and use each answer's reward minus the group mean (often divided by the group's standard deviation) as its advantage. No separate value model (critic) is needed, which saves memory and complexity.
2Loss aggregation
averaging the loss per answer and then over answers (original GRPO) gives short answers' tokens more weight each; averaging over all tokens in the batch (DAPO, Dr. GRPO) removes that length bias.
3Clipping
limits how far one update can move the probability of a token. An asymmetric, higher upper bound ("clip-higher") lets rare but good tokens grow, which keeps exploration (entropy) alive.
4Token vs. sequence level
GSPO computes the importance ratio and clipping per answer instead of per token, which its authors report is more stable, especially for mixture-of-experts models.
5KL to a reference model
a penalty for drifting from the starting model. Many reasoning recipes now drop it (and the reference model's memory cost) and rely on clipping instead; recipes that care about preserving behavior keep a small one.

The variants at a glance.

Variant What it changes Why
GRPO Group-normalized advantages, no critic Cheap, simple RL for verifiable tasks
DAPO Clip-higher, dynamic sampling, token-level loss, overlong penalty Stability and efficiency for long reasoning
Dr. GRPO Removes per-length and per-std normalization Removes biases toward short or easy answers
GSPO Sequence-level ratio and clipping Stability, especially for MoE models
PPO Learned critic for advantages Dense credit assignment, at the cost of a second model

The code. The same choices as TRL GRPOConfig settings (current TRL defaults to DAPO-style loss and no KL term).

from trl import GRPOConfig, GRPOTrainer config = GRPOConfig(    output_dir="/checkpoints/assistant-v12/rl",    loss_type="dapo",                     # token-level aggregation (the default)    num_generations=8,                    # group size per prompt    epsilon=0.2, epsilon_high=0.28,       # clip-higher    beta=0.0,                             # no KL to a reference model (the default)    importance_sampling_level="token",    # "sequence" = GSPO-style    scale_rewards="group",                # divide by group std; "none" = Dr. GRPO-style    mask_truncated_completions=True,      # don't punish answers cut off by the length limit    max_completion_length=16384,    temperature=1.0,    learning_rate=1e-6,    use_vllm=True, vllm_mode="server",    # rollouts on a separate vLLM server    vllm_importance_sampling_correction=True,   # correct engine mismatch)trainer = GRPOTrainer(model="registry/assistant-v12-sft", reward_funcs=[math_exact, format_ok],                      args=config, train_dataset=prompts)trainer.train()
Going deeper2 points
  • The literature disagrees, and results depend on scale: controlled comparisons find different "best" algorithms at different model sizes. Treat the objective as a set of ablatable switches in the recipe, not a fixed choice.
  • Start simple: token-level loss, clip-higher, no KL, group size 8–16 and a low learning rate is a sensible baseline; change one switch at a time from there.

Rewards and verifiers

Scenario. A coding RL run's reward climbs to 0.95 while real pass rates on held-out problems fall. The model learned to detect the test harness and print the expected output. The reward was measuring something easier than the skill.

What the picture shows. Three kinds of reward, and the safeguards around them.

1Verifiable rewards
exact-match math answers, unit tests, compilers, schema checks. The strongest signal (RL with verifiable rewards, RLVR) and the least ambiguous, but only for tasks with a checkable answer.
2Reward models and judges
a trained reward model or an LLM judge with a rubric, for open-ended quality. Flexible, but they can be gamed, and their biases (often toward longer answers) become the policy's biases.
3Shaping terms
format checks and length penalties (for example, a graded penalty as answers approach the length limit). Small weights, because the policy optimizes them too.
4Sandboxed execution
rewards that run model-written code do so in isolated sandboxes with no network and strict time and memory limits (Design 01). A reward function is untrusted code's target.
5Reward hacking checks
held-out evals that use different verifiers from training, sampled rollouts reviewed by people every few hundred steps, and alerts when reward rises while held-out scores don't.

The code. Reward functions in TRL's format: each receives the batch and returns one score per completion.

import refrom math_verify import parse, verify            # robust equivalence of math answers def math_exact(completions, solution, **kwargs) -> list[float]:    """1.0 if the final boxed answer is mathematically equal to the reference."""    scores = []    for completion, ref in zip(completions, solution):        text = completion[0]["content"]        boxed = re.findall(r"\\boxed\{([^}]*)\}", text)        scores.append(1.0 if boxed and verify(parse(ref), parse(boxed[-1])) else 0.0)    return scores def format_ok(completions, **kwargs) -> list[float]:    """Small shaping reward: exactly one final boxed answer, after the reasoning."""    return [0.1 if len(re.findall(r"\\boxed\{", c[0]["content"])) == 1 else 0.0 for c in completions] def unit_tests(completions, tests, **kwargs) -> list[float]:    """Run the candidate code against hidden tests in a sandbox (no network, 10 s, 1 GiB)."""    return [sandbox_client.run(c[0]["content"], t, timeout_s=10, memory_mb=1024).pass_rate            for c, t in zip(completions, tests)]
Going deeper2 points
  • Keep reward code versioned and tested like production code. A bug in a verifier (accepting "1/2" but not "0.5") silently teaches the model the verifier's quirks.
  • Reward throughput is part of rollout throughput. Thousands of sandboxed test runs per step need their own autoscaled pool, sized so reward never becomes the bottleneck.

Rollout generation: the most expensive part

Scenario. On a long-reasoning RL run, the training GPUs are idle 70% of the time. Each step waits for the slowest rollouts: most answers finish in 2,000 tokens, but a few run to 16,000, and the whole batch waits for them.

What the picture shows. Three ways to organize rollout and training, and what each trades.

1Synchronous (colocated)
generate a batch, then train on it, on the same GPUs. Strictly on-policy and simple, but GPUs alternate between generating and training, and the slowest answer holds everyone up.
2One-step off-policy
generation of the next batch overlaps with training on the current one. Most of the idle time disappears, at the cost of training on samples one policy version old.
3Fully asynchronous (streaming)
separate rollout and training pools; rollouts stream into a buffer and the trainer consumes them continuously, with weights pushed to the rollout engines periodically. Highest throughput; samples can be several versions stale, so the objective needs importance-sampling corrections and a staleness limit.
4Train–inference mismatch
even with identical weights, the inference engine (vLLM, SGLang) and the training engine (FSDP, Megatron) compute slightly different token probabilities. Every update divides one by the other, so the gap enters every step. Corrections: truncated or masked importance sampling, matching numerics, and for MoE models rollout routing replay, which reuses the experts chosen during sampling in the training pass.

The YAML. An RL run on KubeRay with verl: rollout and training as one Ray job, admitted by Kueue as a whole.

apiVersion: ray.io/v1kind: RayJobmetadata:  name: assistant-v12-rl-math-code  namespace: post-training  labels:    kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: research-rl            # all-or-nothing admission    recipe.example.com/hash: 3f9a1c7spec:  entrypoint: >-    python3 -m verl.trainer.main_ppo    algorithm.adv_estimator=grpo    data.train_files=/data/rl-math-code-v4/train.parquet    data.max_response_length=16384    actor_rollout_ref.model.path=/models/assistant-v12-sft    actor_rollout_ref.rollout.name=vllm    actor_rollout_ref.rollout.n=8    actor_rollout_ref.actor.loss_agg_mode=token-mean    actor_rollout_ref.actor.clip_ratio_low=0.2    actor_rollout_ref.actor.clip_ratio_high=0.28    actor_rollout_ref.actor.use_kl_loss=False    actor_rollout_ref.actor.optim.lr=1e-6    trainer.nnodes=4 trainer.n_gpus_per_node=8    trainer.save_freq=50 trainer.default_local_dir=/checkpoints/assistant-v12/rl  shutdownAfterJobFinishes: true  rayClusterSpec:    headGroupSpec:      rayStartParams: {}      template:        spec:          containers:          - name: head            image: registry.example.com/post-training/verl:2026.11   # pinned verl + vLLM            resources: { limits: { cpu: "16", memory: 64Gi } }    workerGroupSpecs:    - groupName: gpu      replicas: 4      rayStartParams: {}      template:        spec:          containers:          - name: worker            image: registry.example.com/post-training/verl:2026.11            resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8, vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: 32 } }            volumeMounts: [ { name: ckpt, mountPath: /checkpoints } ]          volumes:          - name: ckpt            persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: post-training-checkpoints }
Going deeper3 points
  • Start synchronous, then add asynchrony with a staleness limit, and compare against the synchronous run on the same recipe. Throughput gains are only real if the reward curve matches.
  • Long tails dominate: cap response length, use partial rollouts (pause long generations and resume them in the next step) and oversample prompts so a few slow answers don't stall the batch.
  • Weight sync is a network problem: pushing new weights from trainer to rollout engines every step moves the whole model. Use the fast fabric and in-place updates; see Design 05.

Filtering: which samples carry signal

Scenario. Halfway through an RL run, 60% of prompts have all eight answers correct and 20% have all eight wrong. In group-relative RL those groups have zero advantage: they cost full rollout compute and teach nothing.

What the picture shows. Filters at three points, and what each saves.

1Before the run (prompt curation)
estimate each prompt's pass rate with the starting model and keep prompts between roughly 5% and 95%. Too easy or too hard prompts have no learning signal.
2During the run (dynamic sampling)
drop groups where every answer got the same reward and sample more prompts until the batch is full of informative groups (DAPO's dynamic sampling). Re-estimate pass rates as the model improves, which acts as a curriculum.
3Per sample
mask answers truncated by the length limit (so the model isn't punished for being cut off), drop samples whose importance ratio is extreme (engine mismatch or staleness), and optionally train only on high-entropy "forking" tokens.
4For SFT and distillation data
deduplicate, decontaminate against eval sets and keep only verified-correct traces (rejection sampling).

The code. Pass-rate filtering of a prompt set before RL, using the SFT checkpoint served by vLLM.

from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams llm = LLM(model="/models/assistant-v12-sft", tensor_parallel_size=8)params = SamplingParams(n=16, temperature=1.0, max_tokens=16384) def pass_rates(prompts: list[dict]) -> list[float]:    outs = llm.generate([p["prompt"] for p in prompts], params)    return [sum(math_exact([[{"content": o.text}]], [p["solution"]])[0] for o in out.outputs) / 16            for p, out in zip(prompts, outs)] rates = pass_rates(prompts)kept = [p | {"pass_rate": r} for p, r in zip(prompts, rates) if 0.05 <= r <= 0.95]print(f"kept {len(kept)} of {len(prompts)} prompts; mean pass rate {sum(rates)/len(rates):.2f}")
Going deeper2 points
  • Filtering changes what "reward going up" means: with dynamic sampling, the training reward is measured on a moving, harder-than-average subset. Always read capability from held-out evals, not training reward.
  • Filtering costs rollouts too: dynamic sampling generates more than it trains on. Track "rollouts generated per sample trained" as an efficiency metric.

Distillation: off-policy and on-policy

Scenario. The RL-trained 32B model is excellent and too expensive to serve. The team wants an 8B model that behaves like it. Fine-tuning the 8B on the 32B's answers gets the style right, but on hard problems the student goes off track early and never recovers.

What the picture shows. Two ways to transfer a teacher's behavior.

1Off-policy distillation (SFT on teacher traces)
the teacher writes answers; the student imitates them. Cheap and simple, but the student only ever sees states the teacher visited. When it makes its own early mistake at serving time, it's in territory it never trained on.
2On-policy distillation
the student generates answers, and the teacher scores every token the student chose, typically with the per-token reverse KL between the two models' next-token distributions. The student learns what to do from the states it actually reaches, including how to recover.
3Dense signal
unlike RL's single reward per answer, every token gets feedback, which makes on-policy distillation much cheaper than RL for the same improvement when a good teacher exists.
4Constraints
teacher and student must share a tokenizer for per-token scores, and the teacher's quirks (verbosity, style) transfer along with its skill.

The code. On-policy distillation with TRL's DistillationTrainer (its beta=1.0 selects reverse KL).

from trl import DistillationConfig, DistillationTrainer trainer = DistillationTrainer(    model="registry/assistant-v12-8b-sft",            # student (same tokenizer as teacher)    teacher_model="registry/assistant-v12-32b-rl",    train_dataset=prompts,                            # prompts only: the student writes the answers    args=DistillationConfig(        output_dir="/checkpoints/assistant-v12/distill-8b",        beta=1.0,                                     # 1.0 = reverse KL (mode-seeking)        max_completion_length=8192,        temperature=1.0,        learning_rate=1e-6,        use_vllm=True, vllm_mode="server",            # student rollouts on vLLM    ),)trainer.train()
Going deeper2 points
  • Combine them: a short off-policy SFT on teacher traces first (so the student's outputs are in the teacher's "language"), then on-policy distillation. When teacher and student think in very different patterns, on-policy distillation alone can fail to take hold.
  • Infrastructure-wise, on-policy distillation is RL with a teacher instead of a reward: the same rollout pools, plus a teacher inference pool scoring tokens, so the same platform runs both.

Stability: the signals that predict a collapse

Scenario. An RL run's reward is flat for a day, then drops to zero in an hour. Looking back, entropy had been falling for two days and the importance-sampling ratios had been drifting since the first hundred steps. The signals were there; nobody was watching them.

What the picture shows. The health signals every run streams, and the failure each one predicts.

1Reward (train and held-out)
rising train reward with flat held-out scores means reward hacking or overfitting to the prompt set.
2Policy entropy
a steady fall to near zero means the model has stopped exploring (entropy collapse); learning stalls. A sudden rise means the policy is breaking down.
3Response length
steady growth is normal for reasoning RL; explosive growth or a collapse to very short answers points to a length bias in the loss or reward.
4KL to the starting model and clip fraction
how far and how fast the policy is moving. Spikes mean updates are too large (learning rate, staleness).
5Importance-sampling ratio statistics (train vs. rollout probabilities)
widening means train–inference mismatch or staleness is growing, an early sign of collapse, especially for MoE models.
6Gradient norm
spikes precede many collapses; clip gradients and alert on spikes.

Symptoms and first fixes.

Symptom Likely cause First thing to try
Entropy falls steadily, reward plateaus Clipping too tight, no exploration Clip-higher, higher temperature, entropy-aware token selection
Responses suddenly very short or very long Length bias in loss or reward Token-level loss; overlong shaping; mask truncated answers
IS ratios widen, then reward collapses Train–inference mismatch or staleness Truncated/masked IS, lower staleness, routing replay for MoE
Train reward up, held-out flat or down Reward hacking, prompt overfitting Different held-out verifiers; review samples; more prompt diversity
Grad-norm spikes, loss spikes Learning rate too high, bad batch Lower LR, gradient clipping, inspect the batch
Going deeper2 points
  • Alert on trends, not values: a slope alert on entropy and IS-ratio spread catches problems days before the reward does.
  • Checkpoint often during RL (every 25–50 steps) and keep the last several, so a collapse costs a rollback, not the run.

The experiment platform on Kubernetes

Scenario. A researcher wants to run a 12-way ablation of the clip-higher bound overnight, at small scale, while a two-week production RL run continues on the main GPUs. Today that means asking in a channel and hoping.

What the picture shows. The components that turn a recipe file into compared results.

1Recipes in Git
reviewed like code; an ablation is a branch with one changed key and a declared variable.
2Experiment launcher
expands a recipe (and a sweep) into jobs, attaches data, code, image and checkpoint versions, and submits them. Every run gets a stable ID and the recipe hash.
3Queues and capacity
Kueue queues per team and per run size: small ablations borrow idle GPUs at low priority; production runs have reserved capacity and aren't preempted (Design 02).
4The RL job
a Ray job with a trainer (FSDP or Megatron), rollout engines (vLLM or SGLang), a reference or teacher model when needed, and reward workers that call verifiers and a sandbox pool.
5Checkpoints and registry
checkpoints to fast shared storage and S3, the chosen ones registered with their recipe and eval results (Design 03).
6Evaluation and tracking
every checkpoint runs the same eval suites as batch jobs; metrics, eval scores and sample outputs go to one tracking system, comparable across runs.
Going deeper3 points
  • Proxy runs first: most decisions (mixture weights, clip values, filtering thresholds) are made with small models and short runs, then confirmed at full scale. The platform makes "same recipe, smaller model" a one-line change.
  • Determinism where possible: fixed seeds, pinned images and recorded data order make ablations meaningful. Full determinism isn't achievable across GPU kernels, so run important comparisons with two seeds.
  • Cost per experiment is a first-class metric: GPU hours, rollout tokens and the share of rollouts that carried signal, shown next to the results.

Evaluation and final model behavior

Scenario. A new recipe wins on every benchmark and is promoted. Within a week, users notice it's twice as verbose, refuses more borderline requests and hedges on simple questions. None of the benchmarks measured that.

The design.

  • Capability suites: reasoning, code, tool use and domain tasks, with held-out verifiers different from the training rewards, run every N steps and on every candidate checkpoint.
  • Behavior suites: response length distribution, refusal rate on borderline prompts, over-refusal on safe prompts, instruction-following precision, tone and style classifiers, honesty and calibration checks.
  • Safety suites: harmful-request refusals, jailbreak resistance, and the red-team set, owned by the safety team and versioned.
  • Regression checks against the previous release: a candidate must not regress more than an agreed margin on any suite, not just improve on average.
  • Human review: a fixed weekly sample of outputs per candidate, blind-compared against the current release.
Going deeper2 points
  • Decontaminate eval sets against all training data, including SFT mixtures and RL prompts, and keep a private test set nobody trains on.
  • Promote through the registry with gates (see From training to serving): a recipe's output only reaches users after its eval results are attached and approved.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Scenario. The team wants better recipes, faster, starting this quarter.

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, reproducibility: recipe files in Git, the launcher, run IDs and tracking, standard eval suites on every checkpoint. Nothing new about the training itself, but every result becomes comparable.
  • Phase 2, RL platform: RayJob-based RL with separate rollout, reward and training components, sandboxed verifiers, health signals and alerts, frequent checkpoints.
  • Phase 3, efficiency: one-step off-policy and then asynchronous rollouts with staleness limits, dynamic sampling, partial rollouts, mismatch corrections.
  • Phase 4, distillation and pipelines: on-policy distillation, multi-stage pipelines (SFT → RL → distill) launched as one recipe.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Config-driven recipes over free-form notebooks: less flexibility for one-off exploration, in exchange for runs that can be reproduced, diffed and compared.
  • Asynchronous RL: much higher GPU utilization, at the cost of off-policy corrections and one more source of instability to monitor.
  • Several frameworks (TRL for SFT and small RL, verl for large RL): the right tool for each scale, at the cost of keeping their configs and metrics aligned.
  • Sandboxed rewards: slower than running tests in-process, but a reward function is exactly where a model will learn to exploit any weakness.

Open questions for the next review.

  • Agentic RL: multi-turn rollouts with tools and environments (browsers, terminals) make rollouts longer, stateful and harder to replay. Does the reward pool become an environment platform?
  • Algorithm choice at our scale: run a controlled comparison of GRPO variants and on-policy distillation on our own tasks, since published rankings change with model size.
  • Bitwise-consistent rollouts: inference engines are starting to offer kernels that match training exactly. When available, can we drop mismatch corrections?
  • Data flywheel: feeding production traffic (with consent and filtering) back into SFT and RL prompt sets.
Design 07 · 12 sections

Design 07: Scaling RL beyond the small-run regime

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. What changes when you scale each axis
  3. Predict before you spend: compute–performance curves
  4. The scaling ladder
  5. Where the time goes: the step-time breakdown
  6. Long trajectories and the long tail
  7. Larger models: two layouts and the weight sync between them
  8. Numerics and MoE: the mismatch that grows with scale
  9. Rewards and environments at scale
  10. Stability over thousands of steps
  11. Failures and recovery on multi-week runs
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we take a post-training recipe that works on a small run (an 8B model, 4K-token answers, a few hundred steps, 32 GPUs) and make it work with more tokens, longer trajectories, larger models, more steps and a much larger compute budget, and how do we find the bottlenecks that only appear once we leave the small-run regime? It builds directly on Design 06 (recipes, objectives, health signals), Design 02 (capacity and queues), Design 03 (training jobs and checkpoints), Design 04 (long-running state and recovery) and Design 05 (the fabric that moves weights).

The short version: scaling RL is two problems at once. The algorithm problem: a recipe that looks best at small scale may hit a lower ceiling at large scale, so we predict with fitted compute–performance curves before committing a big budget. The systems problem: at scale, the bottleneck moves from the trainer to rollout long tails, weight synchronization, numerical mismatch between engines, reward throughput, memory for long contexts, and failures over multi-week runs. The platform runs a scaling ladder (each rung roughly 4× bigger than the last), measures where time and stability go at every rung, and only climbs when the previous rung's curve and bottleneck profile are understood.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. The recipe from Design 06 works: on an 8B model with 4K-token answers it improves math and code steadily for 500 steps on 32 GPUs. The team now wants a 235B mixture-of-experts model, answers up to 64K tokens, multi-turn tool use, 5,000+ steps and a budget of about 200,000 GPU hours. The first attempt at 8× scale ran at 11% GPU utilization, spent 40% of each step waiting for weight sync, and collapsed on day nine with no obvious cause.

What the platform must do.

  • Predict before spending: estimate where a recipe will plateau and how fast it gets there, from runs costing a few percent of the full budget.
  • Find the bottleneck at each scale: break every step's time into rollout, reward, training, weight sync and waiting, and show which one grew as scale grew.
  • Keep GPUs busy despite long tails: answers whose lengths vary 50× must not leave most GPUs idle.
  • Move weights fast: pushing a hundreds-of-billions-parameter policy to the rollout fleet every step without stalling.
  • Stay stable for thousands of steps: detect slow drifts (entropy, mismatch, length) and recover from instability without losing days.
  • Survive failures: a multi-week run on thousands of GPUs will see node failures; resume in minutes, not hours.

Out of scope: the choice of objective and reward itself (Design 06), and the GPU fleet (Design 02).

What changes when you scale each axis

Scenario. The team scales everything at once and can't tell which change caused which problem. They need a map of what each scaling axis breaks, so they can scale one axis at a time.

What the picture shows. The five scaling axes and the bottleneck each one tends to expose first.

1More tokens per step (bigger batches, larger groups)
rollout throughput and reward throughput become the limit; the trainer waits. Larger batches also change the optimization (fewer, larger updates).
2Longer trajectories (16K → 64K+ tokens, multi-turn)
the long tail dominates step time, the KV cache limits how many sequences fit on a rollout GPU, and training activations for long sequences need context parallelism. Multi-turn tool use adds environment latency inside the rollout.
3Larger models (dense 8B → MoE with hundreds of billions of parameters)
training needs tensor, pipeline, expert and context parallelism; rollout engines need their own, different layout; weight sync moves hundreds of gigabytes per step; MoE routing differs between engines.
4More steps (hundreds → thousands)
slow drifts (entropy collapse, length growth, mismatch accumulation) have time to matter, the prompt set gets used up, and hardware failures become certain.
5Larger compute budgets
the cost of a wrong recipe choice grows, so prediction from small runs becomes the most valuable tool, and run-level operations (checkpointing, preemption, quotas) start to matter as much as algorithms.
Going deeper2 points
  • Scale one axis per rung. A rung that changes model size and trajectory length and step count can't tell you which one caused a regression.
  • Some bottlenecks are invisible below a threshold. Weight sync is negligible for 8B over NVLink and dominant for a large MoE over the network; the long tail barely matters at 4K tokens and dominates at 64K. The ladder exists to find those thresholds.

Predict before you spend: compute–performance curves

Scenario. Two recipes are compared at 2,000 GPU hours. Recipe A is clearly ahead. At 30,000 hours, recipe B passes it and keeps rising while A flattens. Choosing from the small comparison would have wasted the budget on the recipe with the lower ceiling.

What the picture shows. Fitting a saturating (sigmoid) curve of held-out performance against compute, and what its parameters mean.

1Ceiling (A)
the performance the recipe approaches with unlimited compute. Choices that change the ceiling matter most at scale.
2Efficiency (B) and midpoint (C_mid)
how quickly the recipe gets to the ceiling, and how much compute it takes to get halfway. Choices that only change efficiency are worth less at large budgets, because every good recipe gets there eventually.
3Fit early, check late
fit on the first part of a run (excluding the noisy start) and check the extrapolation against later checkpoints; the gap between predicted and observed is the trust you can place in the curve.
4Held-out metric, not training reward
fit on a fixed validation set (for example, mean pass rate over 16 samples per problem), since training reward is measured on a moving, filtered subset.

The published study behind this approach fitted such curves across more than 400,000 GPU hours of experiments and found that some design choices mainly shift the ceiling while others (loss aggregation, normalization, curriculum, the off-policy algorithm) mainly change efficiency. Its extrapolation from the first half of a 100,000-GPU-hour run closely matched the second half.

The code. Fit and compare recipes from their eval history (Python, SciPy).

import numpy as npfrom scipy.optimize import curve_fit def sigmoid(C, A, B, C_mid, R0):    """Held-out pass rate as a function of compute C (GPU hours)."""    return R0 + (A - R0) / (1.0 + (C_mid / C) ** B) def fit_recipe(gpu_hours: np.ndarray, pass_rate: np.ndarray, skip_hours: float = 1500):    keep = gpu_hours > skip_hours                     # drop the noisy start    R0 = pass_rate[0]    f = lambda C, A, B, C_mid: sigmoid(C, A, B, C_mid, R0)    (A, B, C_mid), cov = curve_fit(f, gpu_hours[keep], pass_rate[keep],                                   p0=[0.6, 1.0, 5000], bounds=([R0, 0.1, 100], [1.0, 5.0, 1e6]))    return {"A": A, "B": B, "C_mid": C_mid, "A_std": float(np.sqrt(cov[0, 0]))} for name, hist in runs.items():                       # runs: recipe -> (hours, pass_rate) arrays    p = fit_recipe(*hist)    print(f"{name:<14} ceiling A={p['A']:.3f}±{p['A_std']:.3f}  B={p['B']:.2f}  C_mid={p['C_mid']:.0f} h")# Commit the big budget to the recipe with the highest ceiling whose fit is tight,# not the one that is ahead at the budget you happened to measure.
Going deeper2 points
  • Uncertainty matters. A ceiling estimated from a run that hasn't reached its midpoint is weak; the platform shows the confidence interval and refuses to "rank" recipes whose intervals overlap.
  • Curves per axis: fit separate curves for larger models and longer generation lengths; both can raise the ceiling while making early progress look slower.

The scaling ladder

Scenario. Leadership asks "when can we start the big run?" The honest answer is "after the rung below it is understood," and the platform needs to make that concrete.

What the picture shows. A sequence of runs, each roughly 4× the previous, with explicit exit criteria.

1Rung 1, recipe search (~1–2% of budget)
small model, short answers; many ablations; fit curves; pick candidates.
2Rung 2, length
same model, much longer answers; measures the long tail, KV cache pressure and length dynamics.
3Rung 3, model size
the target architecture (for example, the MoE) on fewer steps; exposes parallelism, weight sync and routing mismatch.
4Rung 4, duration
the target model and length for many steps; exposes drift, prompt exhaustion and failure handling.
5The production run
the full budget, with the curve from rung 4 as the forecast it's checked against.
6Exit criteria at every rung
the curve fit is stable, the step-time breakdown is understood (no unexplained waiting), the health signals are flat or explained, and a restart from checkpoint has been tested.

The YAML. A rung is just a recipe overlay: the base recipe plus the axis being scaled (applied by the launcher from Design 06).

# recipes/assistant-v13/ladder/rung3-model-size.yamlextends: recipes/assistant-v13/rl-base.yamlladder:  rung: 3  axis: model_size                       # exactly one axis changes per rung  previous: runs/assistant-v13-rung2-8b-64k  budget_gpu_hours: 12000  exit_criteria:    curve_fit_ceiling_ci: 0.03           # ±0.03 on the ceiling estimate    unexplained_wait_fraction_max: 0.10  # of step time    restart_from_checkpoint_tested: truemodel:  path: registry://base-235b-a22b-moe@v1  trainer_parallelism: { tp: 4, pp: 4, ep: 8, cp: 2 }   # training layout  rollout_parallelism: { tp: 4, ep: 8, dp: 16 }         # inference layout, differentrollout:  max_response_tokens: 65536             # unchanged from rung 2
Going deeper2 points
  • Budget the ladder explicitly: roughly 10–15% of the total compute for rungs 1–4 is a cheap insurance policy against spending the other 85% on the wrong recipe or a run that collapses.
  • Keep a "reference rung" (small, cheap, fixed) that re-runs nightly on the current code; it catches framework regressions before they reach a big run.

Where the time goes: the step-time breakdown

Scenario. At rung 3, a step takes 14 minutes. Nobody knows whether to buy more rollout GPUs, optimize the trainer or fix the network, because the 14 minutes have never been broken down.

What the picture shows. How one RL step's time splits as scale grows, and which part to attack.

1Rollout generation
at small scale, roughly half the step; with long trajectories, commonly most of it. The long tail (the slowest few percent of answers) often decides the whole step.
2Reward and environment time
small for exact-match math; large for sandboxed tests, judges and multi-turn tools.
3Reference and old-policy log-probabilities
an extra forward pass over every token; grows with tokens per step.
4Training (forward + backward + optimizer)
grows with model size and tokens, but usually isn't the largest share in RL.
5Weight sync
negligible for a small model on one node; tens of seconds to minutes for a large model across nodes, every step.
6Idle (bubbles)
GPUs waiting for another stage. The single most useful number to drive down.

The code. Every run emits a span per stage per step; the platform turns them into this breakdown and the "bubble" fraction (OpenTelemetry spans, exported like the traces in Observability).

import timefrom contextlib import contextmanagerfrom opentelemetry import trace, metrics tracer = trace.get_tracer("rl.step")stage_seconds = metrics.get_meter("rl").create_histogram("rl_stage_seconds", unit="s") @contextmanagerdef stage(name: str, step: int, run_id: str, gpus: int):    t0 = time.perf_counter()    with tracer.start_as_current_span(f"rl.{name}", attributes={"step": step, "run": run_id}):        yield    dt = time.perf_counter() - t0    stage_seconds.record(dt, {"stage": name, "run": run_id, "gpus": str(gpus)}) # in the training loopwith stage("rollout", step, run_id, rollout_gpus):     batch = rollout_pool.collect(prompts)with stage("reward", step, run_id, 0):                 rewards = reward_pool.score(batch)with stage("logprobs", step, run_id, train_gpus):      old_lp = trainer.logprobs(batch)with stage("train", step, run_id, train_gpus):         trainer.update(batch, rewards, old_lp)with stage("weight_sync", step, run_id, rollout_gpus): sync.push(trainer.state_dict_shards())
Going deeper2 points
  • Measure GPU-seconds, not seconds: a 60-second stage on 16 rollout GPUs and a 60-second stage on 128 training GPUs cost very different amounts. The breakdown is weighted by the GPUs each stage holds, including GPUs held while idle.
  • Profile the slowest step, not the average: the long tail is in the tail.

Long trajectories and the long tail

Scenario. At 64K-token answers, the median answer finishes in 4 minutes and the slowest 1% take 25. In synchronous RL, every step waits 25 minutes, and 90% of rollout GPUs sit idle for most of it.

What the picture shows. The long-tail problem and the techniques that tame it.

1Over-provision and cut off (active partial rollouts)
start more answers than the batch needs; when enough have finished, stop the rest and keep their partial output; resume them in the next step under the newer policy.
2Asynchrony with a staleness bound
separate rollout and training pools, so the trainer consumes whatever has finished; samples are at most k policy versions old, with importance-sampling corrections.
3Length-aware scheduling
route long-running requests to engines with free KV cache; rebalance during generation; speculative decoding for long answers.
4KV cache capacity
long contexts cap the number of concurrent sequences per rollout GPU; FP8 KV cache and prefix caching (group samples share the prompt) raise it.
5Training long sequences
context parallelism splits one sequence across GPUs; sequence packing and dynamic batch sizes by token count keep training balanced.
6Length dynamics
answer length usually grows during reasoning RL; the length cap, the overlong penalty and truncation masking (Design 06) decide how that interacts with the budget.

Production systems report that rollout can take 50–80% of step time and more, and that partial-rollout and asynchronous designs recover much of it, with the caveat that stale samples must be corrected or repaired.

The YAML. The rollout pool as a vLLM deployment sized for long contexts, separate from training (one group per engine with LeaderWorkerSet for multi-node engines).

apiVersion: leaderworkerset.x-k8s.io/v1kind: LeaderWorkerSetmetadata:  name: rollout-235b  namespace: rl-scale  labels: { kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: rl-rollout }spec:  replicas: 16                                    # 16 engines, 2 nodes each  leaderWorkerTemplate:    size: 2    restartPolicy: RecreateGroupOnPodRestart      # an engine is all-or-nothing    leaderTemplate:      spec:        containers:        - name: vllm          image: registry.example.com/rl/vllm:2026.11-rl          args:          - --model=/weights/current          - --tensor-parallel-size=8          - --pipeline-parallel-size=2          - --enable-expert-parallel          - --max-model-len=81920          - --kv-cache-dtype=fp8                  # more concurrent long sequences          - --enable-prefix-caching               # group samples share the prompt          - --max-num-seqs=256          resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8 } }    workerTemplate:      spec:        containers:        - name: vllm-worker          image: registry.example.com/rl/vllm:2026.11-rl          resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8 } }
Going deeper2 points
  • Partial rollouts change the data: one answer may contain tokens from several policy versions. Record the version per token span so the importance-sampling correction uses the right probabilities.
  • The tail grows with training: as the model learns to think longer, a step-time budget that worked at step 500 fails at step 3,000. Re-check the breakdown regularly.

Larger models: two layouts and the weight sync between them

Scenario. The 235B MoE trains well with one parallel layout but needs a completely different layout to generate efficiently. Every step, the new weights have to get from one layout to the other, across 64 nodes, and that transfer alone takes four minutes.

What the picture shows. The training and rollout layouts, and the paths for moving weights between them.

1Training layout
tensor, pipeline, expert, context and data parallelism (Megatron or FSDP), optimized for memory and backward passes.
2Rollout layout
tensor and expert parallelism with many data-parallel engines, optimized for decoding throughput and KV cache.
3Resharding
each rollout engine needs the full model in its own layout; the trainer's shards must be gathered and re-split. Done naively, this is a full gather through one place.
4Colocated vs disaggregated
colocated (same GPUs, time-shared) reshards in GPU memory, no network; disaggregated (separate pools) must cross the network, but lets each pool scale and keeps both busy.
5Faster sync
bucketed broadcasts over NCCL on the fast fabric, overlapping sync with the next rollouts, sending only changed parameters or compressed deltas, and pipelining layer by layer so engines start before the whole model arrives.

The code. A bucketed, layer-pipelined push from trainer ranks to rollout engines, with the policy version recorded (sketch).

import torch, torch.distributed as dist BUCKET_BYTES = 1 << 30                                       # 1 GiB buckets def push_weights(named_shards, group, version: int, resharder):    """Gather each layer to rollout layout and broadcast in buckets over NCCL."""    bucket, size = [], 0    for name, shard in named_shards:                         # iterate layer by layer        full = resharder.to_rollout_layout(name, shard)      # TP/EP re-split for vLLM        bucket.append((name, full)); size += full.numel() * full.element_size()        if size >= BUCKET_BYTES:            _flush(bucket, group); bucket, size = [], 0    if bucket:        _flush(bucket, group)    dist.broadcast(torch.tensor([version], device="cuda"), src=0, group=group)  # engines tag tokens def _flush(bucket, group):    flat = torch.cat([t.flatten() for _, t in bucket])    dist.broadcast(flat, src=0, group=group)                 # rollout engines load in place
Going deeper2 points
  • Size the sync path like a serving path: a 235B model in BF16 is about 470 GB. At an effective 50 GB/s per receiving engine that's around 10 seconds; through one bottleneck link it's minutes. Use the GPU fabric (Design 05), not the pod network.
  • Measure sync as its own stage and set a budget (for example, under 5% of step time); above it, overlap sync with rollout or move to asynchronous training.

Numerics and MoE: the mismatch that grows with scale

Scenario. At 8B dense, the inference engine's token probabilities and the trainer's match closely. At 235B MoE with FP8 rollouts, a few percent of tokens have probability ratios above 10, and those tokens dominate the gradient. The run looks fine for a week, then collapses.

What the picture shows. Sources of train–inference mismatch, and how each is reduced.

1Different kernels and precision
the inference engine and trainer compute the same function in different ways; low-precision rollouts (FP8) widen the gap. Corrections: truncated or masked importance sampling at the token level, and keeping the final projection to logits in FP32 on both sides.
2MoE routing differences
a tiny numerical difference can send a token to different experts in the two engines, so the probabilities differ a lot. Routing replay records the experts chosen during rollout and reuses them in training.
3Staleness
asynchronous rollouts are from older policies; their ratios are expected to differ, and are corrected the same way.
4Watch the ratio distribution
track the fraction of tokens with ratio beyond a threshold, and the KL between rollout and trainer probabilities, per step. A widening tail is the earliest warning.
5Bitwise-consistent inference
where the engine offers kernels that exactly match the trainer, the mismatch disappears at some throughput cost; worth testing at each rung.

The code. Mismatch metrics and a truncated importance weight, computed from probabilities both engines already return.

import torch def mismatch_metrics(train_logp, rollout_logp, mask, cap: float = 3.0):    """Per-token log ratio between trainer and rollout engine, and a truncated IS weight."""    log_ratio = (train_logp - rollout_logp) * mask    ratio = log_ratio.exp()    n = mask.sum()    stats = {        "mismatch/kl": ((ratio - 1) - log_ratio).sum().item() / n.item(),   # k3 estimator        "mismatch/frac_ratio_gt_2": ((ratio > 2) & mask.bool()).sum().item() / n.item(),        "mismatch/max_ratio": ratio[mask.bool()].max().item(),    }    is_weight = ratio.clamp(max=cap).detach()               # truncated IS (TIS)    return stats, is_weight
Going deeper2 points
  • Precision is a ceiling choice, not just a speed choice. Published scaling work found that FP32 for the logit computation shifted the asymptotic performance, not only stability.
  • Test mismatch before the run: score the same rollouts with both engines on the target model and inspect the ratio histogram; it's a cheap pre-flight check at every rung.

Rewards and environments at scale

Scenario. Moving from math to multi-turn coding agents, each rollout calls tools 20–50 times. The sandbox pool that handled 2,000 test runs per step now gets 150,000 tool calls per step, and rollout GPUs sit idle waiting for sandboxes.

What the picture shows. The reward and environment tier as its own autoscaled service.

1Stateless verifiers
exact match, unit tests, schema checks; scale horizontally on CPU, batched per step.
2Judges and reward models
served on their own GPU pool with vLLM; sized for the step's token count, not for interactive latency.
3Stateful environments for agentic RL
sandboxes, browsers and terminals that live for a whole trajectory; pre-warmed pools and snapshots so starting one takes milliseconds (Design 01).
4Environment stragglers
one slow tool call blocks a trajectory; time out, retry or mark the turn failed, and count failures by environment.
5Back-pressure
rollout engines pause new trajectories when the environment queue is full, instead of piling up idle KV cache.

The YAML. The sandbox pool scales on queue depth, not CPU, so it grows before rollouts stall (KEDA).

apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1kind: ScaledObjectmetadata:  name: rl-sandbox-pool  namespace: rl-scalespec:  scaleTargetRef: { name: sandbox-workers }  minReplicaCount: 200                           # pre-warmed for the step start  maxReplicaCount: 6000  cooldownPeriod: 300  triggers:  - type: prometheus    metadata:      serverAddress: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090      query: sum(rl_env_queue_depth{run="assistant-v13-prod"})      threshold: "25"                            # pending tool calls per worker
Going deeper2 points
  • Environments are deterministic by contract: the same seed and actions give the same observations, so trajectories can be replayed for debugging and for importance-sampling checks.
  • Count environment cost per trajectory: at scale, CPU and sandbox minutes can rival GPU cost for agentic tasks.

Stability over thousands of steps

Scenario. The production run improves for 2,400 steps, then held-out scores start sliding. Entropy fell slowly the whole time, response length doubled since step 1,500, and 30% of prompts now have all-correct groups. Each signal was within its alert threshold; together they predicted the slide.

What the picture shows. Slow drifts that only matter on long runs, and the controls for each.

1Entropy decay
exploration fades over thousands of steps. Controls: clip-higher, temperature, entropy-targeted token selection, and resetting the reference point periodically if KL is used.
2Length growth
answers get longer as the model learns to think more; step time and memory grow with them. Controls: a length curriculum (raise the cap in stages), overlong penalties, and re-planning rollout capacity.
3Prompt exhaustion
the model solves more prompts and the informative set shrinks. Controls: refresh pass-rate estimates, add harder prompts, sample by difficulty, and remove mastered prompts.
4Mismatch accumulation
small ratio drift becomes large. Controls: IS corrections, routing replay, precision checks at intervals.
5Composite alerts
alert on combinations and trends (entropy slope × length slope × informative-prompt fraction), not single thresholds.
6Rollback with change
on a collapse, roll back to the last healthy checkpoint and change something (lower LR, tighter staleness, refreshed prompts); a plain restart usually collapses again at the same point.
Going deeper2 points
  • Keep checkpoints dense enough to roll back cheaply (every 25–50 steps for the latest, every few hundred kept long term), and record the health signals with each so "the last healthy checkpoint" is a query, not a guess.
  • Schedules over a long run: learning-rate decay, length-cap increases and data refreshes are planned in the recipe, so the curve fitted at rung 4 still applies.

Failures and recovery on multi-week runs

Scenario. A 2,048-GPU run on its eleventh day: one GPU throws an uncorrectable memory error. The whole job crashes; restarting takes 70 minutes (rescheduling, loading a 3 TB checkpoint, warming 64 rollout engines). It happens twice a week.

What the picture shows. Making failures cheap rather than rare.

1Separate the blast radius
a failed rollout engine is replaced while the run continues (rollouts are stateless and retryable); only trainer failures require a training restart.
2Fast checkpoints
asynchronous, sharded checkpoints to local NVMe first and object storage in the background, so saving takes seconds of training time (Design 04).
3Fast restarts
hot spare nodes reserved by the queue, pre-pulled images, checkpoints loaded in parallel from the nearest copy, rollout engines warm-started from the new weights.
4Health checks before admission
nodes run GPU, NVLink and network tests before joining; repeat offenders are drained automatically.
5Save the rollout buffer and data cursor
with the checkpoint, so a restart neither repeats nor skips prompts.

The YAML. The trainer as a JobSet with a failure policy that restarts the trainer group while rollout engines (a separate LeaderWorkerSet) keep running.

apiVersion: jobset.x-k8s.io/v1alpha2kind: JobSetmetadata:  name: assistant-v13-prod-trainer  namespace: rl-scale  labels: { kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: rl-production }   # reserved capacity, not preemptible  annotations:    alpha.jobset.sigs.k8s.io/exclusive-topology: network.example.com/fabric-block   # one fabric blockspec:  failurePolicy:    maxRestarts: 50                                   # weeks-long runs will restart    restartStrategy: Recreate  replicatedJobs:  - name: trainer    replicas: 1    template:      spec:        parallelism: 128        completions: 128        backoffLimit: 0        template:          spec:            containers:            - name: megatron              image: registry.example.com/rl/trainer:2026.11              command: ["python3", "-m", "rl.train", "--resume=latest", "--recipe=/recipes/prod.yaml"]              resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8 } }              volumeMounts: [ { name: nvme, mountPath: /local-ckpt } ]            volumes:            - name: nvme              hostPath: { path: /mnt/nvme/ckpt }
Going deeper2 points
  • Track goodput: the fraction of reserved GPU-hours that produced training progress. Failures, restarts, sync and bubbles all subtract from it; it's the run-level metric leadership should see.
  • Rehearse a failure at rung 4: kill a trainer node and a rollout engine on purpose and time the recovery.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, measurement: step-time breakdown, goodput and mismatch metrics on every run, plus the curve-fitting service on eval history.
  • Phase 2, the ladder: rung recipes, exit criteria and the nightly reference rung.
  • Phase 3, systems for long trajectories and large models: disaggregated rollout pools, partial rollouts, bucketed weight sync, routing replay, autoscaled environment tier.
  • Phase 4, run operations: fast checkpoints, hot spares, composite alerts, rollback with change, failure rehearsals.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Spending 10–15% of the budget on the ladder, instead of starting the big run immediately.
  • Disaggregated rollout and training: better utilization and independent scaling, at the cost of network-bound weight sync and more moving parts.
  • Asynchrony and partial rollouts: large throughput gains, at the cost of off-policy samples that must be corrected and monitored.
  • Lower-precision rollouts: faster generation, at the cost of more mismatch; only adopted after the ratio histogram at the target scale is acceptable.

Open questions.

  • How far do curves extrapolate across model sizes? We fit per model size today; a joint fit would let rung 1 predict more.
  • Agentic RL at scale: environments with long, stateful, slow steps may need their own asynchronous design, decoupled from token generation.
  • Weight sync with sparse or delta updates: if only a small fraction of parameters change meaningfully per step, can we send much less?
  • Multi-cluster RL: rollout in one region and training in another, with weights crossing a WAN; viable only with large staleness tolerance.
Design 08 · 12 sections

Design 08: Training for long-horizon reasoning

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Why long horizons are hard
  3. The trajectory as data: turns, snapshots and branch points
  4. Credit assignment: a ladder of methods
  5. Branching rollouts: tree-shaped exploration
  6. Denser rewards without reward hacking
  7. Exploration: curricula over the horizon
  8. Verification for long tasks
  9. Context management: trajectories longer than the window
  10. The infrastructure: environments, trajectories and credit workers
  11. Measuring progress on long tasks
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we train models on tasks where success depends on many intermediate decisions (an 80-turn software fix, a multi-hour research task, a long proof), when the only reliable signal is often a single pass/fail at the very end? It covers how to give useful feedback to the decisions inside a trajectory (credit assignment), how to get more signal than one bit per trajectory (denser rewards), how to keep the model finding new strategies (exploration), and how to know a long task was really solved (verification). It builds on Design 06 (recipes and objectives), Design 07 (scale and long rollouts), Design 01 (environments) and Design 04 (snapshots and state).

The short version: the trajectory is the unit of storage, but the turn (or step) is the unit of credit. Every trajectory is recorded as a sequence of turns with environment snapshots at chosen points. Feedback moves from one end-of-task reward toward per-turn advantages through a ladder of methods: shared trajectory-level advantages, turn-level process rewards, and Monte Carlo value estimates from branching at snapshots. Exploration is helped by curricula over the horizon (start near the goal, then move the start back). Verification is layered, because the longer the task, the more ways a model has to look successful without being so.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. The team trains a coding agent on real repository issues. A typical successful episode is 40–120 turns: read the issue, explore files, reproduce the bug, try a fix, run tests, revise, and submit. The reward is whether hidden tests pass at the end. After RL with trajectory-level GRPO, the agent improves on short issues but not on long ones: it learns to submit early, rarely recovers from a wrong first hypothesis, and on failed episodes every turn, including the excellent ones, gets the same negative signal.

What the platform must do.

  • Assign credit to turns: tell the model which decisions helped or hurt, not just whether the whole episode succeeded.
  • Get more signal per episode: use intermediate checks, milestones and value estimates where they're trustworthy, without teaching the model to game them.
  • Keep exploring: long tasks with a low success rate give almost no learning signal; the platform must create easier starting points and diverse attempts.
  • Verify long tasks robustly: final checks that can't be passed by shortcuts (editing tests, hard-coding outputs, faking progress).
  • Handle long contexts: trajectories longer than the context window, with summarization or memory, without breaking the training math.
  • Make it reproducible: every trajectory can be replayed and branched from any recorded point.

Out of scope: the base RL objective and scaling machinery (Designs 06 and 07), and sandbox security itself (Design 01).

Why long horizons are hard

Scenario. A researcher asks why the recipe that works on 4K-token math problems barely moves on 100-turn tasks. The answer is four problems that are minor for short tasks and dominant for long ones.

What the picture shows. The four problems and how each grows with the number of decisions.

1Sparse rewards
one bit at the end of hundreds of decisions. With a 5% success rate, most groups of attempts are all failures and give no signal at all in group-relative RL.
2Credit assignment
even when the outcome is informative, giving the same advantage to every token spreads the signal thinly across good and bad decisions alike. The useful information per decision shrinks as the trajectory grows.
3Exploration
a long task can fail in many more ways than it can succeed. Random variations rarely stumble onto a full solution, and the model's own habits (submitting early, repeating a failed command) reinforce themselves.
4Verification
final checks see only the end state, and there are more ways to fake an end state in a long task (editing tests, deleting failing code, claiming success). Intermediate checks are even harder to trust.
5Variance
all four combine into high-variance gradient estimates; training needs more samples per useful update, or better estimates of value.
Going deeper2 points
  • Measure success as a function of horizon: plot success rate against the number of turns a task needs. A recipe that only helps short tasks shows a steep drop-off; the goal of this design is to flatten that curve.
  • Most problems show up as "zero-variance groups": track the fraction of groups where every attempt failed or every attempt succeeded. On long tasks it's the clearest early sign that the signal is too sparse.

The trajectory as data: turns, snapshots and branch points

Scenario. To try a different credit method, a researcher needs to restart 1,000 failed episodes from turn 30 and try alternatives. The trajectories were stored as flat text, and the environments are gone. Nothing can be replayed.

What the picture shows. How a trajectory is recorded so it can be scored, replayed and branched.

1Turns
each turn is the model's output (reasoning and an action), the environment's response, and metadata (tokens, policy version, latency).
2Token log-probabilities
