apiVersion: apps/v1kind: Deploymentmetadata:  name: verifier-math-final-answer-3-2-0          # one Deployment per pinned version  namespace: rewards  labels: { app: verifier, verifier: math-final-answer, version: "3.2.0" }spec:  replicas: 20  selector: { matchLabels: { verifier: math-final-answer, version: "3.2.0" } }  template:    metadata: { labels: { app: verifier, verifier: math-final-answer, version: "3.2.0" } }    spec:      containers:      - name: verifier        image: registry.example.com/rewards/math-final-answer@sha256:5e1d...   # immutable        ports: [ { containerPort: 8080 } ]        resources: { limits: { cpu: "2", memory: 2Gi } }        readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 } }---apiVersion: batch/v1kind: CronJobmetadata:  name: verifier-fuzz-nightly  namespace: rewardsspec:  schedule: "17 2 * * *"  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid  jobTemplate:    spec:      template:        spec:          restartPolicy: Never          containers:          - name: fuzz            image: registry.example.com/rewards/fuzz:2026.11            args:            - --verifiers=math-final-answer@3.2.0,code-tests@5.1.0            - --reference=strict-reference@1.4.0            - --policy-samples=s3://rl-runs/assistant-v13-prod/latest/rollouts/   # fresh outputs            - --fail-on=false_positive_rate>0.005            - --report=s3://rewards/fuzz-reports/
Going deeper2 points
  • Pinning by digest: a run records verifier image digests, not tags, so a reward can always be reproduced.
  • Shared with evaluation, separated from training: evaluation verifiers live in the same registry but are different entries, owned by a different team, and never pinned by training runs.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, interface and inventory: one verifier interface with abstention and reasons; all existing verifiers registered with versions; rewards tagged with versions.
  • Phase 2, measurement: gold sets per slice, precision and recall dashboards, training gated on precision.
  • Phase 3, hardening: fuzzing and differential testing in CI and nightly; strict answer contracts; stronger code tests with mutation scores; judge adversarial suites.
  • Phase 4, monitoring and review: the reward-quality monitor with audit verifiers and perturbation tests; the human review service; re-scoring on verifier changes.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Strict contracts cause false negatives: some correct answers are rejected for format; we accept slower learning for fewer false positives, and state the contract in the prompt.
  • Abstention reduces signal: abstained samples teach nothing, but they don't teach anything wrong.
  • Audit scoring and review cost compute and people, in exchange for knowing whether gains are real.
  • Separate training and evaluation verifiers means maintaining two implementations of similar logic.

Open questions.

  • How much noise is tolerable? Evidence suggests moderate false negatives are harmless and false positives are not; where exactly is the line for our tasks and scales?
  • Learned verifiers at scale: can judges trained on human labels and fuzzing outputs become reliable enough for frontier tasks, or will they always be the weakest link?
  • Formal verification coverage: how much of our math and code distribution can be moved to proof assistants and formal specifications?
  • Verifying agent behavior: for long agent trajectories, how do we verify not just the end state but that the process didn't cheat (Design 08)?
Design 11 · 12 sections

Design 11: Multi-task post-training across task families

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. The capability matrix: transfer and interference
  3. Specialization vs generality: four ways to cover many domains
  4. Designing the mixture
  5. Sequential, mixed or staged
  6. RL across domains: rewards, lengths and batches
  7. Interference: detect it, then reduce it
  8. Merging and distilling specialists
  9. Evaluation: scorecards and no-regression gates
  10. Domains as plug-ins: ownership and contracts
  11. The platform on Kubernetes
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we scale post-training recipes across many task families and domains (math, code, agents, instruction following, chat, safety, languages), understand the trade-offs between specialized and general models, and design training mixtures that improve all capabilities together instead of trading one for another? It builds on Design 06 (recipes and mixtures), Design 07 (predicting from small runs), Design 09 (distillation and other-policy data) and Design 10 (verifiers per domain).

The short version: treat the mixture as the product. Each task family has an owner who supplies data, a verifier and an eval suite through a common contract. A central team owns the mixture: the weights, the order and the per-domain settings, chosen with small proxy runs and a measured transfer matrix (how training on one family affects every other). The default path is one generalist trained on a staged mixture, with short refreshes for families that regress; specialists are trained when a family needs more capacity or speed of iteration, and folded back by distillation or merging. A release has to clear a no-regression gate on every family, not just a better average.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. Five teams each improved "their" capability with their own post-training run: a math model, a coding agent, a multilingual chat model, a tool-use model and a safety-tuned model. Leadership wants one assistant. The first combined run (all data mixed at natural proportions) improves code and math, but instruction following drops six points, the multilingual model starts answering Spanish questions in English, and the safety team reports more over-refusals. Each team blames the others' data.

What the platform must do.

  • Make domains pluggable: a new task family arrives as data, verifier and evals through one contract, with an owner.
  • Measure interactions: know how training on each family affects every other family, positively or negatively.
  • Choose mixtures with evidence: weights, order and per-domain settings selected with proxy runs, not by negotiation.
  • Support both paths: one generalist trained on a mixture, and specialists that are later distilled or merged back.
  • Prevent regressions: no release that improves the average while degrading any family beyond an agreed margin.
  • Scale the number of domains: adding the twentieth domain must not take more work than adding the fifth.

Out of scope: the RL objective itself (Design 06), scaling a single run (Design 07).

The capability matrix: transfer and interference

Scenario. Someone claims "code data helps math." Someone else claims "chat data hurts reasoning." Nobody has measured either, and both may be true at different mixture weights.

What the picture shows. A transfer matrix: rows are the family added to training, columns are the evaluated family, cells are the change relative to a baseline mixture.

1Diagonal
the direct effect (training on code improves code). Large and positive, by design.
2Positive off-diagonal (transfer)
families that share skills help each other, such as math and code through step-by-step reasoning, or tool use and agents.
3Negative off-diagonal (interference)
families that pull the model in different directions, such as long reasoning traces making casual chat verbose, or terse coding style hurting explanation quality.
4Asymmetry
A helping B doesn't mean B helps A. The matrix is directional.
5It changes with scale and stage
a matrix measured on a small model or at the SFT stage is a starting hypothesis for a large model or the RL stage, not a fact.

The code. Estimating the matrix from leave-one-in ablations: a baseline mixture plus a small boost of one family at a time (Python).

import numpy as np FAMILIES = ["math", "code", "agents", "instr", "chat", "multiling", "safety"] def transfer_matrix(run_eval, base_mix: dict, boost: float = 0.10, seeds=(0, 1)):    """M[i, j] = change in eval j when family i's weight is raised by `boost` (proxy runs)."""    base = np.mean([run_eval(base_mix, seed=s) for s in seeds], axis=0)       # vector over FAMILIES    M = np.zeros((len(FAMILIES), len(FAMILIES)))    for i, fam in enumerate(FAMILIES):        mix = dict(base_mix); mix[fam] += boost        total = sum(mix.values()); mix = {k: v / total for k, v in mix.items()}        scores = np.mean([run_eval(mix, seed=s) for s in seeds], axis=0)        M[i] = scores - base                                                   # row: effect of adding fam    noise = np.std([run_eval(base_mix, seed=s) for s in (7, 8, 9)], axis=0)    return M, noise                                                            # ignore cells within noise
Going deeper2 points
  • Seed noise is the first thing to measure: many apparent transfer effects are smaller than the variation between seeds. Show the matrix with cells inside the noise band greyed out.
  • Refresh the matrix at every stage: SFT and RL interact differently; RL across domains is known to cause interference even when full-model gradients look nearly orthogonal, because the damage concentrates in a small shared set of parameters.

Specialization vs generality: four ways to cover many domains

Scenario. The coding team argues for keeping a dedicated coding model; the platform team wants one model to serve. Both have a point, and the choice changes training, serving and cost.

What the picture shows. Four strategies, from most specialized to most general.

1Separate specialists plus a router
best per-domain quality and independent iteration; more models to serve, a router that can misroute, and no transfer between domains at inference.
2Specialists merged in weight space
train specialists separately, combine parameters (task arithmetic, TIES, DELLA and similar). Cheap to try, no joint training; results depend strongly on model size and how far each specialist moved.
3One generalist trained on a mixture
one model, transfer between domains, one release; interference must be managed, and every team depends on one training run.
4Specialists distilled into a generalist
specialists act as teachers for one student; combines independent iteration with one served model, at the cost of the distillation run.

The options at a glance.

Strategy Quality per domain Transfer Serving Iteration speed Main risk
Specialists + router Highest None at inference Many models Fast, independent Misrouting, cost
Merge specialists Medium–high Some One model Fast Unpredictable interference
Mixture generalist Medium–high Yes One model Slow, shared Interference, slow loop
Distill specialists High Yes One model Medium Distillation cost, teacher quirks
Going deeper2 points
  • Scale changes the answer: one 2026 study of code models found data-mixture fine-tuning worked better at around 2B parameters, while merging specialists worked better at 7B. Re-test the choice when the model size changes.
  • Hybrid is common: a generalist for most traffic, a few specialists where quality or latency justify them, and periodic distillation of specialists back into the generalist.

Designing the mixture

Scenario. The first mixture used "natural proportions": whatever each team had. Code had 4 million examples and safety had 40,000, so the model saw code 100 times more often, regardless of what either needed.

What the picture shows. The levers that turn many datasets into one training stream.

1Weights, not sizes
each family gets a sampling weight; small, high-value families can be up-sampled (with care about repetition), and large ones down-sampled.
2Temperature sampling
a single knob between natural proportions (temperature 1) and uniform across families (high temperature), useful as a starting point.
3Epoch caps
limit how many times a small family's examples repeat, since repeated data overfits.
4Per-domain settings
maximum lengths, chat templates, system prompts and loss weights can differ by family.
5Search with proxies
choose weights by fitting a simple model of eval scores as a function of mixture weights on small runs, then confirm at scale.
6Minimum shares
every family keeps a floor weight, so no capability silently disappears from training.

The YAML. A multi-domain mixture in the recipe, with per-family settings (extends the recipe format of Design 06).

# recipes/assistant-v14/mixture.yamlmixture:  strategy: weighted  temperature: 2.0                      # starting point before search  floors: { default: 0.02 }             # no family below 2%  max_epochs_per_source: 3  families:    math:      { weight: 0.22, sources: [datasets://math-verified@v6],  max_len: 16384 }    code:      { weight: 0.22, sources: [datasets://code-tests@v9],     max_len: 16384 }    agents:    { weight: 0.14, sources: [envs://swe-tasks@v3],          max_len: 65536 }    instr:     { weight: 0.12, sources: [datasets://ifeval-style@v4],   max_len: 4096 }    chat:      { weight: 0.12, sources: [datasets://chat-prefs@v8],     max_len: 4096 }    multiling: { weight: 0.10, sources: [datasets://chat-ml@v5],        max_len: 4096,                 eval_languages: [es, de, fr, ja, hi] }    safety:    { weight: 0.08, sources: [datasets://safety@v11],        max_len: 4096 }owners:                                  # who answers for each family's data, verifier and evals  math: team-reasoning  code: team-code  safety: team-safety

The code. Fitting a simple response model on proxy runs and choosing weights that maximize the worst family's score (Python).

import numpy as npfrom scipy.optimize import minimize def fit_response(W: np.ndarray, S: np.ndarray):    """W: runs x families (mixture weights), S: runs x families (eval scores). Linear in log-weights."""    X = np.hstack([np.log(W + 1e-3), np.ones((len(W), 1))])    coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, S, rcond=None)    return lambda w: np.hstack([np.log(w + 1e-3), 1.0]) @ coef            # predicted score per family def best_mixture(predict, n, floor=0.02, base_scores=None):    def neg_worst(w):        w = np.abs(w) / np.abs(w).sum()        gains = predict(w) - (base_scores if base_scores is not None else 0)        return -gains.min()                                                # maximize the weakest family    res = minimize(neg_worst, np.full(n, 1 / n), method="Nelder-Mead", options={"maxiter": 4000})    w = np.maximum(np.abs(res.x) / np.abs(res.x).sum(), floor)    return w / w.sum()
Going deeper2 points
  • Optimize for the worst family, or a weighted product, not the average: an average-maximizing mixture happily sacrifices a small family.
  • Mixtures interact with quality: doubling a family's weight with low-quality data hurts more than leaving it alone. Clean the data before tuning its weight.

Sequential, mixed or staged

Scenario. The team trains math RL, then code RL, then chat RL. After the chat stage, math has dropped 8 points. Then they mix everything in each batch, and math and chat both end up worse than with their own runs.

What the picture shows. Three ways to order training across domains.

1Sequential
one domain after another. Simple and easy to attribute, but later stages degrade earlier ones (forgetting and interference).
2Mixed
every batch contains all domains. No forgetting by order, but gradients from different domains interfere within each update; recent work on math, chat and instruction following found both sequential and mixed RL fell short.
3Staged with refreshes
a mixed base, then short focused stages for domains that need more, each followed by a brief refresh of earlier domains. A 2026 study found that a short math refresh after a sequence of code, math, QA and creative-writing RL restored math from about 58 to 66 while largely preserving the other domains.
4Mixed with conflict handling
keep the mixture, but reduce gradient conflict between domains (gradient surgery per module, or per-domain adapters).

The YAML. A staged schedule: mixed base, focused stages and refreshes, each with its own mixture.

# recipes/assistant-v14/schedule.yamlstages:- name: sft-mixed  type: sft  mixture: recipes/assistant-v14/mixture.yaml- name: rl-mixed  type: rl  steps: 1200  mixture: { math: 0.25, code: 0.25, instr: 0.15, chat: 0.15, safety: 0.1, multiling: 0.1 }- name: rl-agents-focus  type: rl  steps: 400  mixture: { agents: 0.7, code: 0.15, instr: 0.15 }       # keep a share of neighbours- name: rl-refresh  type: rl  steps: 80                                               # short: restore, don't retrain  mixture: { math: 0.3, chat: 0.3, multiling: 0.2, safety: 0.2 }  trigger: { any_family_regression_gt: 1.5 }              # only if the gate shows regressionsgates_after_each_stage: evals://multi-family@v3
Going deeper2 points
  • Keep neighbours in focused stages: a focus stage at 70% agents and 30% related families forgets less than a pure agents stage.
  • Refreshes are cheap and targeted: a few dozen to a few hundred steps on the regressed family, after measuring which family regressed, beats re-running a full mixed stage.

RL across domains: rewards, lengths and batches

Scenario. In mixed RL, math rewards are 0/1 with 30% success, chat judge scores cluster between 0.6 and 0.8, and agent episodes are 50 times longer than chat answers. Math and agents dominate the updates; chat barely moves.

What the picture shows. The per-domain differences that distort a mixed RL batch, and the corrections.

1Reward scales differ
binary verifiers, judge scores and shaped rewards have different ranges and variances. Normalize advantages within each prompt group (and report per domain), so no domain dominates through scale alone.
2Lengths differ
token-level loss makes long answers contribute more tokens. Decide explicitly whether a domain should weigh by tokens or by samples, and balance batches by token count per domain.
3Difficulty differs
each domain needs its own pass-rate filter (Design 06); a domain with mostly all-correct groups contributes no signal regardless of its weight.
4Verifiers differ
each domain uses its own verifier from the registry (Design 10), with its own precision gate.
5Rollout cost differs
agent environments cost far more per sample than chat; the scheduler plans rollout capacity per domain so cheap domains don't wait on expensive ones.

The code. Per-domain advantage normalization and token-budgeted batch composition (Python).

from collections import defaultdictimport numpy as np def domain_advantages(groups):    """groups: list of dicts {domain, rewards: [..]} for one prompt each. Normalize within the group."""    out, stats = [], defaultdict(list)    for g in groups:        r = np.asarray(g["rewards"], dtype=float)        std = r.std()        adv = (r - r.mean()) / (std + 1e-6) if std > 0 else np.zeros_like(r)  # zero-variance: no signal        out.append(adv)        stats[g["domain"]].append(float(np.abs(adv).mean()))    return out, {d: float(np.mean(v)) for d, v in stats.items()}             # log signal per domain def compose_batch(pools, token_budget: int, shares: dict):    """Fill each domain's share of the batch by tokens, not by sample count."""    batch = []    for domain, share in shares.items():        budget, used = int(token_budget * share), 0        for s in pools[domain]:            if used + s.num_tokens > budget:                break            batch.append(s); used += s.num_tokens    return batch
Going deeper2 points
  • Log "effective signal" per domain: the mean absolute advantage and the fraction of non-zero-variance groups per domain show which domains are actually being trained in each step.
  • Separate KL or clip settings per domain are possible but add tuning burden; start shared and split only with evidence.

Interference: detect it, then reduce it

Scenario. Chat quality falls a little each time the code share rises. The team wants to know whether the two domains are actually fighting in the updates, and where.

What the picture shows. Signals that show interference, and tools that reduce it.

1Eval deltas per family
the most direct signal; the transfer matrix and per-stage gates measure it.
2Gradient conflict
compute per-domain gradients on a probe batch and their cosine similarity per module; negative cosines in shared modules mark where domains pull in opposite directions.
3Parameter-change overlap
which parameters each domain's updates change most; overlap with opposite signs predicts interference.
4Reducers
gradient surgery (project out conflicting components per module), per-domain adapters or LoRA modules on top of a shared model, more capacity (larger or mixture-of-experts models), conservative updates (small KL to the previous stage), and the refreshes above.

The code. Per-module gradient cosine between two domains on probe batches (PyTorch).

import torch def module_grads(model, loss_fn, batch):    model.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)    loss_fn(model, batch).backward()    return {n: p.grad.detach().flatten().clone() for n, p in model.named_parameters() if p.grad is not None} def conflict_report(model, loss_fn, batch_a, batch_b, top=10):    ga, gb = module_grads(model, loss_fn, batch_a), module_grads(model, loss_fn, batch_b)    rows = []    for name in ga.keys() & gb.keys():        cos = torch.nn.functional.cosine_similarity(ga[name], gb[name], dim=0).item()        rows.append((cos, name))    rows.sort()                                            # most conflicting modules first    return rows[:top]
Going deeper2 points
  • Whole-model cosine hides conflict: two domains can look orthogonal overall while conflicting strongly in a handful of modules; always look per module.
  • Capacity is a real lever: smaller models show more interference. If interference dominates and the data is clean, a larger or MoE model may be cheaper than more mixture tuning.

Merging and distilling specialists

Scenario. The coding team needs to iterate weekly; the generalist retrains monthly. They want to keep a specialist for speed and still get its gains into the generalist.

What the picture shows. Two ways to fold specialists back into one model.

1Weight merging
compute each specialist's "task vector" (its weights minus the shared base) and add scaled task vectors to the base. Methods like TIES and DELLA trim small changes and resolve sign conflicts. Fast and cheap; the merge weights are tuned on evals.
2Multi-teacher distillation
the generalist student generates answers on each domain's prompts, and that domain's specialist grades it token by token (on-policy distillation, Design 06); off-policy teacher data can start it.
3Requirements
a shared base and tokenizer for merging; a shared tokenizer for per-token distillation.
4When to use which
merging for quick combination of closely related specialists from the same base; distillation when specialists diverged a lot, when the student is smaller, or when merging shows interference.

The code. Task-vector merging with trimming and sign agreement (TIES-style, simplified; PyTorch).

import torch def ties_merge(base: dict, specialists: list[dict], weights: list[float], keep: float = 0.2):    merged = {}    for name, b in base.items():        deltas = torch.stack([s[name] - b for s in specialists])            # task vectors        k = max(1, int(keep * deltas[0].numel()))        thresh = deltas.abs().flatten(1).kthvalue(deltas[0].numel() - k + 1, dim=1).values        deltas = deltas * (deltas.abs() >= thresh.view(-1, *[1] * (deltas.dim() - 1)))   # trim small        sign = torch.sign((deltas * torch.tensor(weights).view(-1, *[1] * (deltas.dim() - 1))).sum(0))        agree = (torch.sign(deltas) == sign) & (deltas != 0)                 # keep agreeing signs        w = torch.tensor(weights).view(-1, *[1] * (deltas.dim() - 1))        num = (deltas * agree * w).sum(0)        den = (agree * w).sum(0).clamp(min=1e-8)        merged[name] = b + num / den    return merged
Going deeper2 points
  • Tune merge weights against the multi-family gate, not one domain; a merge that helps code and hurts safety fails the same gate as a training run would.
  • Merging generalists works too: merging several checkpoints from different runs or stages can reduce trade-offs between capabilities; it's a cheap experiment before a new training run.

Evaluation: scorecards and no-regression gates

Scenario. A candidate improves the average by 2.1 points. Inside that average, Hindi chat dropped 5 points and tool-call formatting dropped 3. Under the old "average must go up" rule, it would have shipped.

What the picture shows. How a multi-domain release is judged.

1A scorecard per family
each family's owner defines its suite, metric and acceptable regression margin.
2No-regression gate
a candidate passes only if no family regresses beyond its margin compared with the current release, with seed noise accounted for.
3Aggregate views that resist trade-offs
the minimum over families and a weighted geometric mean, alongside the average; the geometric mean punishes a collapse in one family more than the average does.
4Pareto view
candidates plotted on pairs of families show which trade-offs are available; a candidate dominated on every pair is dropped.
5Behavior across domains
length, refusal and language-consistency checks for every family, since cross-domain side effects often show up as behavior, not accuracy.

The code. The release gate as a function (Python).

import math def release_gate(candidate: dict, current: dict, margins: dict, noise: dict):    """Each dict maps family -> score (higher is better). Returns (passed, report)."""    report, passed = {}, True    for fam, margin in margins.items():        delta = candidate[fam] - current[fam]        tolerance = margin + 2 * noise.get(fam, 0.0)              # don't fail on seed noise        ok = delta >= -tolerance        report[fam] = {"delta": round(delta, 2), "allowed": -round(tolerance, 2), "ok": ok}        passed &= ok                                                # one regression fails the release    geo = math.exp(sum(math.log(max(candidate[f], 1e-6)) for f in margins) / len(margins))    report["_aggregate"] = {"min": min(candidate[f] for f in margins), "geomean": round(geo, 2)}    return passed, report
Going deeper2 points
  • Margins are negotiated once, not per release: owners set them in advance; changing a margin to let a release through needs explicit sign-off.
  • Language-consistency checks: for multilingual families, measure answering in the language of the question; it's a common casualty of reasoning-heavy mixtures.

Domains as plug-ins: ownership and contracts

Scenario. A sixth team wants to add legal reasoning. Last time a new domain was added, it took six weeks of meetings and broke the safety evals.

What the picture shows. The contract a task family must satisfy to join the mixture.

1Data
versioned datasets or environments, deduplicated and decontaminated against all eval sets, with licenses recorded.
2Verifier or judge
registered with measured precision (Design 10).
3Eval suite and margin
what "better" and "no worse" mean for this family.
4Owner and on-call
who answers when the family regresses or its verifier is exploited.
5Admission test
a proxy run adding the family at a small weight; the transfer row and column for the new family are measured, and the gate must pass for every existing family.
6Central ownership of the mixture
domain teams own their family; the mixture team owns weights, order and the release gate.
Going deeper2 points
  • Decontamination is cross-domain: a new family's data must be checked against every family's eval sets, not just its own.
  • Budget for the long tail of domains: small domains get a floor weight and can be grouped ("specialized professional domains") with shared evals, so adding one doesn't require a full study.

The platform on Kubernetes

Scenario. Training specialists, merging them, distilling and evaluating across seven families is a dozen jobs with dependencies. Today it's a spreadsheet and a chat thread.

What the picture shows. The pieces that run multi-task post-training.

1Domain registry
families, owners, data, verifiers, eval suites and margins.
2Mixture service
stores mixtures and schedules, runs proxy sweeps, fits response models and proposes weights.
3Training jobs
the mixed generalist runs and specialist runs, on the queues from Design 02.
4Per-domain rollout and reward pools
verifiers, judges and environments for each family, scaled independently (Design 07).
5Combination jobs
merging and distillation of specialists.
6Evaluation and gate
every candidate is scored on every family, and the gate decides promotion.
7Workflow engine
chains these steps (train specialists → merge or distill → evaluate → gate) as one auditable pipeline.

The YAML. One pipeline as an Argo Workflow: specialists in parallel, then merge, then the multi-family gate.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1kind: Workflowmetadata:  generateName: assistant-v14-combine-  namespace: post-trainingspec:  entrypoint: pipeline  templates:  - name: pipeline    dag:      tasks:      - name: code-specialist        template: train        arguments: { parameters: [ { name: recipe, value: recipes/specialists/code-v9.yaml } ] }      - name: agents-specialist        template: train        arguments: { parameters: [ { name: recipe, value: recipes/specialists/agents-v4.yaml } ] }      - name: merge        template: merge        dependencies: [code-specialist, agents-specialist]          # run after both      - name: gate        template: evaluate        dependencies: [merge]  - name: train    inputs: { parameters: [ { name: recipe } ] }    resource:                                                       # submit a Kueue-managed JobSet      action: create      successCondition: status.terminalState == Completed      manifest: |        apiVersion: jobset.x-k8s.io/v1alpha2        kind: JobSet        metadata:          generateName: specialist-          labels: { kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: post-training }        spec:          replicatedJobs:          - name: trainer            template:              spec:                parallelism: 4                completions: 4                template:                  spec:                    restartPolicy: Never                    containers:                    - name: train                      image: registry.example.com/rl/trainer:2026.11                      args: ["--recipe={{inputs.parameters.recipe}}"]                      resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8 } }  - name: merge    container:      image: registry.example.com/post-training/merge:2026.11      args: ["--method=ties", "--base=registry://assistant-v14-base",             "--specialists=registry://code-v9,registry://agents-v4", "--tune-on=evals://multi-family@v3"]  - name: evaluate    container:      image: registry.example.com/evals/runner:2026.11      args: ["--candidate=registry://assistant-v14-merged", "--gate=gates/no-regression.yaml"]
Going deeper2 points
  • Proxy sweeps are the bulk of the compute: dozens of small mixture runs per decision. Run them at low priority on borrowed capacity.
  • Every artifact carries its lineage: which specialists, merge weights, mixture and data versions produced a candidate, so a regression can be traced to its source.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, contract and gate: the domain registry and contract, per-family scorecards and the no-regression gate on the current release process.
  • Phase 2, measurement: proxy-run infrastructure, the transfer matrix, seed-noise estimates and per-domain RL signal metrics.
  • Phase 3, mixtures: response-model weight search, staged schedules with refreshes, per-domain batch composition.
  • Phase 4, combination: specialist pipelines with merging and multi-teacher distillation, and conflict-reduction methods where interference is measured.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • No-regression gates slow releases: some improvements wait until a regression elsewhere is fixed.
  • Proxy-run evidence is imperfect: mixtures chosen at small scale are confirmed at scale, and sometimes changed.
  • Specialists add moving parts: more training runs and a combination step, in exchange for faster iteration in the domains that need it.
  • Central mixture ownership: domain teams give up control of their weight in exchange for a fair, measured process.

Open questions.

  • Scaling laws for mixtures: how well do optimal weights found on small models transfer to large ones?
  • Capacity vs mixture: at what point is a larger or MoE model cheaper than ever more careful mixture tuning?
  • Merging RL-trained specialists: RL changes few parameters per domain; does that make RL specialists easier to merge than SFT specialists?
  • Automatic refreshes: can the platform detect a regression and schedule a targeted refresh without a person deciding?
Design 12 · 12 sections

Design 12: Experiment analysis and debugging for post-training

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Where the noise comes from
  3. Separating real improvements from noise
  4. Designing ablations that decide something
  5. Diagnosing a regression by bisection
  6. Diffing two runs
  7. Probes on every checkpoint
  8. Behavior analysis: reading outputs at scale
  9. Data attribution: which data caused the change?
  10. Looking inside: activation probes
  11. The analysis platform on Kubernetes
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we develop a deep empirical understanding of post-training runs, so that we can diagnose regressions, separate real improvements from noise, design better ablations, and build the probes and analyses that make training less opaque? It sits on top of everything the earlier designs produce: recipes and health signals (Design 06), scaling ladders (Design 07), off-policy metrics (Design 09), verifier quality (Design 10) and multi-family evals (Design 11).

The short version: every claim about a run is a statistical claim, and every run is a dataset. The platform stores per-question eval results (not just averages) for every checkpoint, so comparisons are paired and come with error bars. Ablations are declared with a hypothesis and a decision rule before they run. Regressions are found by bisecting over recipe, data and code versions. And a fixed set of probes (log-probabilities on reference answers, per-layer update sizes, behavior statistics, linear probes on activations) runs on every checkpoint, so "what changed inside the model" has an answer before anyone asks.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. A researcher reports that a new reward-shaping term improves the reasoning benchmark by 1.8 points. Two weeks later, a re-run with a different seed shows −0.4. Meanwhile, a regression in tool-call formatting shipped because nobody connected it to a data refresh three runs earlier, and a long RL run's entropy collapse is "explained" by four different theories in the team channel.

What the platform must do.

  • Quantify uncertainty: every reported difference comes with a confidence interval from paired, per-question data.
  • Make ablations decisive: one declared variable, matched compute, enough seeds and questions to detect the effect size that matters.
  • Find regressions fast: narrow a regression to a specific change (recipe key, data version, code commit) in hours.
  • Look inside runs: standard probes on every checkpoint, comparable across runs.
  • Explain behavior changes: connect a change in outputs to the data or reward that caused it.
  • Keep it cheap enough to always run: analysis that's only done for important runs is never available when needed.

Out of scope: the training systems themselves (Designs 06–09) and production monitoring of served models.

Where the noise comes from

Scenario. The same recipe, run three times with different seeds, scores 61.2, 62.9 and 60.7 on the reasoning suite. A 1.8-point "improvement" is inside that range.

What the picture shows. The sources of variation in a reported score, from the eval to the training run.

1Question sampling
an eval is a sample of possible questions; a 500-question suite has a standard error of around 2 points at 60% accuracy.
2Generation sampling
with temperature above zero, the same model gives different answers; averaging several samples per question reduces this part.
3Training seed and data order
different seeds give different models; for RL this variation is often larger than for SFT.
4Nondeterministic kernels and infrastructure
different GPU counts, kernels or batch splits change results slightly even with the same seed.
5Checkpoint choice
picking the best of several checkpoints on the same eval used to report it inflates the result.
6Decomposition
measuring each source once per recipe family tells you what to spend on: more questions, more samples per question, or more training seeds.

The code. Estimating the components from a small grid of seeds × generation samples (Python).

import numpy as np def variance_components(scores: np.ndarray):    """scores[s, g, q]: training seed s, generation sample g, question q (0/1 or fractional)."""    S, G, Q = scores.shape    per_seed = scores.mean(axis=(1, 2))                       # score of each trained model    within_seed_gen = scores.mean(axis=2).var(axis=1, ddof=1).mean()   # generation sampling, whole-suite    q_means = scores.mean(axis=(0, 1))    question_se = np.sqrt(q_means.var(ddof=1) / Q)            # suite-level sampling error    return {        "seed_sd": float(per_seed.std(ddof=1)),               # training seed / data order        "generation_sd": float(np.sqrt(within_seed_gen)),        "question_se": float(question_se),    }
Going deeper2 points
  • Seed variance is a property of the recipe: some recipes are much noisier than others; a noisy recipe needs more seeds before any comparison, and that noise is itself a reason to prefer a quieter recipe.
  • Never select and report on the same eval: choose checkpoints on a validation split and report on a separate test split.

Separating real improvements from noise

Scenario. Model B scores 62.0 and model A 60.8 on the same 600 questions. Is B better? The unpaired standard errors overlap; but most questions are answered identically by both, and the paired analysis tells a different story.

What the picture shows. The statistical practices the platform applies to every comparison.

1Paired differences
compare models question by question on the same questions; the variance of the difference is much smaller than the variance of each score, because shared difficulty cancels out. Evaluation-statistics work recommends inference on question-level paired differences rather than population-level summary statistics.
2Clustered standard errors
questions often come in groups (several questions on one document, several tests per coding task); treat each group as one cluster, or the error bars are too narrow.
3Small evals need care
with fewer than a few hundred questions, normal-approximation intervals can badly understate uncertainty; use exact or Bayesian intervals, or bootstrap at the cluster level.
4Multiple comparisons
comparing 20 evals at 95% confidence produces one false "significant" result on average; control the false discovery rate or pre-declare the primary metric.
5Power analysis
decide in advance the smallest effect worth detecting and compute how many questions, samples and seeds are needed.

The code. A paired comparison with clustered standard errors, plus the number of questions needed to detect a given effect (Python).

import numpy as npfrom scipy import stats def paired_compare(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray, clusters: np.ndarray | None = None):    """a, b: per-question scores of two models on the same questions (means over samples)."""    d = b - a    n = len(d)    if clusters is None:        se = d.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n)    else:                                                     # cluster-robust SE        ids = np.unique(clusters)        sums = np.array([d[clusters == c].sum() - d[clusters == c].size * d.mean() for c in ids])        se = np.sqrt((sums ** 2).sum()) / n * np.sqrt(len(ids) / (len(ids) - 1))    z = d.mean() / se    return {"diff": d.mean(), "ci95": (d.mean() - 1.96 * se, d.mean() + 1.96 * se),            "p": 2 * (1 - stats.norm.cdf(abs(z))), "n": n} def questions_needed(effect: float, sd_diff: float, alpha=0.05, power=0.8) -> int:    """Questions needed to detect a paired mean difference `effect` (power analysis)."""    z = stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha / 2) + stats.norm.ppf(power)    return int(np.ceil((z * sd_diff / effect) ** 2))
Going deeper2 points
  • Report the interval, not the star: a result "+1.2 [−0.3, +2.7]" carries more information than "not significant", and stops both over- and under-claiming.
  • Seeds are the outer layer: paired question-level statistics handle eval noise; training-seed variance still needs several runs per arm. Compare arms with seeds as the unit, and questions within them.

Designing ablations that decide something

Scenario. An ablation changed the learning rate and the reward weight together, ran one seed each, and was evaluated on the suite the researcher happened to have open. Nobody can say what it showed.

What the picture shows. The elements of an ablation that produces a decision.

1Hypothesis and decision rule, declared first
what effect is expected, on which primary metric, and what result leads to which action.
2One declared variable
the launcher enforces that the recipe diff touches only the declared keys (Design 06).
3Matched compute
arms get the same tokens or GPU hours; otherwise "better" may just mean "trained longer".
4Enough seeds and questions
from the power analysis, not from habit.
5Proxy scale with a confirmation step
run at small scale; confirm the winner at the target scale before adopting it (Design 07).
6Factorial designs for interacting choices
when two settings plausibly interact (learning rate and batch size), a small 2×2 grid shows the interaction that two one-at-a-time ablations miss.

The YAML. An ablation declared with its hypothesis, budget and decision rule; the launcher refuses to run it without these.

# ablations/2026-11/overlong-penalty.yamlhypothesis: "An overlong penalty starting at 14K tokens improves math-hard without hurting length-sensitive chat evals."base_recipe: recipes/assistant-v14/rl-math-code.yamlvariable:  rewards.overlong_penalty: [off, {start: 14336, end: 16384}]   # the only key allowed to differbudget: { matched_by: tokens, tokens_per_arm: 2.0e9 }seeds: 3                                          # from the power analysis belowpower: { min_effect: 1.0, metric_sd_diff: 6.5, questions: 1200 }primary_metric: evals://math-hard@v5/pass@1guardrails:                                       # must not regress beyond these  evals://chat-length@v2/mean_tokens: { max_increase_pct: 5 }  evals://ifeval@v4/strict: { max_drop: 0.8 }decision:  adopt_if: "primary.ci95.low > 0 and all guardrails pass"  reject_if: "primary.ci95.high < 0.5"  otherwise: "extend seeds to 5, then decide"      # no open-ended 'interesting' outcomes
Going deeper2 points
  • Pre-registering doesn't forbid exploration: exploratory analysis is fine and often where insight comes from; it's labeled as exploratory, and a decision needs a confirmatory run.
  • Keep the ablation record even when it fails: a library of negative results stops the same idea from being re-tested every quarter.

Diagnosing a regression by bisection

Scenario. Tool-call formatting dropped 3 points between release candidates rc1 and rc5. In between: two data refreshes, a verifier version bump, a trainer upgrade and nine recipe changes. Reading diffs hasn't found it.

What the picture shows. Narrowing a regression to one change, the way git bisect narrows a bug.

1Enumerate the changes
every difference between the good and bad candidates as a list of atomic changes: recipe keys, data versions, verifier versions, code commits, image digests.
2Order them
by time, or group by kind (data, reward, code, recipe).
3Bisect with proxy runs
apply half the changes to the good recipe, run a short proxy, evaluate the regressed metric (with enough questions to see the effect), and keep the half that reproduces it.
4Check the checkpoint dimension too
within one run, evaluate intermediate checkpoints to find when the regression appeared; a sudden drop points to a data shard or a schedule event.
5Confirm by reverting
revert only the identified change on the bad recipe; the regression should disappear.

The code. Bisection over a list of changes with a proxy-run oracle (Python).

def bisect_changes(good_recipe, changes: list, regressed, apply):    """changes: atomic diffs between good and bad. regressed(recipe) runs a proxy and returns True if the    metric is significantly worse than the good recipe (paired test). apply(recipe, subset) applies diffs."""    lo, hi = 0, len(changes)                       # invariant: changes[:hi] reproduce, changes[:lo] don't    assert regressed(apply(good_recipe, changes)), "regression doesn't reproduce at proxy scale"    while hi - lo > 1:        mid = (lo + hi) // 2        if regressed(apply(good_recipe, changes[:mid])):            hi = mid        else:            lo = mid    culprit = changes[hi - 1]    return culprit                                  # confirm: revert only this on the bad recipe
Going deeper2 points
  • Interactions break bisection: if the regression needs two changes together, linear bisection points to the second one; when reverting it alone doesn't fully fix things, bisect the remaining changes with it applied.
  • Proxy fidelity first: before bisecting, confirm the regression reproduces at proxy scale; if it only appears at full scale, bisect over checkpoints and data shards of the full run instead.

Diffing two runs

Scenario. Two runs with "almost the same" config end 4 points apart. The team needs to see where, during training, they started to diverge, and on which signals.

What the picture shows. A run diff: two runs aligned on the same axis and compared on every signal.

1Config diff
the exact differences in recipe, data, code and image versions, from lineage.
2Aligned curves
all metrics aligned by tokens or samples seen (not wall-clock or step, which differ with batch size).
3First divergence
the earliest point where any signal's difference exceeds its seed-noise band; the signal that diverges first is usually closest to the cause.
4Eval-level diff
per-question paired differences at matched checkpoints; which question types moved.
5Sample diff
outputs of both runs on the same prompts at matched checkpoints, side by side.
Going deeper2 points
  • Seed-noise bands come from reference runs: keep two or three seeds of the reference recipe so every signal has a known spread to compare against.
  • Divergence in health signals often precedes divergence in evals by hundreds of steps: entropy, length or importance-ratio spread typically move first.

Probes on every checkpoint

Scenario. After an RL run, the model is better at math but worse at one style of instruction. Nobody can tell when that started or whether the model's knowledge changed or only its behavior.

What the picture shows. Cheap, fixed measurements run on every saved checkpoint.

1Reference log-probability probes
the model's log-probability of fixed reference answers (correct solutions, preferred responses, held-out text). A falling log-probability on held-out general text is an early sign of forgetting; on preferred responses, of a style shift.
2Distribution probes
entropy and top-token probabilities on a fixed prompt set; length and format statistics of generated answers.
3Distance probes
KL to the base model on fixed prompts; per-layer and per-module relative update size since the last checkpoint.
4Behavior probes
small, fast suites for refusals, language consistency, tool-call validity and verbosity.
5One table per run
every probe value per checkpoint, so runs can be compared at any point, not just at the end.

The code. A reference log-probability probe and per-module update sizes (PyTorch, Transformers).

import torch @torch.no_grad()def ref_logprob(model, tok, pairs, device="cuda"):    """pairs: [(prompt, reference_answer)]. Mean per-token log-prob of the reference answers."""    total, count = 0.0, 0    for prompt, ref in pairs:        p = tok(prompt, return_tensors="pt").input_ids.to(device)        r = tok(ref, return_tensors="pt", add_special_tokens=False).input_ids.to(device)        ids = torch.cat([p, r], dim=1)        logits = model(ids).logits[:, p.size(1) - 1:-1]        lp = torch.log_softmax(logits.float(), -1).gather(-1, r.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1)        total += lp.sum().item(); count += r.numel()    return total / count def update_sizes(prev: dict, cur: dict) -> dict:    """Relative change per module between two checkpoints' state dicts."""    return {n: ((cur[n].float() - prev[n].float()).norm() / (prev[n].float().norm() + 1e-8)).item()            for n in cur if n in prev}
Going deeper2 points
  • Probes must be cheap: a probe set that takes an hour won't run on every checkpoint; keep each to minutes on one GPU and run them in parallel.
  • Version the probe sets like eval suites, and never train on them.

Behavior analysis: reading outputs at scale

Scenario. Users say the new model "feels different." Benchmarks are flat. Somebody needs to read thousands of outputs and say how.

What the picture shows. Turning many outputs into a description of behavior change.

1Paired samples
the same prompts answered by both models, at matched settings.
2Automatic statistics
length, formatting, hedging phrases, refusals, language, code-block use, tool calls, per prompt category.
3Model-assisted labeling
a model labels each pair against a taxonomy (more verbose, more cautious, different structure, wrong language), validated on a human-labeled sample.
4Clustering
embed the differences and cluster them, so unexpected changes appear as clusters nobody defined in advance.
5Human review of each cluster
a few examples per cluster read by people, who name the behavior and decide whether it matters.
Going deeper2 points
  • The taxonomy grows: every new behavior found by clustering becomes a label and, if it matters, a behavior eval (Design 11).
  • Check the labeler: model labels are measured against human labels like any verifier (Design 10).

Data attribution: which data caused the change?

Scenario. A run picked up a habit of ending answers with a summary table. The team suspects one of 40 data sources, but it could also be the reward model.

What the picture shows. Methods for tracing a behavior back to data, from cheapest to most precise.

1Search
find training examples (SFT data, high-reward rollouts) that show the behavior; often enough to spot the source.
2Rollout and reward analysis
in RL, compare the reward of outputs with and without the behavior; a reward model that prefers the behavior will teach it.
3Gradient similarity
compare the gradient of "produce this behavior" on probe prompts with gradients of training examples; examples with high similarity are candidates.
4Slice ablations
remove or down-weight a candidate source in a proxy run and check that the behavior goes away. This is the confirmation step.

The code. Ranking training examples by gradient similarity to a behavior probe, using a small set of parameters for speed (PyTorch).

import torch def grad_vec(model, loss, params):    g = torch.autograd.grad(loss, params, retain_graph=False)    return torch.cat([x.flatten() for x in g]) def attribute(model, behavior_loss_fn, examples, example_loss_fn, params, top=20):    """params: a few chosen modules (e.g. last layers' MLPs). Returns examples most aligned with the behavior."""    target = grad_vec(model, behavior_loss_fn(model), params)    target = target / target.norm()    scores = []    for ex in examples:        g = grad_vec(model, example_loss_fn(model, ex), params)        scores.append((torch.dot(g / (g.norm() + 1e-8), target).item(), ex["id"], ex["source"]))    scores.sort(reverse=True)    return scores[:top]                  # candidates: confirm with a slice ablation
Going deeper2 points
  • Attribution suggests, ablation confirms: gradient similarity is approximate; never remove data on attribution scores alone.
  • For RL, the reward is data too: many behavior changes come from what the verifier or reward model prefers, not from prompts.

Looking inside: activation probes

Scenario. Refusals rose after a safety-data update. The team wants to know whether the model's internal sense of "harmful request" changed, or only its threshold for acting on it.

What the picture shows. Simple tools for looking at internal representations across checkpoints.

1Linear probes
train a small classifier on hidden states at one layer to predict a property (harmful vs harmless request, language, task type); probe accuracy across checkpoints shows whether the property is still represented.
2Directions
the difference between mean activations of two groups (for example, requests that were refused vs answered) gives a direction; its projection shows how strongly each prompt activates it.
3Comparison across checkpoints
if the representation stays the same but the behavior changes, the change is in how the model acts on the representation; if the representation itself moves, the model now "sees" requests differently.
4Limits
these are coarse tools; they help form and test hypotheses, not prove mechanisms.

The code. A linear probe on one layer's activations, trained once and applied to several checkpoints (PyTorch, scikit-learn).

import numpy as npimport torchfrom sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression @torch.no_grad()def layer_acts(model, tok, prompts, layer: int, device="cuda"):    out = []    for p in prompts:        ids = tok(p, return_tensors="pt").input_ids.to(device)        hs = model(ids, output_hidden_states=True).hidden_states[layer]        out.append(hs[0, -1].float().cpu().numpy())          # last-token representation    return np.stack(out) def probe_across(checkpoints, tok, prompts, labels, layer=20):    X0 = layer_acts(checkpoints[0], tok, prompts, layer)    clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(X0, labels)   # train on the first checkpoint    return [clf.score(layer_acts(m, tok, prompts, layer), labels) for m in checkpoints]
Going deeper2 points
  • Use held-out prompts for probe accuracy, and compare with a probe trained on each checkpoint separately; the gap shows how much the representation moved.
  • Keep it in proportion: activation probes are a useful lens for post-training questions, but the decision still rests on behavior evals.

The analysis platform on Kubernetes

Scenario. Probes and evals run when someone remembers to start them, results live in personal notebooks, and per-question results are thrown away after the average is computed.

What the picture shows. The pieces that make analysis automatic.

1Checkpoint events
every registered checkpoint emits an event.
2Eval and probe jobs
triggered by the event, they run the standard suites and probes on low-priority capacity and store per-question and per-probe results.
3Results store
a columnar store keyed by run, checkpoint, suite, question and sample; everything comparisons need.
4Analysis service
paired comparisons, variance components, run diffs and bisection, as APIs and notebooks on the same data.
5Ablation registry
declared ablations, their outcomes and decisions, including negative results.

The YAML. An Argo Events sensor that runs probes and evals whenever a checkpoint is registered.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1kind: Sensormetadata:  name: checkpoint-analysis  namespace: analysisspec:  dependencies:  - name: ckpt-registered    eventSourceName: model-registry          # emits on every new checkpoint    eventName: checkpoint-registered  triggers:  - template:      name: probes-and-evals      k8s:        operation: create        source:          resource:            apiVersion: batch/v1            kind: Job            metadata:              generateName: analyze-              labels:                kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: analysis                kueue.x-k8s.io/priority-class: analysis-low      # borrows idle GPUs            spec:              backoffLimit: 1              template:                spec:                  restartPolicy: Never                  containers:                  - name: analyze                    image: registry.example.com/analysis/runner:2026.11                    args: ["CHECKPOINT_URI", "--suites=standard@v7", "--probes=standard@v3",                           "--store-per-question=true"]           # never keep only averages                    resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 1 } }        parameters:        - src: { dependencyName: ckpt-registered, dataKey: body.uri }          dest: spec.template.spec.containers.0.args.0      # replaces CHECKPOINT_URI          operation: overwrite
Going deeper2 points
  • Per-question storage is cheap, compared with the GPU time spent producing it; throwing it away makes paired analysis impossible later.
  • Analysis code is versioned too: a changed probe or statistic gets a new version, and dashboards say which version they show.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, data: per-question eval storage, checkpoint events, standard probes on every checkpoint.
  • Phase 2, statistics: paired comparisons and intervals in every report; variance components per recipe family; power analysis in the ablation launcher.
  • Phase 3, debugging: run diffing, change bisection, behavior clustering.
  • Phase 4, depth: data attribution, activation probes, and the ablation library.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • More seeds and questions cost compute, in exchange for fewer wrong decisions and fewer re-runs.
  • Declared ablations slow down quick tries: exploratory runs remain allowed but can't, by themselves, change a recipe.
  • Always-on probes take GPU time on every checkpoint, kept low by small, fast probe sets on borrowed capacity.

Open questions.

  • Cheaper seed variance: can a few short runs predict the seed variance of a long one?
  • Better attribution for RL: how to attribute behavior to rollouts and reward decisions, not just to prompts?
  • Early predictors: which probe values at 10% of a run best predict its final evals?
  • Automated diagnosis: can the platform propose the likely cause of a regression from run diffs and probes before a person looks?
Design 13 · 12 sections

Design 13: End-to-end execution, from idea to production-scale runs

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. From idea to production: stages and gates
  3. Contracts between teams
  4. Data quality: contracts, validation and lineage
  5. Verifier and environment readiness
  6. Capacity planning for big runs
  7. Reliable pipelines: pre-flight, failure classes and recovery
  8. Scaling a recipe up
  9. Running the run: reviews, incidents and decisions
  10. From successful run to repeatable recipe
  11. The platform on Kubernetes
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do research, systems, infrastructure and data teams work together to get experiments from an idea to production-scale runs, with training pipelines that are reliable, data and verifiers whose quality is known, and successful experiments turned into repeatable, scalable recipes? It ties the earlier designs together: capacity and queues (Design 02), training infrastructure (Design 03), recipes (Design 06), scaling (Design 07), verifiers (Design 10), mixtures (Design 11) and analysis (Design 12).

The short version: the path from idea to production is a pipeline with explicit stages, contracts and gates, not a series of favours. Each stage (proxy, scale-up, production run, recipe release) has an entry checklist, an owner and a gate. The hand-offs between teams are contracts: a run spec for infrastructure, a data contract for data, a verifier contract for rewards, and a recipe manifest for whoever runs it next. Big runs start only after pre-flight checks pass; while they run, failures are classified and handled automatically; and a run that worked becomes a recipe release that CI can re-run.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. A small-scale RL experiment shows a clear gain in March. It reaches a production-scale run in June. In between: the data it used turned out to include eval questions, its verifier couldn't handle the throughput of a large run, the first two large runs died on infrastructure problems nobody owned, and the final recipe existed only in a researcher's branch. When she went on leave, nobody could reproduce it.

What the platform must do.

  • Shorten idea-to-scale time: weeks, not months, for an experiment that has earned it.
  • Make hand-offs explicit: each team knows what it receives, what it promises and how quality is checked.
  • Make big runs reliable: problems found before the run starts, failures during the run handled in minutes.
  • Guarantee data and verifier quality: checked automatically at every stage, not discovered after training.
  • Turn experiments into recipes: a successful run becomes a versioned, reproducible recipe anyone can re-run.
  • Keep a record: decisions, incidents and results in one place.

Out of scope: the technical content of each component, which the earlier designs cover.

From idea to production: stages and gates

Scenario. Nobody can say what "ready for a big run" means. Some experiments jump straight to 512 GPUs; others sit at proxy scale for months waiting for someone to decide.

What the picture shows. The stages an experiment moves through, with a gate between each.

1Idea and proxy
a declared ablation at small scale (Design 12). Gate: a confirmed effect with an interval, on the primary metric and guardrails.
2Scale-up
the scaling ladder (Design 07): longer, larger, more steps. Gate: stable curve fit, understood step-time breakdown, pre-flight checks passing.
3Production run
the full budget on reserved capacity. Gate: multi-family no-regression evaluation (Design 11).
4Recipe release
the run's configuration, data and verifier versions packaged as a recipe that CI can reproduce. Gate: a reproduction at reference scale matches.
5Owners per stage
research leads the first two; the run's operational owner (from systems) leads the production run; the recipe owner keeps the release reproducible.
Going deeper2 points
  • Gates are light at the start and heavy at the end: a proxy run needs a recipe file; a production run needs everything. Heavy gates early kill exploration.
  • Time in each stage is a metric: where experiments wait is where the process needs work.

Contracts between teams

Scenario. Infrastructure learns about a 1,024-GPU run two days before it should start. The data team learns that their dataset is being used for RL when the run is already in progress. The verifier team learns its service is in the critical path when it falls over.

What the picture shows. The hand-offs between teams, each a document with a schema and an owner.

1Run spec (research → infrastructure)
size, duration, topology, storage and network needs, start window, priority. Submitted when the scale-up stage starts, not when the run starts.
2Data contract (data → research)
schema, versions, freshness, decontamination status, licenses, PII handling and validation results.
3Verifier contract (rewards → research)
versions, measured precision per slice, throughput limits and on-call (Design 10).
4Recipe manifest (research → everyone)
the complete, pinned description of how to run it again.
5Incident and decision log (everyone)
what went wrong, what was decided and why.

The YAML. A run spec submitted to infrastructure at the start of scale-up.

# runspecs/assistant-v14-rl-prod.yamlrun: assistant-v14-rl-prodowner: { research: alice, operations: rl-ops-oncall }stage: productionsize: { nodes: 128, gpus_per_node: 8, accelerator: h100 }duration_estimate: { gpu_hours: 180000, wall_days: 8 }topology: { same_fabric_block: true }                  # see Design 02storage: { checkpoint_tb: 4.2, checkpoint_interval_min: 30, dataset_tb: 1.1 }dependencies:  verifiers: [math-final-answer@3.2.0, code-tests@5.1.0]   # must meet throughput below  verifier_throughput_rps: 1800  sandbox_pool_peak: 4000window: { earliest_start: 2026-12-01, latest_start: 2026-12-08 }priority: production
Going deeper2 points
  • Contracts are versioned and validated by machines: a run spec missing a field or a data contract missing decontamination status is rejected by CI, not by a meeting.
  • Every contract names an on-call: a hand-off without a contact for 3 a.m. isn't a hand-off.

Data quality: contracts, validation and lineage

Scenario. The March experiment's gain was partly from eval contamination: a scraped dataset contained a third of the benchmark's questions, paraphrased.

What the picture shows. The checks every dataset passes before it can be used in a recipe.

1Schema and format
fields present, chat templates valid, lengths within limits, languages labeled.
2Deduplication
exact and near-duplicate removal within and across sources.
3Decontamination
n-gram and embedding-similarity checks against every eval set the organization uses, including paraphrase detection.
4Safety and compliance
PII detection and removal, license recorded, sensitive-content filters.
5Quality signals
per-source quality scores and spot-check samples reviewed by people.
6Versioned snapshots and lineage
every dataset version is immutable, with the code and inputs that produced it, so a recipe pins exact data.

The code. Validation run on every new dataset version before it's published (Python).

import hashlibfrom datasketch import MinHash, MinHashLSH def ngram_minhash(text, n=8, perm=128):    m = MinHash(num_perm=perm)    toks = text.lower().split()    for i in range(max(1, len(toks) - n + 1)):        m.update(" ".join(toks[i:i + n]).encode())    return m def build_eval_index(eval_texts, threshold=0.5):    lsh = MinHashLSH(threshold=threshold, num_perm=128)    for i, t in enumerate(eval_texts):        lsh.insert(f"eval-{i}", ngram_minhash(t))    return lsh def validate(rows, eval_index, max_len=32768):    report = {"rows": len(rows), "schema_errors": 0, "exact_dupes": 0, "contaminated": 0}    seen = set()    for r in rows:        if not r.get("messages") or r["messages"][-1]["role"] != "assistant":            report["schema_errors"] += 1        h = hashlib.sha256(str(r["messages"]).encode()).hexdigest()        report["exact_dupes"] += h in seen; seen.add(h)        text = " ".join(m["content"] for m in r["messages"])        if eval_index.query(ngram_minhash(text)):            report["contaminated"] += 1                                   # blocks publication    report["ok"] = report["schema_errors"] == 0 and report["contaminated"] == 0    return report
Going deeper2 points
  • Decontaminate against all evals, every time an eval is added: a new eval set triggers re-checking existing datasets, not just new ones.
  • Data bugs look like model behaviors: a wrong chat template in one source shows up as an odd habit after training; schema checks per source are cheap insurance.

Verifier and environment readiness

Scenario. The verifier that served a 32-GPU proxy run at 40 requests per second gets 1,800 per second in the production run. Latency rises from 200 ms to 9 s, rollouts stall, and GPU utilization falls to 20%.

What the picture shows. What must be true of rewards and environments before a big run.

1Quality gate
precision per slice above threshold on current policy outputs, fuzzing clean (Design 10).
2Throughput test
a load test at the run's expected peak request rate and payload sizes, with latency targets.
3Capacity reservation
sandbox pools and judge GPUs reserved and pre-warmed for the run's duration.
4Failure behavior
what happens when the verifier is slow or down: rollouts pause and retry, never default to "pass".
5Version pinning
the run pins verifier and environment image digests; no changes during the run without an explicit decision.

The code. A pre-flight check the launcher runs before a production run (Python).

import asyncio, time, statistics, httpx async def load_test(url, payloads, rps: int, seconds: int = 60):    lat, errors = [], 0    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=30) as client:        async def one(p):            nonlocal errors            t0 = time.perf_counter()            try:                r = await client.post(url, json=p); r.raise_for_status()                lat.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)            except Exception:                errors += 1        for _ in range(seconds):            tick = time.perf_counter()            await asyncio.gather(*(one(payloads[i % len(payloads)]) for i in range(rps)))            await asyncio.sleep(max(0, 1 - (time.perf_counter() - tick)))    p99 = statistics.quantiles(lat, n=100)[98] if lat else float("inf")    return {"p99_s": p99, "error_rate": errors / (rps * seconds)} def preflight(runspec, verifier_registry):    results = {}    for v in runspec["dependencies"]["verifiers"]:        meta = verifier_registry.get(v)        results[v] = {            "precision_ok": all(s["precision"] >= s["gate"] for s in meta["slices"]),            "load": asyncio.run(load_test(meta["url"], meta["sample_payloads"],                                          rps=runspec["dependencies"]["verifier_throughput_rps"])),        }        results[v]["ok"] = results[v]["precision_ok"] and results[v]["load"]["p99_s"] < 2.0 \            and results[v]["load"]["error_rate"] < 0.001    return results
Going deeper2 points
  • Load-test with realistic payloads: policy outputs late in a run are longer than early ones; test with long outputs.
  • Fail closed: a reward service error must never be read as a pass; it's the cheapest reward hack there is.

Capacity planning for big runs

Scenario. A production run needs 1,024 GPUs for eight days. Two days in, the cluster's reserved block expires; nobody had checked the reservation's end date against the run's estimate.

What the picture shows. Turning a run spec into reserved, ready capacity.

1Estimate from the ladder
GPU hours and wall-clock from rung measurements (Design 07), plus a margin for restarts and evals.
2Match capacity sources
reserved blocks for the run's duration with margin, on-demand only for overflow (Design 02).
3Reserve in the queue
the run's queue gets guaranteed quota for the window; other work borrows around it.
4Reserve the dependencies
verifier, sandbox and judge capacity, storage throughput for checkpoints.
5Dry run
a short run on the actual reserved nodes before the window starts, to catch hardware and topology problems.

The code. A capacity estimate with margins from ladder measurements (Python).

def capacity_plan(tokens_total, tokens_per_gpu_hour, gpus, restart_rate_per_day=0.3,                  restart_cost_h=0.5, eval_overhead=0.06, safety_margin=0.15):    gpu_hours = tokens_total / tokens_per_gpu_hour    wall_h = gpu_hours / gpus    days = wall_h / 24    lost_h = days * restart_rate_per_day * restart_cost_h             # expected restart losses    wall_h = (wall_h + lost_h) * (1 + eval_overhead)    reserve_h = wall_h * (1 + safety_margin)                          # reservation must cover this    return {"gpu_hours": round(gpu_hours), "expected_wall_days": round(wall_h / 24, 1),            "reserve_days": round(reserve_h / 24, 1)} print(capacity_plan(tokens_total=4.0e11, tokens_per_gpu_hour=2.6e6, gpus=1024))
Going deeper2 points
  • Track estimate accuracy: compare each run's estimate with its actual; bias in estimates is fixed by calibrating tokens-per-GPU-hour from the latest rung, not by bigger margins.
  • Reservations are commitments: an unused reservation costs as much as a used one; release early if the run finishes early.

Reliable pipelines: pre-flight, failure classes and recovery

Scenario. The first production run died on day one: a typo in a data path that the 32-GPU proxy never hit. The second died on day three: a node's GPU fault was retried as if it were a code bug, failing the whole job after the retry limit.

What the picture shows. How a production run avoids preventable failures and handles the rest.

1Pre-flight smoke run
a few steps of the production configuration on a small slice of the reserved nodes, touching every code path: data loading from every source, a checkpoint save and load, a verifier call, a weight sync and an eval.
2Failure classes
infrastructure failures (GPU faults, node loss, network) are retried on other nodes without counting against the job; code and configuration errors fail fast and page the run owner; data errors quarantine the shard and continue or stop by policy.
3Checkpoint verification
every checkpoint is test-loaded once after it's written; a corrupt checkpoint is found then, not when needed.
4Watchdogs
stalled-step detection (no progress for N minutes), NaN detection and health-signal alerts (Design 06).
5On-call and runbooks
a named operations owner per production run, with runbooks for each failure class.

The YAML. A pod failure policy that separates infrastructure failures from code errors (Kubernetes Job API).

apiVersion: batch/v1kind: Jobmetadata:  name: assistant-v14-preflight  namespace: post-training  labels: { kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: rl-production }spec:  completions: 16  parallelism: 16  completionMode: Indexed  backoffLimit: 6  podFailurePolicy:    rules:    - action: Ignore                         # node drained / GPU fault: retry, don't count      onPodConditions:      - type: DisruptionTarget    - action: FailJob                        # exit code 42 = config or code error: stop now      onExitCodes:        containerName: trainer        operator: In        values: [42]    - action: Count                          # anything else counts against backoffLimit      onExitCodes:        containerName: trainer        operator: NotIn        values: [0, 42]  template:    spec:      restartPolicy: Never      containers:      - name: trainer        image: registry.example.com/rl/trainer@sha256:1f0c...        args: ["--recipe=/recipes/prod.yaml", "--preflight", "--steps=20",               "--touch-all-sources", "--test-checkpoint-roundtrip", "--test-verifiers"]        resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8 } }
Going deeper2 points
  • Exit codes are an API: the trainer exits with distinct codes for config errors, data errors and internal errors, so the platform can react correctly.
  • Count failures by class over time: a rising rate of one infrastructure class on certain nodes is a hardware problem to fix, not noise to retry.

Scaling a recipe up

Scenario. The recipe that worked at 64 GPUs used a batch of 256 prompts. At 1,024 GPUs, someone multiplied the batch by 16 and kept the learning rate. The run was stable and learned much less per sample.

What the picture shows. What has to change, and what must not, when a recipe moves from proxy to production scale.

1Keep the science fixed
objective, reward, data mixture and filtering stay the same unless the ladder showed a reason to change them.
2Change the systems deliberately
parallelism layout, micro-batch sizes, number of rollout engines and weight-sync configuration are re-tuned for the new size.
3Batch and learning rate together
if the global batch changes, the learning rate and number of steps are re-validated at a rung, not assumed.
4Length and time budgets
maximum response length, timeouts and checkpoint intervals reflect the longer, larger run.
5The scale-up diff is reviewed
every key that differs between the proxy recipe and the production recipe is listed and justified.

The code. A scale-up diff check that separates "systems" keys from "science" keys (Python).

SYSTEMS_KEYS = {"parallelism", "micro_batch", "rollout.engines", "weight_sync", "checkpoint_interval",                "timeouts", "resources"} def flatten(d, prefix=""):    out = {}    for k, v in d.items():        key = f"{prefix}.{k}" if prefix else k        out.update(flatten(v, key) if isinstance(v, dict) else {key: v})    return out def scale_up_review(proxy: dict, prod: dict, justified: set):    a, b = flatten(proxy), flatten(prod)    changed = {k for k in a.keys() | b.keys() if a.get(k) != b.get(k)}    science = {k for k in changed if not any(k.startswith(s) for s in SYSTEMS_KEYS)}    unjustified = science - justified                                    # science changes need a reason    return {"systems_changes": sorted(changed - science), "science_changes": sorted(science),            "blocked": sorted(unjustified)}
Going deeper2 points
  • Scale-up surprises go back down the ladder: if production behaves differently from the last rung, reproduce at the rung before adjusting the production run.
  • Systems changes can change science: different parallelism or precision changes numerics; the mismatch checks of Design 07 run after any layout change.

Running the run: reviews, incidents and decisions

Scenario. On day five of a production run, three people noticed entropy dropping. Each assumed someone else was handling it. On day seven, the run collapsed.

What the picture shows. The operational rhythm of a production run.

1Roles
a research owner (is it learning the right thing?) and an operations owner (is it running well?), both named in the run spec.
2Daily run review
fifteen minutes on health signals, evals at the latest checkpoints, throughput, cost and open issues.
3Incident process
any automatic alert or human concern opens an incident with an owner; decisions (pause, roll back, change a setting) are recorded with the evidence.
4Change control during the run
live changes (learning rate, staleness limit, mixture) go through the run's change log, never directly.
5Post-run review
what worked, what broke, what the next run should change; the results feed the recipe and the runbooks.
Going deeper2 points
  • The decision log is part of the recipe release: a recipe that needed three mid-run interventions isn't a recipe yet; those interventions become part of it or become fixed problems.
  • Automatic controls first: controllers from Design 09 handle common problems; people handle what's new.

From successful run to repeatable recipe

Scenario. The production run succeeded. Three months later, the next version starts from "what we did last time", and nobody can reconstruct the exact data mixture or the verifier version.

What the picture shows. What a recipe release contains, and how it stays reproducible.

1Pinned inputs
base checkpoint, dataset snapshots, verifier and environment versions, container image digests.
2Configuration
the full recipe and schedule, including the systems settings for each supported scale.
3Evidence
eval results with intervals, the scale-up record, the decision log and known issues.
4Runbook
how to run it, what to watch, what to do when known problems appear.
5Reproduction in CI
a scheduled job re-runs the recipe at reference scale on current infrastructure and compares with the recorded results, so infrastructure or library drift is caught.

The YAML. A recipe release manifest, the unit a future run starts from.
