# releases/assistant-v14-rl@1.0.0/manifest.yamlrelease: assistant-v14-rlversion: 1.0.0base_checkpoint: registry://assistant-v14/sft@sha256:7c1e...data:  - datasets://math-verified@v6 # snapshot id: ds-2026-11-02-a91f  - datasets://code-tests@v9  - envs://swe-tasks@v3verifiers: [math-final-answer@3.2.0, code-tests@5.1.0]images: { trainer: "sha256:1f0c...", vllm: "sha256:88ab...", verifier-math: "sha256:5e1d..." }recipe: recipes/assistant-v14/rl-math-code.yaml@3f9a1c7scales:  reference: { gpus: 64,   steps: 300,  expected: { math-hard: [61.0, 63.4] } }   # CI reproduction band  production: { gpus: 1024, steps: 4200 }evidence:  evals: results://assistant-v14-rl-prod/final  decision_log: runs/assistant-v14-rl-prod/decisions.mdknown_issues: ["entropy dips at ~step 2,400; controller handles it (see runbook §3)"]owner: team-reasoning
Going deeper2 points
  • Reproduction bands come from seed variance: the CI check passes when the reference run lands inside the interval measured for that recipe (Design 12), not when it matches a single number.
  • Recipes have a lifecycle: active, superseded or deprecated; a deprecated recipe keeps its manifest so old results remain explainable.

The platform on Kubernetes

Scenario. Each stage of the path uses a different set of scripts, and the state of an experiment lives in a mix of tickets, chats and branches.

What the picture shows. The components that carry an experiment from idea to recipe.

1Experiment tracker
the stage, owners, contracts and gates for each experiment, linked to its runs.
2Contract validators in CI
run specs, data contracts, verifier contracts and recipe manifests checked on every change.
3Launcher
turns recipes and run specs into Kueue-managed jobs, runs pre-flight checks, and refuses launches that fail them.
4Data platform
versioned snapshots, validation and lineage.
5Reward platform
verifier registry and pools (Design 10).
6Training infrastructure
queues, reserved capacity, JobSets and RayJobs (Designs 02, 03).
7Run operations
dashboards, alerts, controllers, incident and decision logs.
8Recipe registry and reproduction CI
releases, manifests and scheduled reproduction runs.

The YAML. A scheduled reproduction of the recipe release at reference scale, triggered from CI (GitHub Actions).

# .github/workflows/reproduce-recipes.yamlname: reproduce-recipeson:  schedule: [ { cron: "23 3 * * 1" } ]          # weekly, Monday 03:23 UTC  workflow_dispatch: {}jobs:  reproduce:    runs-on: ubuntu-latest    strategy:      matrix: { release: [assistant-v14-rl@1.0.0, assistant-v14-sft@2.1.0] }    steps:    - uses: actions/checkout@v4    - name: Submit reference run      run: |        python3 tools/launch.py --release "releases/${{ matrix.release }}/manifest.yaml" \          --scale reference --queue research-small --wait    - name: Compare with expected band      run: |        python3 tools/compare_band.py --release "releases/${{ matrix.release }}/manifest.yaml" \          --run latest --fail-outside-band          # drift in infra or libraries fails the check
Going deeper2 points
  • One identifier everywhere: the experiment ID appears in run specs, jobs, checkpoints, eval results and recipe releases, so any artifact leads back to the decision that created it.
  • Dashboards per stage: how many experiments are in each stage, how long they wait, and why they fail gates.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, visibility: stages, owners and the experiment tracker; run specs submitted at scale-up; decision logs for production runs.
  • Phase 2, quality gates: data validation and decontamination in CI; verifier readiness checks; launcher pre-flight.
  • Phase 3, reliability: failure classes and pod failure policies, checkpoint verification, watchdogs, on-call and runbooks.
  • Phase 4, repeatability: recipe releases, scale-up reviews and reproduction CI.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Gates add steps: a few days of checks before a large run, in exchange for not losing weeks to preventable failures.
  • Reserved capacity costs money while idle, in exchange for runs that start on time and finish.
  • Contracts formalize relationships: some flexibility is lost, and much less is lost in miscommunication.
  • Reproduction CI uses compute weekly, in exchange for catching drift before a new version depends on an old recipe.

Open questions.

  • How light can early gates be while still catching the problems that are expensive later?
  • Automatic run reviews: can the analysis platform (Design 12) draft the daily run review?
  • Shared ownership at the boundary: who owns a failure that is half data and half verifier, and how is that decided quickly?
  • Recipes across model generations: how much of a recipe release carries over to the next base model, and how is that tested?
Design 14 · 12 sections

Design 14: Reliable infrastructure for large-scale RL training

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Anatomy of an RL system and its failure domains
  3. Reliability targets: failure rates, goodput and checkpoint intervals
  4. Node health: burn-in, continuous checks and automatic drain
  5. Trainer fault tolerance: from fast restarts to per-step recovery
  6. Rollout fleet resilience
  7. Weight synchronization you can trust
  8. The reward and environment tier: fail closed, degrade gracefully
  9. Checkpointing the whole RL state
  10. Stragglers, hangs and silent errors
  11. Observability, SLOs and fault injection
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we design and build infrastructure that keeps large-scale RL training running (thousands of GPUs, weeks of wall-clock time, many cooperating services) when hardware fails every few hours, services slow down, and some failures are silent? Design 07 covers what changes when RL scales and Design 13 covers how runs get from idea to production. This design is about the infrastructure underneath: failure domains, node health, fault tolerance for each RL component, whole-state checkpointing, stragglers and silent errors, and how reliability is measured and tested.

The short version: assume something is always broken, and make each break cost seconds of one component instead of hours of the whole run. The RL system is split into failure domains with different recovery strategies: the trainer is stateful and synchronous (fast checkpoint, fast restart, or per-step recovery across replica groups); rollout engines, verifiers and environments are stateless or cheaply restorable (retry, replace, route around). Nodes are continuously health-checked and drained before they break a job. All RL state (not only weights) is checkpointed asynchronously and verified. And reliability is a measured number, goodput, with an SLO, tested on purpose with fault injection.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. The RL platform runs a 2,048-GPU training job with 512 more GPUs of rollout engines, a 6,000-pod sandbox pool and a judge fleet. In the first month: a GPU failure roughly every few hours, two silent NaN events from a bad GPU, a network flap that hung all NCCL collectives for 40 minutes, a verifier deploy that returned errors read as "fail" for an hour, and a checkpoint that couldn't be loaded when it was needed. Goodput was 61%.

What the platform must do.

  • Contain failures: a broken GPU, engine, verifier or sandbox affects the smallest possible part of the system.
  • Recover in minutes: automatic detection, replacement and resumption, without a person in the loop for common failures.
  • Lose little work: checkpoints frequent and cheap enough that a restart loses minutes, not hours.
  • Catch silent failures: slow nodes, numerical corruption and hung collectives are detected, not discovered from the loss curve.
  • Measure reliability: goodput and recovery times as tracked numbers with targets.
  • Prove it: fault injection in staging and during rehearsals, so recovery paths are known to work.

Out of scope: algorithmic stability (Designs 06–09) and the run's organizational process (Design 13).

Anatomy of an RL system and its failure domains

Scenario. One sandbox node's disk filled up. Rollouts that used it hung, the trainer waited for a full batch, and the whole 2,048-GPU job sat idle for 25 minutes. A failure in the cheapest component stopped the most expensive one.

What the picture shows. The components of a large RL system, grouped by how they fail and recover.

1Trainer (stateful, synchronous)
thousands of GPUs in collectives; one failed rank stops all of them. Recovery: restart from checkpoint, or per-step recovery across replica groups.
2Rollout engines (stateless, independent)
each engine can fail alone; in-flight requests are retried elsewhere. Recovery: replace.
3Reward and environment tier (stateless or snapshot-backed)
verifiers, judges and sandboxes. Recovery: retry, circuit-break, replace.
4Coordination state
the sample buffer, the controller, weight versions and the data cursor. Small but critical; must be durable and replicated.
5Storage and network
checkpoint storage, object storage, the GPU fabric and the pod network. Shared by everything; failures here are wide.
6The rule
failures flow toward the trainer as delays, never as stops. Every dependency of the trainer has a timeout, a fallback and a bound on how long the trainer will wait.
Going deeper2 points
  • Map the blast radius explicitly: for each component, write down what stops when it fails; anything that can stop the trainer, apart from the trainer itself, is a design bug.
  • Decoupling buys reliability as well as throughput: the asynchronous designs of Design 07 and Design 09 mean a slow rollout tier reduces fresh data instead of halting training.

Reliability targets: failure rates, goodput and checkpoint intervals

Scenario. Someone proposes checkpointing every 4 hours "to save storage." Someone else proposes every 5 minutes "to be safe." Neither has done the arithmetic.

What the picture shows. How failure rates turn into lost time, and how to choose the checkpoint interval.

1Failures scale with size
a job's failure rate is roughly the per-node rate times the number of nodes. Meta's Llama 3 405B run on 16,384 H100 GPUs saw 419 unexpected interruptions in 54 days, about one every three hours, with GPUs or their memory responsible for about half.
2Lost time per failure
detection time + restart time + recomputation since the last checkpoint (on average half the interval).
3Checkpoint cost
the time training is paused to save; asynchronous checkpointing reduces it to seconds.
4Optimal interval
roughly the square root of (2 × checkpoint cost × mean time between failures), the Young–Daly approximation. Faster checkpoints allow shorter intervals.
5Goodput
the fraction of reserved GPU time that produced training progress. The target (for example, 90%+) is set per run and tracked daily.

The code. Expected goodput and the best checkpoint interval for a job (Python).

import math def plan(nodes, node_mtbf_h, ckpt_cost_s, restart_s, detect_s, step_overhead=0.0):    job_mtbf_s = node_mtbf_h * 3600 / nodes                       # failures add up across nodes    interval_s = math.sqrt(2 * ckpt_cost_s * job_mtbf_s)          # Young–Daly approximation    ckpt_overhead = ckpt_cost_s / interval_s    lost_per_failure = detect_s + restart_s + interval_s / 2    failure_overhead = lost_per_failure / job_mtbf_s    goodput = (1 - ckpt_overhead) * (1 - failure_overhead) * (1 - step_overhead)    return {"job_mtbf_h": round(job_mtbf_s / 3600, 2), "ckpt_interval_min": round(interval_s / 60, 1),            "goodput": round(goodput, 3)} # 256 nodes, a node fails every ~60 days on average; sync vs async checkpoint, slow vs fast restartprint(plan(256, 60 * 24, ckpt_cost_s=300, restart_s=1800, detect_s=300))   # sync, slow restartprint(plan(256, 60 * 24, ckpt_cost_s=8,   restart_s=240,  detect_s=30))    # async, hot spares
Going deeper2 points
  • Restart time matters as much as checkpoint interval: with failures every few hours, a 30-minute restart costs more than any checkpoint policy can recover.
  • Measure, don't assume, node MTBF: use the fleet's own failure history per hardware generation; it changes with age and firmware.

Node health: burn-in, continuous checks and automatic drain

Scenario. A node with a GPU throwing intermittent memory errors joins the training job. It doesn't fail outright; it fails the job twice a day for a week, each time looking like a new problem.

What the picture shows. The health lifecycle of a GPU node.

1Burn-in before admission
new or repaired nodes run GPU diagnostics, memory tests, NVLink and network bandwidth tests and a short multi-node collective test before they can join training pools.
2Continuous passive checks
GPU error counters (XID errors, ECC and row-remap events), thermals, PCIe and NIC errors, collected per node.
3Periodic active checks
short diagnostic runs during idle windows or between jobs.
4Automatic drain
a node that fails a check is tainted so no new pods land on it, its workloads are moved, and it goes to repair; a node that fails repeatedly is retired.
5Feedback from jobs
if one node appears in several job failures, it's drained even if its checks pass.

The YAML. A health-check DaemonSet that taints a node when its GPU checks fail (the check script uses NVIDIA DCGM; node tainting through the API).

apiVersion: apps/v1kind: DaemonSetmetadata:  name: gpu-health  namespace: gpu-opsspec:  selector: { matchLabels: { app: gpu-health } }  template:    metadata: { labels: { app: gpu-health } }    spec:      serviceAccountName: gpu-health            # RBAC: patch nodes (taints) only      nodeSelector: { nvidia.com/gpu.present: "true" }      tolerations: [ { operator: Exists } ]     # keep running on tainted nodes      priorityClassName: system-node-critical      containers:      - name: check        image: registry.example.com/gpu-ops/health:2026.11        args:        - --interval=60s        - --dcgm-level=1                        # quick passive checks; level 3 in idle windows        - --xid-fatal=48,63,64,74,79,94,95      # treat these XIDs as fatal        - --on-fail=taint:gpu-health=failed:NoSchedule        - --report=http://fleet-health.gpu-ops:8080/events        env:        - name: NODE_NAME          valueFrom: { fieldRef: { fieldPath: spec.nodeName } }        securityContext: { privileged: true }   # DCGM needs device access        resources: { limits: { cpu: "500m", memory: 512Mi } }
Going deeper2 points
  • Drain gently during a run: a failing node in a running job is replaced at the next checkpoint or restart, not by killing the job immediately, unless the failure is already fatal.
  • Track node history: every node's failures and repairs are recorded; repeat offenders are retired before they fail another run.

Trainer fault tolerance: from fast restarts to per-step recovery

Scenario. Each trainer failure took the whole 256-node job down for 35 minutes: rescheduling pods, pulling images, re-forming NCCL groups and loading a 3 TB checkpoint. Four failures a day cost more than two hours of 2,048 GPUs.

What the picture shows. Three levels of trainer fault tolerance, each building on the previous.

1Fast full restart
hot spare nodes reserved in the queue, images pre-pulled, checkpoints loaded in parallel from local copies or peers; the whole job restarts in a few minutes.
2In-place restart
only the failed pod is replaced and the job restarts its processes without rescheduling the healthy pods, avoiding the pod-level work.
3Per-step recovery across replicas
with replicated data-parallel groups (DDP or HSDP), a failed replica group drops out, training continues with the rest, and the group rejoins by copying state from a healthy peer. Libraries like torchft implement this, allowing membership changes at the training step granularity instead of stopping the world.
4Collective timeouts
NCCL watchdog timeouts set so a hung collective fails in minutes, not hours; the failure is then handled like any other.

The YAML. A JobSet failure policy: infrastructure failures restart without using up the restart budget; configuration errors stop immediately.

apiVersion: jobset.x-k8s.io/v1alpha2kind: JobSetmetadata:  name: rl-trainer-prod  namespace: rl-scale  labels: { kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: rl-production }spec:  failurePolicy:    maxRestarts: 20    restartStrategy: Recreate    rules:    - name: infra-disruption                       # node drained, GPU fault, preemption      action: RestartJobSetAndIgnoreMaxRestarts     # doesn't consume the budget      onJobFailureReasons: [PodFailurePolicy]    - name: config-error      action: FailJobSet                            # exit 42: don't retry a bad config      onJobFailureReasons: [BackoffLimitExceeded]      targetReplicatedJobs: [launcher]  replicatedJobs:  - name: trainer    replicas: 1    template:      spec:        parallelism: 256        completions: 256        backoffLimit: 0        podFailurePolicy:          rules:          - action: FailJob            onPodConditions: [ { type: DisruptionTarget } ]        template:          spec:            restartPolicy: Never            containers:            - name: trainer              image: registry.example.com/rl/trainer@sha256:1f0c...              env:              - { name: TORCH_NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING, value: "1" }              - { name: TORCH_NCCL_HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT_SEC, value: "300" }   # hung collective → error              args: ["--resume=latest", "--ckpt-load=peer-first"]              resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8 } }  - name: launcher    replicas: 1    template:      spec:        backoffLimit: 0        template:          spec:            restartPolicy: Never            containers:            - name: validate              image: registry.example.com/rl/trainer@sha256:1f0c...              args: ["--validate-config-only"]      # exits 42 on config errors
Going deeper2 points
  • Per-step recovery has requirements: replicated data-parallel groups, a coordination service, and enough memory headroom to run with one group missing; it pays off most at very large scale.
  • Measure each recovery phase: detection, scheduling, image, process start, collective setup, checkpoint load. The slowest phase is the one to fix.

Rollout fleet resilience

Scenario. One vLLM engine started returning garbled output after a driver error but kept passing its HTTP health check. For two hours, 1/64 of rollouts were nonsense with near-zero rewards.

What the picture shows. Keeping a large fleet of inference engines healthy and its failures invisible to the trainer.

1Stateless engines
any request can be retried on another engine; partial generations are discarded or resumed according to policy.
2Timeouts and hedging
each request has a deadline; requests in the slowest tail are re-issued on another engine and the first answer wins.
3Deep health checks
beyond "is it up," engines periodically answer a fixed canary prompt; output and log-probabilities are compared with expected values, catching silent corruption.
4Quarantine
an engine that fails a canary or produces abnormal statistics (rewards, lengths, log-probabilities far from its peers) is drained and replaced.
5Rolling weight updates
new weights are loaded engine by engine (or group by group), so the fleet never goes fully offline.

The code. A rollout client with deadlines, retries on another engine and hedged requests (Python, asyncio).

import asyncio, random async def generate(engines, request, deadline_s=600, hedge_after_s=120, max_attempts=3):    """Send to one engine; if slow, hedge on a second; retry elsewhere on failure."""    tried, attempt = set(), 0    while attempt < max_attempts:        attempt += 1        primary = random.choice([e for e in engines.healthy() if e not in tried]); tried.add(primary)        tasks = {asyncio.create_task(primary.generate(request))}        try:            done, _ = await asyncio.wait(tasks, timeout=hedge_after_s)            if not done:                                            # slow: hedge on another engine                backup = random.choice([e for e in engines.healthy() if e not in tried]); tried.add(backup)                tasks.add(asyncio.create_task(backup.generate(request)))                done, _ = await asyncio.wait(tasks, timeout=deadline_s - hedge_after_s,                                             return_when=asyncio.FIRST_COMPLETED)            for t in done:                if not t.exception():                    for other in tasks - {t}: other.cancel()                    return t.result()        except Exception:            pass        for t in tasks: t.cancel()        engines.report_failure(primary)                              # feeds quarantine decisions    raise TimeoutError("rollout failed on all attempts")             # the buffer skips this prompt
Going deeper2 points
  • Compare engines with their peers: per-engine reward, length and log-probability distributions should match the fleet; an outlier engine is suspect even when it responds.
  • Hedging costs capacity: hedge only the slowest few percent, and count hedged duplicates in the throughput budget.

Weight synchronization you can trust

Scenario. A weight push was interrupted halfway by a network flap. Half of one engine's layers were new and half were old. It served for an hour before anyone noticed.

What the picture shows. Making weight distribution atomic, verifiable and recoverable.

1Stage, then swap
new weights are written to a staging buffer on each engine; the engine switches versions only when the full set has arrived and verified.
2Checksums per bucket
each transferred bucket carries a checksum; a mismatch triggers a re-send of that bucket.
3Version handshake
after the swap, each engine reports its version and a fingerprint (for example, the log-probability of a canary prompt); the coordinator checks them.
4Timeouts and fallback path
if the fast path (NCCL over the GPU fabric) fails or times out, engines load the version from object storage instead.
5Version-tagged tokens
every generated token carries the version that produced it (Design 09), so a mistake is traceable and correctable.

The code. Staged, checksummed weight loading with an atomic swap on the engine side (Python sketch).

import hashlib, torch class WeightReceiver:    def __init__(self, model):        self.model, self.staging, self.expected = model, {}, {}     def begin(self, version: int, manifest: dict):          # manifest: bucket_id -> (names, sha256)        self.version, self.expected, self.staging = version, manifest, {}     def receive(self, bucket_id: str, tensors: dict[str, torch.Tensor]) -> bool:        h = hashlib.sha256()        for name in sorted(tensors):            h.update(tensors[name].contiguous().view(torch.uint8).cpu().numpy().tobytes())        if h.hexdigest() != self.expected[bucket_id][1]:            return False                                     # coordinator re-sends this bucket        self.staging.update({n: t.to("cuda", non_blocking=True) for n, t in tensors.items()})        return True     def commit(self) -> int:        if set(self.staging) != {n for names, _ in self.expected.values() for n in names}:            raise RuntimeError("incomplete weight set; keeping current version")        with torch.no_grad():            for name, p in self.model.named_parameters():                p.copy_(self.staging[name])                  # swap only when everything arrived        self.staging.clear()        return self.version
Going deeper2 points
  • Checksums on GPU: hashing large tensors on CPU is slow; compute a cheap GPU-side checksum (for example, sums over strided slices) per bucket and keep the full hash for the object-storage path.
  • Staging needs memory: a full staging copy doubles weight memory; with tight memory, stage per layer and swap layer by layer between requests.

The reward and environment tier: fail closed, degrade gracefully

Scenario. A verifier deploy started returning HTTP 500 for 30% of requests. The reward client treated errors as score 0. For an hour, the policy was punished for correct answers that happened to hit the broken pods.

What the picture shows. Patterns that keep reward failures from corrupting training or stalling it.

1Errors are not scores
a failed reward call is an error, retried or marked "no reward" (excluded from the loss), never a 0 or a 1 (Design 10).
2Circuit breakers
when a verifier's error rate crosses a threshold, calls stop for a cooling period; affected samples wait or are skipped.
3Back-pressure
when the reward queue is long, rollout engines slow down new trajectories instead of piling up work.
4Bulkheads
separate pools per verifier and per environment type, so one overloaded verifier doesn't starve the others.
5Sandbox hygiene
leaked or stuck sandboxes are reaped by age; pools are refilled before they run dry.
6Pinned versions during a run
verifier deploys during a run are explicit, canaried and reversible.

The code. A circuit breaker around reward calls that turns failures into "no reward", never into a score (Python).

import time class RewardBreaker:    def __init__(self, call, max_error_rate=0.05, window=200, cooldown_s=60):        self.call, self.max, self.window, self.cooldown = call, max_error_rate, window, cooldown_s        self.results, self.open_until = [], 0.0     def score(self, task, completion) -> float | None:        if time.time() < self.open_until:            return None                                   # breaker open: no reward, sample excluded        try:            r = self.call(task, completion)            self._record(ok=True)            return r        except Exception:            self._record(ok=False)            return None                                   # an error is never a score     def _record(self, ok: bool):        self.results = (self.results + [ok])[-self.window:]        errs = self.results.count(False) / len(self.results)        if len(self.results) >= 50 and errs > self.max:            self.open_until = time.time() + self.cooldown  # stop hammering a failing service            self.results.clear()
Going deeper2 points
  • Track "no reward" rate per verifier as a first-class metric; a rise means data is being lost even if training looks fine.
  • Graceful degradation is a policy: decide in advance whether a run pauses, continues with fewer domains, or slows down when a verifier is unavailable.

Checkpointing the whole RL state

Scenario. After a restart from checkpoint, the run repeated 40,000 prompts it had already trained on, the controller forgot that it had tightened the staleness limit, and the replay buffer was empty. The model was restored; the run wasn't.

What the picture shows. Everything a restart needs, and how it's saved without stopping training.

1Model and optimizer
sharded, saved asynchronously (copy to host memory, then write in the background).
2Data and sampling state
data cursors per source, curriculum position, RNG states.
3RL state
the sample buffer (or enough of it), in-flight rollout bookkeeping, weight version, controller settings and history.
4Two tiers
frequent saves to local NVMe or peer memory for fast restarts; less frequent copies to object storage for durability.
5Verification
every checkpoint is test-loaded (or checksum-verified against its manifest) once; only verified checkpoints are eligible for restart.
6Retention
keep the latest several, plus periodic ones for rollback (Design 07).

The code. Asynchronous sharded checkpointing of model, optimizer and RL state with PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint (sketch).

import json, torch.distributed as distimport torch.distributed.checkpoint as dcpfrom torch.distributed.checkpoint.state_dict import get_state_dict pending = None def save_rl_checkpoint(step, model, optimizer, rl_state: dict, path_local: str):    """rl_state: data cursors, RNG, buffer index, weight version, controller settings (small, JSON-able)."""    global pending    if pending is not None:        pending.result()                               # at most one save in flight    model_sd, optim_sd = get_state_dict(model, optimizer)    state = {"model": model_sd, "optim": optim_sd}    pending = dcp.async_save(state, checkpoint_id=f"{path_local}/step-{step}")   # training continues    if dist.get_rank() == 0:        with open(f"{path_local}/step-{step}.rl.json", "w") as f:            json.dump({"step": step, **rl_state}, f)   # buffer contents saved separately by the buffer service    return pending
Going deeper2 points
  • The buffer service checkpoints itself: it persists its contents (or an index into stored rollouts) on the same step boundary, so trainer and buffer agree on what has been consumed.
  • Upload in the background, verify in the background: the trainer only waits for the copy to host memory; upload and test-load run on separate processes.

Stragglers, hangs and silent errors

Scenario. Step time crept from 41 to 52 seconds over two days. No failures, no alerts. One GPU was thermally throttling, and every collective waited for it.

What the picture shows. The failures that don't announce themselves, and how each is detected.

1Stragglers
one slow rank slows every synchronous step. Detect with per-rank step and collective timings; the outlier rank is the suspect.
2Hangs
a collective that never completes. Detect with collective watchdogs and "no progress for N minutes" monitors; dump stack traces from every rank before restarting.
3Silent data corruption
a faulty GPU computes wrong values without errors. Detect with loss and gradient-norm spikes, NaN and infinity checks, cross-replica checksum comparisons of parameters, and periodic re-computation of a fixed probe on every GPU.
4Silent rollout corruption
an engine producing wrong output (see the rollout section); detected by canaries and peer comparison.
5Response
isolate the suspect node, verify with a targeted diagnostic, roll back to a checkpoint from before the corruption started if it affected training.

The code. Finding straggler ranks from per-rank step timings gathered each step (PyTorch Distributed).

import torch, torch.distributed as dist def straggler_check(step_time_s: float, step: int, z_threshold=4.0, log=print):    """Gather every rank's compute time for this step; flag ranks far above the median."""    t = torch.tensor([step_time_s], device="cuda")    all_t = [torch.zeros_like(t) for _ in range(dist.get_world_size())]    dist.all_gather(all_t, t)    if dist.get_rank() == 0:        times = torch.cat(all_t)        med = times.median()        mad = (times - med).abs().median() + 1e-6        z = (times - med) / (1.4826 * mad)                      # robust z-score        slow = (z > z_threshold).nonzero().flatten().tolist()        if slow:            log({"step": step, "straggler_ranks": slow, "times": times[slow].tolist(), "median": med.item()})        return slow
Going deeper2 points
  • Time compute separately from communication: a rank that is slow in compute is the straggler; ranks that are slow in communication are often waiting for it.
  • Keep a known-good probe per GPU: a tiny fixed computation with a known result, run every few hundred steps on every GPU, catches many silent corruption cases cheaply.

Observability, SLOs and fault injection

Scenario. The platform team believes recovery takes "about five minutes." The last three real recoveries took 9, 31 and 47 minutes. Nobody had measured, and one recovery path had never been exercised.

What the picture shows. Measuring reliability, and testing it on purpose.

1SLOs per run
goodput, time to detect, time to recover, maximum work lost per failure, and "no reward" rate.
2Failure ledger
every interruption recorded with its class, component, node, detection time, recovery time and root cause; reviewed weekly.
3Dashboards by failure domain
trainer, rollout fleet, reward tier, storage, network, each with its own health and recovery metrics.
4Fault injection
in staging and in rehearsal runs, kill trainer pods, crash rollout engines, inject network delay, fail a verifier and corrupt a checkpoint; confirm each recovery path and time it.
5Game days before big runs
a scheduled exercise where the on-call team handles injected failures on a rehearsal run.

The YAML. Injecting failures with Chaos Mesh in a rehearsal namespace: kill a rollout engine every 15 minutes and add latency to the verifier.

apiVersion: chaos-mesh.org/v1alpha1kind: Schedulemetadata:  name: kill-rollout-engine  namespace: rl-rehearsalspec:  schedule: "*/15 * * * *"  type: PodChaos  historyLimit: 5  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid  podChaos:    action: pod-kill    mode: one                                   # one random engine each time    selector:      namespaces: [rl-rehearsal]      labelSelectors: { app: rollout-engine }---apiVersion: chaos-mesh.org/v1alpha1kind: NetworkChaosmetadata:  name: slow-verifier  namespace: rl-rehearsalspec:  action: delay  mode: all  selector:    namespaces: [rl-rehearsal]    labelSelectors: { app: verifier-math }  delay: { latency: "2s", jitter: "500ms" }     # does back-pressure hold?  duration: "20m"
Going deeper2 points
  • Untested recovery paths don't work: any recovery path that hasn't run in the last month is assumed broken until a rehearsal proves otherwise.
  • The failure ledger drives investment: the top three causes of lost goodput each quarter get engineering time; everything else waits.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, measure: goodput, failure ledger, per-phase recovery timing, node health history.
  • Phase 2, contain: timeouts and fallbacks on every trainer dependency, reward circuit breakers, rollout retries and hedging, node burn-in and automatic drain.
  • Phase 3, recover fast: asynchronous whole-state checkpointing with verification, hot spares, peer checkpoint loading, JobSet failure policies, verified weight sync.
  • Phase 4, harden: straggler and silent-corruption detection, per-step trainer recovery at the largest scales, regular fault injection and game days.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Hot spares cost GPUs that sit idle most of the time, in exchange for minutes-long restarts.
  • Deep health checks and canaries use capacity on every node and engine, in exchange for catching silent failures.
  • Per-step recovery adds complexity in the trainer and coordination; used only where restart cost justifies it.
  • Fault injection breaks things on purpose, in rehearsal namespaces only, in exchange for knowing that recovery works.

Open questions.

  • Silent corruption at scale: how much periodic verification is enough, and what does it cost?
  • Per-step recovery with expert and pipeline parallelism: replica-group recovery works best for data parallelism; how far can it extend to other parallel dimensions?
  • Predictive maintenance: can node telemetry predict failures early enough to drain nodes before they fail a run?
  • Cross-cluster resilience: should one RL run span clusters so a cluster-level failure only slows it down?
Design 15 · 12 sections

Design 15: Evaluation and benchmarking infrastructure

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Three questions, one platform
  3. Suite definitions and the harness
  4. Running evals at scale
  5. The results store and lineage
  6. Measuring model progress
  7. Training throughput benchmarks
  8. Inference throughput and latency benchmarks
  9. Uptime and availability
  10. Regression detection and benchmark CI
  11. The platform on Kubernetes and reporting
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we build infrastructure that measures three things continuously and consistently: how much the models are improving (progress), how fast training and inference run (throughput), and how reliably training and serving stay up (uptime)? Design 12 covers the statistics for comparing runs, Design 10 covers verifier quality, and Design 14 covers what makes training reliable. This design is the measurement platform underneath them: suite definitions, eval execution at scale, the results store, performance benchmarks, uptime SLOs and regression detection.

The short version: one definition, one runner, one store per kind of measurement. Every eval suite and benchmark is a versioned definition (data, prompts, sampling, scorer, hardware); one scheduler runs them on shared capacity with caching; every result lands in one store with full lineage, per question or per request. Model progress, training throughput, inference throughput and uptime each have a small set of agreed metrics, measured the same way every time, and benchmark CI catches regressions from model changes and from software or hardware upgrades alike.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. On Monday, three dashboards disagree: the research tracker shows the new checkpoint 2 points better on reasoning, the release dashboard shows it 1 point worse (different prompt template), and the eval took three days because it waited behind training jobs. The serving team reports 2,300 tokens per second per GPU from a benchmark nobody else can reproduce; a driver upgrade quietly cost 12% of training throughput two weeks ago; and the platform's 99.9% uptime report disagrees with users' experience of two outages.

What the platform must do.

  • One definition per measurement: a suite or benchmark means exactly one thing, versioned, wherever it's run.
  • Fast, cheap evals: results for a new checkpoint within hours, not days, at predictable cost.
  • Full lineage: every number traceable to the model, data, code, harness and hardware that produced it.
  • Performance as a first-class measurement: training and inference throughput benchmarked the same way across models, versions and hardware.
  • Honest uptime: availability measured from the user's side for serving and as goodput for training.
  • Catch regressions automatically: from model changes, eval changes and infrastructure changes.

Out of scope: statistical methods (Design 12), verifier design (Design 10), production traffic monitoring beyond uptime SLIs.

Three questions, one platform

Scenario. Research, infrastructure and serving teams each built their own measurement tooling. The tools overlap in function and disagree in results.

What the picture shows. The three kinds of measurement, what each one measures and who uses it.

1Model progress
capability, behavior and safety eval suites run on checkpoints and release candidates. Used by researchers, release gates and leadership.
2Throughput
training performance (tokens per second per GPU, model FLOPs utilization, step time) and inference performance (time to first token, inter-token latency, throughput at a latency target). Used by infrastructure, serving and capacity planning.
3Uptime
serving availability measured as SLIs from the user's side, and training availability measured as goodput. Used by on-call, platform owners and customers.
4Shared foundation
a definition registry, a scheduler on shared GPU capacity, a results store with lineage, and benchmark CI. Built once, used by all three.
Going deeper2 points
  • Separate the question from the tool: "is the new checkpoint better?" and "did the driver upgrade slow us down?" share the same machinery (definitions, runs, comparisons against a baseline), even though the metrics differ.
  • Each metric has an owner: who defines it, who approves changes to its definition, and who is paged when it regresses.

Suite definitions and the harness

Scenario. The reasoning score differed by 3 points between two dashboards because one used a chat template with a system prompt and the other didn't. Both were labeled "math-hard".

What the picture shows. Everything that determines an eval result, captured in one versioned definition.

1Data
the exact dataset version and split, with a content hash.
2Prompting
template, system prompt, few-shot examples, chat formatting, tool definitions.
3Sampling
temperature, top-p, number of samples per question, maximum tokens, stop sequences, seeds.
4Scoring
the verifier or judge and its version (Design 10), the metric (pass@1, pass@k, accuracy) and the aggregation (per-question mean, clusters).
5Harness version
the eval code itself, pinned by image digest.
6Any change makes a new version
"math-hard@v5" always means the same thing; dashboards say which version they show.

The YAML. A suite definition in the registry.

# suites/math-hard/v5.yamlsuite: math-hardversion: 5owner: team-reasoningdata:  source: datasets://math-hard-heldout@v3  sha256: 9b1e4c...  split: test  questions: 1200  clusters: problem_family              # for clustered standard errors (Design 12)prompt:  template: templates/math-cot@v2        # includes the final-answer contract  system: null  few_shot: 0sampling: { temperature: 0.6, top_p: 0.95, samples: 8, max_tokens: 16384, seed: 1234 }scoring:  verifier: math-final-answer@3.2.0  metric: pass@1                         # mean over 8 samples  report: [pass@1, pass@8, abstain_rate]harness: registry.example.com/evals/harness@sha256:41aa...cost_estimate: { gpu_hours_per_70b: 3.1 }
Going deeper2 points
  • Templates belong to the model family: the same suite runs with each model's own chat template; the definition references "the model's template", resolved and recorded at run time.
  • Deprecate, don't edit: when a suite saturates or has label errors, a new version replaces it; the old version stays runnable so historical results remain comparable.

Running evals at scale

Scenario. A release candidate needs 40 suites, each with several samples per question: about 2 million generations. Run naively, one suite at a time on one node, it takes three days.

What the picture shows. How the scheduler turns "evaluate this checkpoint" into fast, cheap work.

1Fan-out
each (checkpoint, suite) is split into shards of questions; shards run in parallel.
2Shared inference servers
shards send requests to vLLM servers for the checkpoint, sized to the work, instead of each shard loading the model itself.
3Generation cache
generations are cached by a key of (model weights hash, prompt, sampling settings, seed); re-scoring with a new verifier or re-running a dashboard doesn't regenerate.
4Priorities
release-candidate evals preempt routine checkpoint evals; both borrow idle GPUs from training queues at lower priority (Design 02).
5Retries and partial results
failed shards are retried; results stream in, so partial scores are visible early with their uncertainty.

The code. A shard worker: cached generation against a shared server, then scoring (Python).

import hashlib, json, asyncio, httpx def cache_key(weights_sha: str, prompt: str, sampling: dict, sample_idx: int) -> str:    raw = json.dumps([weights_sha, prompt, sampling, sample_idx], sort_keys=True)    return hashlib.sha256(raw.encode()).hexdigest()                     # same inputs → same key async def run_shard(questions, suite, model, cache, scorer, server_url, concurrency=64):    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency)    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=900) as client:        async def one(q, i):            key = cache_key(model["weights_sha"], q["prompt"], suite["sampling"], i)            text = cache.get(key)            if text is None:                async with sem:                    r = await client.post(f"{server_url}/v1/completions", json={                        "model": model["name"], "prompt": q["prompt"], "seed": suite["sampling"]["seed"] + i,                        **{k: v for k, v in suite["sampling"].items() if k not in ("samples", "seed")}})                    r.raise_for_status()                    text = r.json()["choices"][0]["text"]                cache.put(key, text)            res = scorer.verify(q, text)            return {"qid": q["id"], "sample": i, "score": res.score, "verdict": res.verdict, "cache_key": key}        jobs = [one(q, i) for q in questions for i in range(suite["sampling"]["samples"])]        return await asyncio.gather(*jobs)
Going deeper2 points
  • Determinism isn't guaranteed: batched inference can change outputs slightly even with fixed seeds. Store generations; recomputing is not the same as re-reading.
  • Cost per suite is tracked: GPU hours per suite per model size, so suites that cost more than they inform can be trimmed.

The results store and lineage

Scenario. A leadership slide quotes "71.4" for a model. Nobody can find which checkpoint, suite version or harness produced it.

What the picture shows. One store for all measurements, with the lineage that makes every number traceable.

1Granularity
evals per question and sample; inference benchmarks per request; training benchmarks per step; uptime per probe or per minute of SLI data.
2Lineage on every row
model or checkpoint ID and weights hash, suite or benchmark definition version, harness image digest, hardware type and count, software versions (driver, CUDA, framework), run ID.
3Columnar format
stored as partitioned Parquet (or a table format on top of it), so per-question analysis and dashboard aggregation read the same data.
4Derived tables
aggregates (scores with intervals, throughput curves, SLO compliance) computed from the raw rows by versioned jobs; dashboards read only derived tables.
5Immutability
rows are never edited; corrections are new rows with a new definition or scorer version.

The code. Writing eval rows with lineage as partitioned Parquet (Python, PyArrow).

import pyarrow as pa, pyarrow.parquet as pq SCHEMA = pa.schema([    ("run_id", pa.string()), ("checkpoint", pa.string()), ("weights_sha", pa.string()),    ("suite", pa.string()), ("suite_version", pa.int32()), ("harness_digest", pa.string()),    ("verifier", pa.string()), ("qid", pa.string()), ("cluster", pa.string()),    ("sample", pa.int16()), ("score", pa.float32()), ("verdict", pa.string()),    ("gen_cache_key", pa.string()), ("hardware", pa.string()), ("ts", pa.timestamp("s")),]) def write_results(rows: list[dict], root="s3://evals/results"):    table = pa.Table.from_pylist(rows, schema=SCHEMA)    pq.write_to_dataset(table, root_path=root,                        partition_cols=["suite", "suite_version", "checkpoint"])   # fast per-suite reads
Going deeper2 points
  • Every published number has a link: dashboards and reports render numbers with a link to the query that produced them.
  • Keep generations separately: generation text lives in object storage keyed by cache key; rows reference it, so the store stays small enough to query quickly.

Measuring model progress

Scenario. The team's flagship benchmark rose from 55% to 89% in a year. Half the remaining errors turn out to be label mistakes, and the top three models are within noise of each other. The benchmark no longer measures progress.

What the picture shows. Tracking progress over time, and checking that the evals can still measure it.

1Progress views
each family's score over checkpoints and releases, with intervals (Design 12); a capability index that combines families with stated weights, alongside the per-family scores.
2Held-out and public
private held-out suites (never trained on, rarely shown) next to public benchmarks; a gap that grows between them suggests contamination or overfitting to public benchmarks.
3Eval health
saturation (scores near the ceiling), discriminative power (can the suite separate models that differ?), label error rate (sampled human review of disagreements between strong models and labels), and contamination checks against training data.
4Suite lifecycle
new suites enter as experimental, become official once their health is measured, and retire when saturated.

The code. Eval health checks from the results store: saturation and how well a suite separates recent checkpoints (Python).

import numpy as np def suite_health(scores_by_model: dict[str, np.ndarray], ceiling=1.0):    """scores_by_model: model -> per-question mean scores on the same questions."""    models = sorted(scores_by_model, key=lambda m: scores_by_model[m].mean())    means = np.array([scores_by_model[m].mean() for m in models])    headroom = ceiling - means.max()                                   # saturation    separable = 0    for a, b in zip(models, models[1:]):                               # adjacent models        d = scores_by_model[b] - scores_by_model[a]        se = d.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(d))        separable += d.mean() > 2 * se    return {"best": round(means.max(), 3), "headroom": round(headroom, 3),            "adjacent_pairs_separated": f"{separable}/{len(models) - 1}"}   # low → retire or replace
Going deeper2 points
  • Saturation hides regressions too: near the ceiling, a real regression may look like noise; keep harder versions of saturated suites.
  • Label audits are cheap: reviewing the questions every strong model gets "wrong" finds most label errors with little effort.

Training throughput benchmarks

Scenario. After a routine driver upgrade, training throughput dropped 12%. It was found two weeks later, in a cost report, because the production run's slowdown was blamed on "the new data mix."

What the picture shows. Standard training benchmarks that make throughput comparable across time, hardware and software.

1Standard workloads
a small set of fixed training jobs (for example, a dense 8B and a MoE model at fixed parallelism and sequence length), run for a few hundred steps after warm-up.
2Metrics
tokens per second per GPU, model FLOPs utilization (MFU: achieved model FLOPs over hardware peak), step time and its breakdown (compute, communication, data loading), memory headroom.
3Matrix
each benchmark across hardware types and the software stack (driver, CUDA, NCCL, PyTorch, framework versions).
4Triggers
every software or image change to the training stack, every new hardware pool, and nightly on a reference pool.
5Production comparison
the production run's own throughput is compared with the benchmark on the same hardware and stack; a gap means the run (data, config) is the cause, not the platform.

The code. MFU from measured throughput for a dense transformer (Python).

def mfu(tokens_per_s_per_gpu: float, n_params: float, n_layers: int, seq_len: int, d_model: int,        peak_flops_per_gpu: float) -> float:    """Model FLOPs utilization: training FLOPs per token ≈ 6N + 12·L·s·d (attention), forward + backward."""    flops_per_token = 6 * n_params + 12 * n_layers * seq_len * d_model    return tokens_per_s_per_gpu * flops_per_token / peak_flops_per_gpu # 8B dense model, 8K sequence, BF16 dense peak ~989 TFLOP/s on H100 SXMprint(f"{mfu(4300, 8.0e9, 32, 8192, 4096, 989e12):.1%}")
Going deeper2 points
  • MFU and goodput answer different questions: MFU measures how efficiently a step runs; goodput (Design 14) measures how much of the reserved time produced steps. Report both.
  • Benchmark the RL loop too: for RL, also benchmark rollout throughput, weight-sync time and reward latency at fixed settings (Design 07).

Inference throughput and latency benchmarks

Scenario. The serving team reports 2,300 tokens per second per GPU. The capacity team measures 900. Both are right: one measured at maximum batch with no latency limit, the other at the product's latency target with real prompt lengths.

What the picture shows. Measuring inference performance as a curve, not a single number.

1Metrics
time to first token (TTFT), inter-token latency or time per output token, end-to-end latency, requests and tokens per second, and their percentiles.
2Load sweep
run at increasing request rates; plot throughput against latency. Throughput only means something together with the latency at which it was measured.
3Throughput at the SLO
the headline number is the highest throughput at which p95 TTFT and p95 inter-token latency stay within the product's targets.
4Realistic traffic
prompt and output length distributions from production (or a replay), shared prefixes, multi-turn conversations; not uniform synthetic lengths.
5Same tool, same configs
a standard, model-server-agnostic load generator such as the Kubernetes community's Inference Perf (which supports vLLM, SGLang and other servers, and real or synthetic datasets) run from the same configs by every team.

The YAML. An Inference Perf load sweep against a serving deployment, run as a Kubernetes Job.

apiVersion: v1kind: ConfigMapmetadata: { name: perf-chat-70b, namespace: benchmarks }data:  config.yml: |    api: { type: chat, streaming: true }    data:      type: shareGPT                   # realistic conversation lengths; or a production replay    load:      type: constant      stages:                          # sweep request rates; 3 minutes each      - { rate: 5,  duration: 180 }      - { rate: 10, duration: 180 }      - { rate: 20, duration: 180 }      - { rate: 40, duration: 180 }    server:      type: vllm      model_name: assistant-70b-rc3      base_url: http://assistant-70b-rc3.serving.svc:8000    report:      request_lifecycle: { summary: true, per_stage: true, per_request: true }    storage:      google_cloud_storage: { bucket_name: perf-results, path: chat-70b/rc3 }---apiVersion: batch/v1kind: Jobmetadata: { name: perf-chat-70b-rc3, namespace: benchmarks }spec:  backoffLimit: 0  template:    spec:      restartPolicy: Never      containers:      - name: inference-perf        image: quay.io/inference-perf/inference-perf:latest   # pin by digest in practice        args: ["--config_file", "/cfg/config.yml"]        volumeMounts: [ { name: cfg, mountPath: /cfg } ]        resources: { limits: { cpu: "8", memory: 16Gi } }      volumes: [ { name: cfg, configMap: { name: perf-chat-70b } } ]
Going deeper2 points
  • The load generator can be the bottleneck: check its own CPU and network use; at high rates run several generator pods.
  • Benchmark the whole path: include the gateway and router in some runs (Design 03); the server alone and the full path give different, both useful, numbers.

Uptime and availability

Scenario. The platform reported 99.9% uptime for the month: every pod was running. Users experienced two outages: one where the gateway returned errors for 25 minutes while pods were healthy, and one where latency was ten times normal for an hour.

What the picture shows. Measuring uptime as users and training runs experience it.

1Serving SLIs
the fraction of requests that succeed and meet the latency target, measured at the gateway (real traffic) and by synthetic probes from outside the cluster (catches total outages with no traffic).
2SLOs and error budgets
for example, 99.5% of requests good over 30 days; the budget is the allowed bad fraction, and burn-rate alerts fire when it's being used up too fast.
3Training availability
goodput per run and the failure ledger (Design 14); "the cluster was up" isn't training uptime.
4Eval and benchmark availability
the measurement platform has its own SLO (results for a release candidate within N hours), since slow evals delay every decision.
5Reports from the same data
monthly uptime reports are computed from the SLI data, not from component health.

The YAML. Recording and alerting rules for a serving SLO with multi-window burn-rate alerts (Prometheus Operator).

apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1kind: PrometheusRulemetadata: { name: chat-api-slo, namespace: monitoring }spec:  groups:  - name: chat-api-sli    rules:    - record: sli:chat_good_ratio:rate5m                   # good = success AND under latency target      expr: |        sum(rate(gateway_requests_total{route="chat",code!~"5.."}[5m])            - rate(gateway_requests_slow_total{route="chat",threshold="ttft_2s"}[5m]))        / sum(rate(gateway_requests_total{route="chat"}[5m]))    - record: sli:chat_good_ratio:rate1h      expr: |        sum(rate(gateway_requests_total{route="chat",code!~"5.."}[1h])            - rate(gateway_requests_slow_total{route="chat",threshold="ttft_2s"}[1h]))        / sum(rate(gateway_requests_total{route="chat"}[1h]))  - name: chat-api-burn    rules:    - alert: ChatSLOFastBurn                                 # 99.5% SLO → budget 0.005      expr: |        (1 - sli:chat_good_ratio:rate5m) > (14.4 * 0.005)        and (1 - sli:chat_good_ratio:rate1h) > (14.4 * 0.005)   # burning 2% of budget per hour      for: 2m      labels: { severity: page }
Going deeper2 points
  • Synthetic probes catch silent outages: when the gateway is down, there may be no failed requests to count; an external probe every 30 seconds sees it.
  • Latency is part of availability: a 10× slower response is an outage for an interactive product; it counts against the SLO.

Regression detection and benchmark CI

Scenario. Every upgrade of vLLM, PyTorch or the GPU driver is "probably fine." Nobody runs the benchmarks before rollout because they take a day to set up.

What the picture shows. Benchmarks wired into change management.

1Triggers
a new model checkpoint (evals), a change to the serving or training image (performance benchmarks), a new hardware pool (both), and a nightly schedule (all, on reference hardware).
2Baselines
each benchmark compares with the rolling baseline for the same definition and hardware, using its known run-to-run variation.
3Gates
image changes can't roll out to production pools if a benchmark regresses beyond its threshold; model releases need the eval gate (Design 11).
4Trend detection
slow drifts (a 1% loss per week) are caught by change-point detection on the nightly series, not by single comparisons.
5Triage
a regression opens an issue with the diff between the two runs' lineage (what changed in model, image, driver, hardware).

The code. Comparing a new benchmark result with its rolling baseline using a robust threshold (Python).

import numpy as np def check_regression(history: list[float], new: float, higher_is_better=True,                     k: float = 4.0, min_rel: float = 0.02):    """history: recent results for the same benchmark + hardware + definition."""    h = np.asarray(history[-20:])    med = np.median(h)    mad = np.median(np.abs(h - med)) * 1.4826 + 1e-9                     # robust spread    delta = (new - med) if higher_is_better else (med - new)    regressed = delta < -max(k * mad, min_rel * abs(med))                # beyond noise AND material    return {"baseline": round(med, 2), "new": round(new, 2), "rel_change": round(delta / med, 4),            "regressed": bool(regressed)} print(check_regression([4310, 4295, 4322, 4301, 4318, 4290, 4307], 3790))   # driver upgrade: −12%
Going deeper2 points
  • Benchmarks need their own variance estimates: some are stable to 0.5%, others vary by 5% run to run; one threshold for all produces either noise or blindness.
  • Pin the benchmark itself: the benchmark harness and its configs are versioned; a change to the benchmark resets the baseline explicitly.

The platform on Kubernetes and reporting

Scenario. Measurements exist, but each audience reads a different spreadsheet. Leadership wants one page per week; on-call wants live SLOs; researchers want per-question drill-down.

What the picture shows. The components and the views built on them.

1Definition registry
eval suites, training and inference benchmarks, SLOs, all versioned with owners.
2Measurement scheduler
turns triggers into Kueue-managed jobs (sharded evals, benchmark jobs) on borrowed or reserved capacity; manages vLLM servers for evals and the generation cache.
3Collectors
Prometheus for SLIs and live metrics, benchmark tools writing raw results, eval shards writing per-question rows.
4Results store and derived tables
Parquet with lineage; versioned aggregation jobs.
5Views
a research view (per-question drill-down, comparisons with intervals), an infrastructure view (throughput matrices, regression history), an operations view (SLOs, error budgets, goodput) and a weekly report generated from derived tables.
Going deeper2 points
  • Generated reports, not hand-made ones: the weekly report is a template filled from derived tables, with each number linked to its query; hand-edited numbers are where disagreements start.
  • Measurement has a budget: evals and benchmarks get a fixed share of GPU capacity, and the platform reports what each suite and benchmark costs, so the budget is spent on what informs decisions.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, definitions and store: suite and benchmark registry, per-question and per-request results with lineage, one dashboard per audience reading derived tables.
  • Phase 2, scale: the sharded eval scheduler with shared inference servers, generation cache and priorities; release-candidate evals within hours.
  • Phase 3, performance and uptime: standard training and inference benchmarks with hardware and software matrices; serving SLIs, synthetic probes, SLOs and burn-rate alerts.
  • Phase 4, CI and health: benchmark gates on image and model changes, change-point detection on nightly series, eval health and suite lifecycle.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Versioned definitions slow down quick changes: a new prompt template means a new suite version and a new baseline, in exchange for numbers that mean the same thing everywhere.
  • Benchmark CI delays upgrades by hours, in exchange for not discovering a 12% slowdown in a cost report.
  • User-side uptime looks worse than component uptime, and is the number that matches what users experience.
  • Measurement capacity is reserved, so some GPUs aren't training; the measurement SLO justifies it.

Open questions.

  • Cheaper evals: how small can a suite be (via question selection) while keeping its ranking of models?
  • Evaluating agents: long, stateful agent evals need environments and much more compute per question (Design 08); how should they be scheduled and cached?
  • Comparable performance across generations: how to compare throughput across very different model architectures and hardware fairly?
  • Production signals as evals: which production metrics (user ratings, retries, abandonment) are reliable enough to sit beside offline evals in progress views?
Design 16 · 12 sections

Design 16: Data collection and feedback pipelines: from human signal to reward models to training

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. The feedback loop
  3. Kinds of human signal
  4. What to ask: active sampling
  5. Campaigns: task design and guidelines
  6. Rater quality and label quality
  7. Production feedback
  8. Training reward models
  9. Evaluating and calibrating reward models
  10. Using the signal in training, without over-optimizing
  11. Governance and the platform on Kubernetes
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we build the data collection and feedback pipelines that close the loop between human signal, reward modeling and training, so that what people prefer reliably turns into better models, week after week? Design 10 covers rewards that can be checked automatically; this design covers the rewards that come from people: preference comparisons, ratings, edits and production feedback, and the reward models trained on them. It connects to Design 06 (how preferences and reward models are used in training), Design 11 (mixtures and gates) and Design 15 (measurement).

The short version: treat human signal as the scarcest and most expensive data in the system, and spend it where the model is most uncertain. Collection is organized as campaigns with versioned task definitions, guidelines and quality controls. Every label carries its rater, guideline version and quality scores, so bad labels can be found and re-weighted later. Active sampling chooses what to ask people: comparisons where the reward model is unsure, new domains and the current policy's own outputs. Reward models are trained, evaluated and calibrated against fresh human labels before use, and monitored for over-optimization during training. Production feedback flows back with consent, privacy filtering and bias correction. And the whole loop runs on a fixed cadence, so each model generation is trained on feedback about the previous one.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. The team collects 40,000 preference comparisons a month from a vendor. Six months in: inter-rater agreement is 63% and nobody knows which raters are reliable; half the comparisons are between two answers from last year's model; the reward model prefers longer answers by a wide margin; RL against it improved the reward model's score by 30% while human win rate barely moved; and millions of thumbs-up and thumbs-down events from the product sit unused because nobody is sure they can be used.

What the platform must do.

  • Collect the right signal: decide which kinds of human feedback to collect for which goals, and what to ask about.
  • Control quality: measure rater reliability and label quality continuously, and use that in training.
  • Spend the budget well: direct labeling effort to the comparisons that improve the reward model most.
  • Build trustworthy reward models: trained on versioned data, evaluated on fresh human labels, calibrated, and checked for known biases.
  • Use production signal responsibly: with consent, privacy protection and correction for the biases of implicit feedback.
  • Close the loop on a cadence: each training round uses feedback on the current model, not the model from months ago.

Out of scope: automatic verifiers (Design 10) and the RL algorithms that consume rewards (Designs 06–09).

The feedback loop

Scenario. The data team, the reward-model team and the training team each run their part on their own schedule. A training run in May used a reward model trained in February on comparisons collected in December, about a model that no longer existed.

What the picture shows. The loop from human signal to a deployed model and back, and the latency of each step.

1Sample
choose prompts and pairs of responses from the current policy (and candidates) to show people.
2Collect
raters compare, rate or edit, following versioned guidelines; production users give explicit and implicit feedback.
3Curate
quality control, de-duplication, privacy filtering, and assembly into versioned preference datasets.
4Model
train and evaluate reward models; for some uses, the preferences go directly into DPO-style training.
5Train
RL against the reward model or preference optimization; gates before release (Design 11).
6Deploy and observe
production feedback and evals on the new model feed the next round.
7Cadence
a fixed cycle (for example, two weeks) with explicit freshness targets: most comparisons used in a round are about the current model.
Going deeper2 points
  • Staleness matters for human data too: comparisons between two outputs from an old model teach the reward model about mistakes the current model no longer makes (Design 09 for the same idea in RL data).
  • Each step has an owner and a latency target: the loop is only as fast as its slowest step, usually collection or reward-model evaluation.

Kinds of human signal

Scenario. The team asks raters for 1–7 quality ratings because they're quick. The ratings drift from week to week, and two raters' "5" mean different things. Pairwise comparisons of the same responses are far more consistent.

What the picture shows. The main kinds of human signal, what each is good for and what it costs.

1Pairwise preferences
"which response is better?", optionally with a strength and a reason. Consistent across raters; the standard input for reward models and DPO.
2Rubric ratings
yes/no or graded answers to specific criteria (correct, follows instructions, safe, concise). More informative than one overall score; good for diagnosing which property differs.
3Edits and corrections
a rater rewrites a response to be good. Expensive, but yields high-quality demonstrations and a natural preference pair (edited over original).
4Demonstrations
experts write the response from scratch. The most expensive; used for new capabilities and SFT.
5Production signal
thumbs up or down, regenerations, copies, edits, abandoned conversations. Cheap and plentiful; noisy, biased and subject to consent and privacy rules.

The signals at a glance.

Signal Cost per item Consistency Best for Main risk
Pairwise preference Low High Reward models, DPO Ties and weak preferences
Rubric ratings Medium Medium–high Diagnosis, multi-objective rewards Rubric drift
Edits High High Demonstrations + pairs Rater style imprinting
Demonstrations Highest Varies New capabilities, SFT Cost, rater skill
Production feedback Very low Low Coverage, real usage Bias, privacy, consent
Going deeper2 points
  • Collect reasons with preferences: a short reason or rubric tags on each comparison make the reward model debuggable and let you build per-property reward models later.
  • Match signal to expertise: coding and medical comparisons need domain experts; general helpfulness can use broader pools. Route tasks by required skill.

What to ask: active sampling

Scenario. Most of the monthly budget goes to comparisons where the reward model is already 95% confident and right. They add almost nothing. Meanwhile the reward model has never seen comparisons from the new agentic tool-use feature.

What the picture shows. Strategies for choosing which prompts and pairs go to human raters.

1Uncertainty
pairs where an ensemble of reward models disagrees, or where the predicted preference is near 50%.
2On-policy pairs
responses from the current policy (and from candidate checkpoints), so labels describe the mistakes the model makes now.
3Coverage
quotas per domain, language and feature, including new features with no data yet.
4Disagreement with other signals
pairs where the reward model disagrees with verifiers, judges or production feedback.
5Random slice
a fixed share sampled uniformly, to measure the reward model's accuracy without selection bias.
6Budget split
the mix of these strategies is a configuration of the campaign, reviewed each round.

The code. Selecting comparisons by reward-model ensemble disagreement, with per-domain quotas and a random slice (Python).

import numpy as np def pref_prob(rm, prompt, a, b) -> float:    """P(a preferred over b) under a Bradley–Terry reward model."""    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(rm.score(prompt, a) - rm.score(prompt, b)))) def select_pairs(candidates, ensemble, quotas: dict, random_share=0.15, seed=0):    """candidates: dicts with domain, prompt, a, b. Returns pairs to send to raters."""    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)    scored = []    for c in candidates:        p = np.array([pref_prob(rm, c["prompt"], c["a"], c["b"]) for rm in ensemble])        uncertainty = p.std() + (0.5 - abs(p.mean() - 0.5))       # disagreement + closeness to 50%        scored.append((uncertainty, c))    chosen = []    for domain, n in quotas.items():        pool = [x for x in scored if x[1]["domain"] == domain]        n_rand = int(n * random_share)        top = sorted(pool, key=lambda x: -x[0])[: n - n_rand]        rest = [x for x in pool if x not in top]        rand = [rest[i] for i in rng.choice(len(rest), size=min(n_rand, len(rest)), replace=False)]        chosen += [dict(c, selection="uncertainty") for _, c in top]        chosen += [dict(c, selection="random") for _, c in rand]           # unbiased accuracy estimate    return chosen
Going deeper2 points
  • Record why each pair was selected: the selection strategy is a column; reward-model accuracy is reported on the random slice, since uncertainty-selected pairs are hard by construction.
  • Don't over-mine hard pairs: many ambiguous pairs are ambiguous for people too; low agreement on a slice means the guideline, not the model, needs work.

Campaigns: task design and guidelines

Scenario. A vendor batch came back with 71% of comparisons marked "tie". The guideline said to mark a tie "when both answers are acceptable." Almost everything was acceptable.

What the picture shows. What a collection campaign defines before any rater sees a task.

1Task type and UI
side-by-side comparison with randomized order, rubric questions, optional edit box, and a required short reason.
2Guidelines
versioned, with worked examples and explicit rules for hard cases (both wrong, both fine but different, partially correct, unsafe content).
3Scale design
preference strength (for example, "much better / better / slightly better / tie") with ties discouraged and defined narrowly.
4Rater pool and routing
required expertise, languages and qualifications per task.
5Quality controls
gold questions, overlap for agreement, time limits and attention checks.
6Volume, deadline and budget,
and the sampling configuration from the previous section.

The YAML. A campaign definition, versioned like a suite or a recipe.

# campaigns/2026-11-coding-agent/campaign.yamlcampaign: coding-agent-prefs-2026-11owner: team-feedbacktask:  type: pairwise  ui: side_by_side  randomize_order: true                       # position bias control  scale: [much_better, better, slightly_better, tie]  tie_rule: "only when neither response is better on any rubric item"  rubric: [correct, follows_instructions, safe, concise, tool_use_appropriate]  require_reason: trueguidelines: guidelines/coding-agent@v4raters:  pool: experts-software  qualifications: [python-senior, guideline-coding@v4-quiz]sampling:  source: policies/assistant-v14-rc2 + policies/assistant-v14-rc3  strategy: { uncertainty: 0.6, coverage: 0.25, random: 0.15 }  quotas: { python: 3000, typescript: 1500, sql: 800, tool_use: 1700 }quality:  gold_rate: 0.05                             # 5% hidden gold comparisons  overlap: { rate: 0.15, raters_per_item: 3 } # for agreement  min_seconds_per_item: 45budget: { items: 7000, max_cost_usd: 84000, deadline: 2026-11-28 }
Going deeper2 points
  • Pilot every campaign: a few hundred items with internal experts first; measure agreement and tie rate, and fix the guideline before scaling.
  • Guidelines change labels: a guideline version is part of each label's lineage; mixing labels from different versions is a decision, not an accident.

Rater quality and label quality

Scenario. Agreement across all raters is 63%. When computed per rater, most agree with each other at about 75%, and four raters agree with nobody, at chance level. They had been labeling 18% of the data.

What the picture shows. Measuring and using label quality at the level of individual raters and items.

1Gold questions
comparisons with expert-agreed answers, mixed in without marking; accuracy per rater over time.
2Agreement
overlap items labeled by several raters; agreement per rater with the majority, and per slice.
3Behavior signals
time per item, position preference (always picking the left response), tie rate, reason length.
4Rater reliability weights
estimated from gold accuracy and agreement (or a latent-class model such as Dawid–Skene) and stored on each label.
5Actions
retrain or remove unreliable raters; down-weight or relabel their past items; route hard slices to experts.

The code. Per-rater gold accuracy, agreement with the majority and position bias (Python, pandas).

import pandas as pd def rater_report(labels: pd.DataFrame, gold: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:    """labels: item_id, rater, choice ('A'|'B'|'tie'), shown_left ('A'|'B'). gold: item_id, answer."""    g = labels.merge(gold, on="item_id")    gold_acc = (g.choice == g.answer).groupby(g.rater).mean().rename("gold_acc")    majority = labels.groupby("item_id").choice.agg(lambda s: s.mode().iat[0]).rename("majority")    m = labels.join(majority, on="item_id")    multi = m.groupby("item_id").rater.transform("count") >= 3    agree = (m[multi].choice == m[multi].majority).groupby(m[multi].rater).mean().rename("agree_majority")    left = (labels.choice == labels.shown_left).groupby(labels.rater).mean().rename("picks_left")    ties = (labels.choice == "tie").groupby(labels.rater).mean().rename("tie_rate")    rep = pd.concat([gold_acc, agree, left, ties], axis=1)    rep["weight"] = (rep.gold_acc.fillna(0.5) - 0.5).clip(lower=0) * 2      # 0 at chance, 1 at perfect    return rep.sort_values("weight")
Going deeper2 points
  • Low agreement is information: if experts disagree on a slice, the preference may be genuinely subjective; consider modeling it as such (or splitting by user need) rather than forcing a single label.
  • Use weights in training: the reward model's loss weights each comparison by rater reliability and preference strength, instead of dropping data with a hard threshold.

Production feedback

Scenario. The product records millions of thumbs-up and thumbs-down events, regenerations and edits each week. The data has never been used: nobody knows which users consented, the text contains personal data, and thumbs-down mostly come from a few heavy users.

What the picture shows. Turning product events into training signal safely.

1Consent first
only conversations from users and organizations whose settings allow training use are eligible; the consent state at the time of the conversation is recorded with each event.
2Privacy filtering
PII detection and removal, removal of secrets and credentials, exclusion of sensitive categories, and aggregation or minimum-count rules before anything is shown to raters.
3Signal extraction
explicit (thumbs, ratings, written feedback) and implicit (regenerate, edit, copy, abandon); each mapped to a weak preference with a known reliability.
4Bias correction
feedback comes from a skewed subset of users and situations; reweight by user and topic, cap each user's influence, and never treat absence of feedback as approval.
5Join with model lineage
each event carries the model version, system prompt and features active at the time.
6Use mainly for selection
production signal is best used to decide what to send to raters (which conversations went wrong) and as a weak auxiliary signal, not as ground truth.

The code. A production feedback event filtered for consent and privacy before entering the pipeline (Python).

import refrom dataclasses import dataclass EMAIL = re.compile(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+")SECRET = re.compile(r"(?i)(api[_-]?key|token|password)\s*[:=]\s*\S+") @dataclassclass FeedbackEvent:    conversation_id: str    user_id_hash: str    org_training_opt_in: bool          # consent state at the time of the conversation    model_version: str    signal: str                        # thumbs_up | thumbs_down | regenerate | edit | abandon    prompt: str    response: str def admit(ev: FeedbackEvent, pii_detector, per_user_count: dict, cap_per_user=20):    if not ev.org_training_opt_in:        return None                                         # never enters the pipeline    if per_user_count.get(ev.user_id_hash, 0) >= cap_per_user:        return None                                         # limit any one user's influence    text = "\n".join([ev.prompt, ev.response])    if pii_detector.has_sensitive(text):        return None                                         # sensitive categories excluded    clean = SECRET.sub("[REDACTED]", EMAIL.sub("[EMAIL]", text))    per_user_count[ev.user_id_hash] = per_user_count.get(ev.user_id_hash, 0) + 1    return {"conversation_id": ev.conversation_id, "model_version": ev.model_version,            "signal": ev.signal, "text": clean, "weak_label_reliability": {"thumbs_down": 0.6,            "thumbs_up": 0.55, "regenerate": 0.65, "edit": 0.7, "abandon": 0.52}[ev.signal]}
Going deeper2 points
  • Privacy review is a gate, not a step: the privacy and legal owners approve each new use of production data, and the pipeline enforces their rules in code.
  • Implicit signals are confounded: a regeneration may mean a bad answer or curiosity; measure each signal's agreement with rater judgments before giving it weight.

Training reward models
