Scenario. The reward model is retrained "when someone has time," on whatever comparisons are in the bucket, with no record of which data or which raters went into which version.

What the picture shows. A reward model as a versioned artifact with explicit data and objectives.

1Data
a versioned preference dataset: chosen and rejected responses, preference strength, rater weights, selection strategy and guideline version.
2Objective
the Bradley–Terry loss on score differences, with an optional margin from preference strength and a small term that keeps rewards centered near zero.
3Base model
usually initialized from a recent policy checkpoint of similar or larger size, so the reward model understands what the policy writes.
4Ensembles
several reward models (different seeds or data subsets) give uncertainty estimates for active sampling and for detecting over-optimization.
5Per-property models
when rubric data exists, separate reward heads for correctness, safety and style can be combined with explicit weights.

The code. Training a reward model with TRL's RewardTrainer on a preference dataset with margins from preference strength (Python).

from datasets import load_datasetfrom trl import RewardConfig, RewardTrainer STRENGTH_MARGIN = {"much_better": 1.0, "better": 0.5, "slightly_better": 0.2} prefs = load_dataset("parquet", data_files="s3://feedback/prefs/assistant-v14/v7/*.parquet")["train"]prefs = prefs.filter(lambda r: r["choice"] != "tie" and r["rater_weight"] > 0.2)prefs = prefs.map(lambda r: {"margin": STRENGTH_MARGIN[r["strength"]] * r["rater_weight"]})prefs = prefs.select_columns(["chosen", "rejected", "margin"])   # conversational chosen/rejected trainer = RewardTrainer(    model="registry/assistant-v14-sft",                  # start from a recent policy checkpoint    train_dataset=prefs,    args=RewardConfig(        output_dir="/checkpoints/rm/assistant-v14-rm-v7",        max_length=8192,        center_rewards_coefficient=0.01,                 # keep rewards centered near zero        learning_rate=1e-6,        num_train_epochs=1,                              # one pass: reward models overfit fast        per_device_train_batch_size=8,        bf16=True,    ),)trainer.train()
Going deeper2 points
  • One epoch is usually enough: reward models overfit preference data quickly; more data beats more epochs.
  • Version everything together: reward model version = base checkpoint + dataset version + training config; the RL recipe pins it (Design 06).

Evaluating and calibrating reward models

Scenario. The new reward model has 78% accuracy on its validation split. In RL it pushes answers to be 40% longer, and people prefer the RL model less than before. The validation split shared the length bias of the training data.

What the picture shows. What a reward model must pass before it's used in training.

1Accuracy on fresh, random-slice human labels
per domain and language, on the current policy's outputs, not only on a split of the training data.
2Calibration
when the model says 80% preference, people agree about 80% of the time; checked with reliability curves.
3Bias probes
length (does adding padding raise the score?), sycophancy (does agreeing with the user raise it?), formatting, position, confident tone; each measured with controlled pairs.
4Agreement with other signals
verifiers where available, LLM judges and production feedback, per slice.
5Best-of-n check
pick the best of n samples with the reward model and have people compare with random samples; a reward model that doesn't improve best-of-n for people isn't ready for RL.
6Release gate
thresholds on all of the above, tied to the model version.

The code. A length-bias probe: does padding a response with neutral text raise its reward? (Python).

import numpy as np FILLER = (" To summarize, the key points above address the question."          " Let me know if you need further detail.") def length_bias(rm, items, n_fill=(1, 2, 4)):    """items: (prompt, response). Score change when neutral filler is appended."""    out = {}    for k in n_fill:        deltas = [rm.score(p, r + FILLER * k) - rm.score(p, r) for p, r in items]        out[f"+{k}x filler"] = float(np.mean(deltas))    return out                                    # should be ≈ 0 or negative; positive → length bias
Going deeper2 points
  • Bias probes become training data: controlled pairs where the padded or sycophantic response is worse can be added to the preference data to teach the reward model the right direction.
  • Re-evaluate on the RL policy's outputs: a reward model accurate on the starting policy's outputs can be inaccurate on outputs from later in RL; evaluate on fresh samples during the run.

Using the signal in training, without over-optimizing

Scenario. RL against the reward model raised its score by 30%. Human evaluation found only a small win. Pushing further made people prefer the model less.

What the picture shows. The ways preference data reaches the model, and how to stop before over-optimization.

1RL against a reward model
flexible and strong; the reward model is a proxy, and optimizing it too hard hurts the true objective. A well-known study of reward model over-optimization found that the true (gold) score first rises and then falls as optimization against a proxy reward model increases.
2Direct preference optimization
DPO-style training on the preference pairs themselves; no separate reward model, less exposed to reward hacking, but offline (pairs not from the current policy) unless refreshed every round.
3Best-of-n and rejection sampling
pick high-reward samples and train on them; simple and robust, with its own over-optimization at large n.
4Controls
a KL penalty or trust region to the starting policy, early stopping on human or held-out-judge win rate (not reward-model score), reward-model ensembles (optimize a conservative combination such as the mean minus the spread), and reward models refreshed with on-policy labels each round.

The code. A conservative reward from a reward-model ensemble for RL (Python).

import numpy as np def conservative_reward(ensemble, prompt, response, k: float = 1.0) -> float:    """Mean minus k × std across reward models: uncertain regions get less reward."""    s = np.array([rm.score(prompt, response) for rm in ensemble])    return float(s.mean() - k * s.std())          # discourages exploiting one model's quirks
Going deeper2 points
  • The stopping rule uses people: a small, fresh human win-rate evaluation every few hundred steps decides when to stop, because the reward model can't tell you when it's being over-optimized.
  • Mix in verifiable rewards: where tasks are checkable, verifiers (Design 10) anchor the policy; preference rewards cover what they can't.

Governance and the platform on Kubernetes

Scenario. A legal request asks which training runs used conversations from a particular customer. Answering takes three weeks of manual searching.

What the picture shows. The components that run the loop, and the lineage that makes it auditable.

1Sampling service
generates candidate pairs from current policies and selects them with the campaign's strategy.
2Annotation platform
internal or vendor tools behind one API: tasks out, labels back, with rater IDs, timings and guideline versions.
3Quality service
gold scoring, agreement and rater weights; flags for relabeling.
4Feedback ingestion
production events filtered for consent and privacy.
5Preference datasets
versioned, immutable snapshots with lineage to every source item (campaign, rater, conversation, consent state).
6Reward model training and evaluation
Kueue-managed jobs; the evaluation gate before any RL recipe can pin a reward model.
7Retention and deletion
source data expires per policy, and deletion requests propagate to datasets (and are recorded for models trained on them).

The YAML. The loop's recurring part as an Argo CronWorkflow: every two weeks, sample from the current policy, create the campaign, then retrain and evaluate the reward model when labels arrive.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1kind: CronWorkflowmetadata:  name: feedback-loop  namespace: feedbackspec:  schedule: "17 6 * * 1"                     # Mondays; the template skips odd weeks  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid  workflowSpec:    entrypoint: loop    templates:    - name: loop      steps:      - - name: sample          template: run          arguments: { parameters: [ { name: cmd, value: "sample --policy=current --campaign=next" } ] }      - - name: launch-campaign          template: run          arguments: { parameters: [ { name: cmd, value: "campaign launch --from=sampled --wait-labels=10d" } ] }      - - name: quality          template: run          arguments: { parameters: [ { name: cmd, value: "quality score --campaign=latest --reweight" } ] }      - - name: dataset          template: run          arguments: { parameters: [ { name: cmd, value: "dataset snapshot --consent-check --pii-check" } ] }      - - name: train-rm          template: run          arguments: { parameters: [ { name: cmd, value: "rm train --dataset=latest --ensemble=4" } ] }      - - name: eval-rm          template: run          arguments: { parameters: [ { name: cmd, value: "rm eval --gate=gates/rm-release.yaml" } ] }    - name: run      inputs: { parameters: [ { name: cmd } ] }      container:        image: registry.example.com/feedback/pipeline:2026.11        command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]        args: ["feedbackctl {{inputs.parameters.cmd}}"]
Going deeper2 points
  • Lineage answers legal questions in minutes: every preference row points to its sources and consent state; every reward model and training run points to its datasets.
  • Rater welfare and fairness are part of the platform: clear guidelines, reasonable task times, and review of content that may be disturbing, with opt-outs and support.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, lineage and quality: campaign definitions, label lineage (rater, guideline, selection), gold questions and agreement, rater weights.
  • Phase 2, on-policy loop: sampling from the current policy, active selection with a random slice, a fixed cadence.
  • Phase 3, reward model discipline: versioned reward models, the evaluation gate (fresh labels, calibration, bias probes, best-of-n), ensembles and over-optimization stopping rules.
  • Phase 4, production signal: consent and privacy filtering, bias correction, production feedback for selection and as weak signal.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • On-policy collection costs more than reusing old comparisons, in exchange for labels about the mistakes the model makes now.
  • Gold and overlap items use budget (often 15–20% of items), in exchange for knowing label quality.
  • Strict consent and privacy rules leave production data unused, in exchange for trust and compliance.
  • Human stopping rules slow RL with periodic evaluations, in exchange for not over-optimizing a proxy.

Open questions.

  • AI feedback at scale: where can model-generated preferences (judges, constitutions) replace human labels, and how is their quality checked against people?
  • Pluralistic preferences: when people genuinely disagree, should reward models predict a distribution or condition on the user?
  • Long, agentic tasks: how do people give feedback on 100-step agent trajectories (Design 08) without reading all of them?
  • Feedback value: can we estimate, before collecting, how much a batch of labels will improve the trained model?

  11. Measuring and tuning the scheduler
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we schedule a shared GPU fleet so that accelerators stay busy: distributed jobs start all at once or not at all (gang scheduling), small jobs don't fragment nodes that big jobs need (bin-packing), and many teams share the fleet fairly (quotas and fair share)? Design 02 covers the multi-cluster picture (which cluster a job goes to); this design goes inside one cluster, into the mechanics of admission, placement, preemption and measurement. For how kube-scheduler filters and scores nodes, see the scheduler deep dive; this design builds on it.

The short version: separate "when may this job start" from "where do its pods go", and measure where every GPU-hour went. Kueue decides admission: a job is admitted only when its whole gang fits its quota and, with topology-aware scheduling, the physical topology. kube-scheduler places pods with a bin-packing profile on GPU nodes, so partially used nodes fill up first and whole nodes stay free for big gangs. Teams get nominal quotas in cohorts with borrowing, lending limits and fair-share preemption; priorities and backfill keep idle quota working. And a GPU-hour accounting breaks idle time into causes (fragmented, reserved-but-idle, waiting for a gang, preempted work) so each one can be attacked.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. A 1,024-GPU cluster (128 nodes × 8 H100) serves six teams. Finance reports 58% of GPU-hours doing useful work. A 256-GPU training job has waited three days; meanwhile 180 GPUs are free, scattered as 1–3 GPUs per node across 90 nodes. Last week two 64-GPU jobs (one GPU per pod) each got 40 of their pods running and then waited for each other for six hours, holding 80 GPUs idle. One team runs notebooks on 96 GPUs that are busy 8% of the time, and another team says the queue is unfair because "the same team always gets the GPUs."

What the platform must do.

  • Start distributed jobs atomically: all pods of a gang start together, or none hold resources.
  • Keep large jobs placeable: small jobs mustn't scatter across nodes that a large job needs whole.
  • Guarantee each team a share: a nominal quota that's available when the team needs it.
  • Lend idle capacity: unused quota works for others, and is reclaimed quickly when its owner returns.
  • Be fair over time: teams that used less recently get priority for borrowed capacity.
  • Explain idle time: every idle GPU-hour attributed to a cause.

Out of scope: which cluster a job runs in (Design 02), node health (Design 14), and GPU sharing inside one device beyond its role in bin-packing.

Where GPU-hours go

Scenario. "58% utilization" is the only number anybody has. It doesn't say whether to buy GPUs, fix the scheduler or talk to the notebook team.

What the picture shows. A breakdown of all GPU-hours in a period into categories with different fixes.

1Busy
allocated and doing useful work (measured by GPU activity, not just allocation).
2Allocated but idle
pods holding GPUs while idle: notebooks, jobs stuck in data loading, services sized for peak. Fix: idle culling, right-sizing, sharing smaller slices.
3Waiting for a gang
GPUs held by some pods of a job whose other pods can't start. Fix: all-or-nothing admission.
4Fragmented
free GPUs that no pending job can use because they're scattered. Fix: bin-packing and defragmentation.
5Free and unusable by policy
quota reserved for a team that isn't using it, not lent. Fix: borrowing and lending limits.
6Lost to preemption
work computed then discarded when a job was preempted before its next checkpoint. Fix: checkpoint-aware preemption.
7Truly free
nothing pending could use it. Fix: more demand, or fewer GPUs.

The code. Classifying each GPU-minute from scheduler and DCGM data (Python sketch).

from collections import Counter def classify(gpu_minute, pending_jobs, quota_state):    """gpu_minute: dict with allocated, util (0..1, DCGM), job_state, node_free_gpus, owner_queue."""    if gpu_minute["allocated"]:        if gpu_minute["job_state"] == "waiting_for_gang":            return "waiting_for_gang"                          # some pods up, others pending        if gpu_minute["util"] < 0.05:            return "allocated_idle"        if gpu_minute.get("discarded_by_preemption"):            return "lost_to_preemption"        return "busy"    fits = [j for j in pending_jobs if j["gpus_per_pod"] <= gpu_minute["node_free_gpus"]]    if pending_jobs and not fits:        return "fragmented"                                    # free, but no pending pod fits here    if fits and not quota_state.can_admit_any(fits):        return "blocked_by_quota_policy"    return "free" def breakdown(minutes, pending_at, quota_at):    c = Counter(classify(m, pending_at(m["t"]), quota_at(m["t"])) for m in minutes)    total = sum(c.values())    return {k: round(v / total, 3) for k, v in c.most_common()}
Going deeper2 points
  • Allocation is not utilization: a GPU can be allocated and idle; DCGM activity metrics (SM activity, tensor activity) say whether it's working.
  • Report the breakdown per team and per queue: the fix for "allocated but idle" is a conversation with a team; the fix for "fragmented" is a scheduler change.

Two layers: admission and placement

Scenario. When a job is pending, users look at pod events from kube-scheduler and see "0/128 nodes are available." The real reason is that the job's queue is out of quota, which kube-scheduler doesn't know about.

What the picture shows. Who decides what, from job submission to running pods.

1Admission (Kueue)
a job is created suspended and becomes a Workload in a LocalQueue. Kueue admits it when its whole request fits the ClusterQueue's quota (possibly by borrowing), in priority and fairness order, and optionally when it fits the physical topology. Admission is all-or-nothing for the whole job.
2Placement (kube-scheduler)
once admitted, pods are created and the scheduler filters and scores nodes for each pod (scheduler deep dive). Profiles decide scoring: bin-packing for GPU pools.
3Devices (device plugin or DRA)
the node assigns specific GPUs (or slices) to the container.
4One status per layer
"pending admission: queue over quota" and "admitted, pods unschedulable" are different problems with different owners.
Going deeper2 points
  • Kueue doesn't replace kube-scheduler: Kueue decides when a workload starts and against which quota; kube-scheduler still decides which node each pod lands on. Topology-aware scheduling is the point where Kueue also looks at nodes, so that what it admits can actually be placed together.
  • Upstream is moving toward workload-aware scheduling: kube-scheduler is gaining native awareness of pod groups; the admission/placement split in this design stays valid as that matures.

Gang scheduling: all or nothing

Scenario. Two 64-GPU jobs were created at the same time. The scheduler placed pods from both as GPUs freed up: 40 pods of each ran, and neither could start training without all 64. Both held 40 GPUs idle for six hours.

What the picture shows. Why per-pod scheduling deadlocks distributed jobs, and the two mechanisms that prevent it.

1The deadlock
distributed training can't make progress with some of its workers; per-pod scheduling lets two jobs each take part of the free capacity and wait forever.
2Quota-level all-or-nothing
Kueue admits a workload only if its full request fits the quota, so two jobs can't both be admitted into capacity that only fits one.
3Physical fit (topology-aware scheduling)
quota fit doesn't guarantee node fit; TAS checks that the pods can actually be placed (and placed close together) before admitting.
4Ready-pods timeout (waitForPodsReady)
after admission, if all pods aren't ready within a timeout, the workload is evicted, its pods deleted, and it's requeued with backoff. A recovery timeout handles pods that fail later.
5Workload types that know their gang
JobSet, LeaderWorkerSet, RayJob and PyTorchJob present all their pods as one workload with PodSets.

The YAML. Kueue configuration for ready-pods gang semantics and fair sharing (Configuration v1beta2).

apiVersion: config.kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: Configurationnamespace: kueue-systemwaitForPodsReady:  timeout: 10m                         # all pods ready within 10 min of admission, or requeue  recoveryTimeout: 5m                  # a pod failing later must recover within 5 min  blockAdmission: false                # TAS handles physical fit; don't serialize admissions  requeuingStrategy:    timestamp: Eviction    backoffBaseSeconds: 60    backoffMaxSeconds: 1800    backoffLimitCount: 10              # then the workload is deactivated for a human to look atfairSharing:  preemptionStrategies: [LessThanOrEqualToFinalShare, LessThanInitialShare]
Going deeper2 points
  • Choose the timeout from data: it must cover image pulls and model loading for large jobs; measure time-to-all-ready per job size and set the timeout above its 99th percentile.
  • blockAdmission trades throughput for safety: serializing admissions avoids deadlocks without TAS, but leaves capacity idle while each job starts; with TAS checking physical fit, it's usually unnecessary.

Topology-aware gang placement

Scenario. A 64-GPU job is admitted and placed across three network blocks; its all-reduce runs 30% slower than the same job in one block. A gang that fits but is spread out wastes accelerators too.

What the picture shows. Placing a gang within the smallest network domain that fits it.

1Topology levels
zone → block → rack → host, from node labels set by the cloud provider or a topology discovery tool.
2Required vs preferred
podset-required-topology waits until one domain can hold the whole PodSet; podset-preferred-topology tries the domain and falls back to wider ones.
3Slices
for very large jobs, split the PodSet into slices (for example, 16 pods each) that must each fit one rack, without requiring the whole job in one block.
4Groups
co-locate several PodSets of one workload (leader and workers of an inference server) in the same domain.
5Interaction with bin-packing
keeping whole racks and blocks free (next section) is what makes required topology placement possible without long waits.

The YAML. A Topology, a ResourceFlavor that uses it, and a JobSet requiring one block with racks of 16 pods.

apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: Topologymetadata: { name: gpu-fabric }spec:  levels:  - nodeLabel: network.example.com/block  - nodeLabel: network.example.com/rack  - nodeLabel: kubernetes.io/hostname---apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: ResourceFlavormetadata: { name: h100-fabric }spec:  nodeLabels: { gpu.example.com/class: h100 }  topologyName: gpu-fabric                       # enables TAS for this flavor---apiVersion: jobset.x-k8s.io/v1alpha2kind: JobSetmetadata:  name: pretrain-ft-64  labels: { kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: llm-team }spec:  replicatedJobs:  - name: workers    replicas: 1    template:      spec:        parallelism: 8        completions: 8        completionMode: Indexed        template:          metadata:            annotations:              kueue.x-k8s.io/podset-required-topology: network.example.com/block      # whole job, one block              kueue.x-k8s.io/podset-slice-required-topology: network.example.com/rack              kueue.x-k8s.io/podset-slice-size: "4"                                  # 4 pods (32 GPUs) per rack          spec:            containers:            - name: trainer              image: registry.example.com/train:2026.11              resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8 } }
Going deeper2 points
  • Topology labels must be accurate: a wrong block label puts a "same block" job across the fabric. Validate labels against measured bandwidth during node burn-in (Design 14).
  • Required topology can wait forever: set a policy for how long a job may wait for its domain before it's offered a preferred (wider) placement, if its owner allows it.

Bin-packing to reduce fragmentation

Scenario. The default scoring spreads pods to the least-allocated nodes. Over a week, 1-, 2- and 4-GPU jobs land on almost every node, and no node has 8 free GPUs, though 180 GPUs are free in total.

What the picture shows. How scoring policy decides whether free GPUs end up usable or scattered.

1Spreading (least allocated)
good for CPU services' resilience; for GPUs, it scatters small jobs and destroys whole free nodes.
2Bin-packing (most allocated)
prefer the node that is already most used, so small jobs fill partly used nodes and whole nodes stay free.
3Weighted by resource
score GPU allocation most heavily, so the GPU dimension drives placement on GPU nodes.
4Separate profiles
a bin-packing scheduler profile for GPU pools, the default spreading profile for CPU services.
5Fragmentation metric
the share of free GPUs that sit on nodes with fewer than 8 free, and the largest gang that could start right now.

The YAML. A kube-scheduler profile that bin-packs GPUs (KubeSchedulerConfiguration v1).

apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1kind: KubeSchedulerConfigurationprofiles:- schedulerName: default-scheduler                 # CPU services keep spreading- schedulerName: gpu-binpack                       # GPU workloads set spec.schedulerName: gpu-binpack  pluginConfig:  - name: NodeResourcesFit    args:      scoringStrategy:        type: MostAllocated                        # prefer fuller nodes        resources:        - { name: nvidia.com/gpu, weight: 10 }     # GPUs dominate the score        - { name: cpu, weight: 1 }        - { name: memory, weight: 1 }  plugins:    score:      disabled:      - name: NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation      # balancing fights packing

The code. A fragmentation report: how much free capacity is usable by gangs of each size (Python).

def fragmentation(free_per_node: list[int], gpus_per_node: int = 8):    total_free = sum(free_per_node)    whole = sum(f for f in free_per_node if f == gpus_per_node)    report = {"free_gpus": total_free, "whole_free_nodes": whole // gpus_per_node,              "fragmented_share": round(1 - whole / total_free, 3) if total_free else 0.0}    for pod_gpus in (1, 2, 4, 8):        report[f"pods_of_{pod_gpus}_that_fit"] = sum(f // pod_gpus for f in free_per_node)    return report # 90 nodes with 1–3 free GPUs, 2 whole free nodesprint(fragmentation([2] * 60 + [1] * 15 + [3] * 15 + [8] * 2))
Going deeper2 points
  • Bin-packing has costs: packed nodes concentrate risk (a node failure hits more jobs) and can create noisy neighbours; keep packing for GPU batch work, not latency-critical services.
  • Your scheduler deep dive applies here: scoring plugins and weights interact (scheduler deep dive); test a new profile on a replay of real submissions before switching.

Defragmentation and right-sizing

Scenario. Even with bin-packing, long-running 1-GPU notebooks pin GPUs on dozens of nodes. Packing only affects new pods; the cluster needs a way to fix what's already scattered.

What the picture shows. Ways to recover whole nodes and avoid wasting whole GPUs on small work.

1Pool by job shape
a small-job pool (or partitioned GPUs) for notebooks and 1–2 GPU jobs, and a large-job pool kept for gangs of whole nodes.
2Partition GPUs for small work
MIG slices, time-slicing or MPS for notebooks and small inference, configured below Kueue with the device plugin or Dynamic Resource Allocation; the quota counts slices, not whole GPUs.
3Compaction
periodically migrate preemptible, checkpointable small jobs off sparsely used nodes (evict and requeue them), so their nodes become whole again; only when a pending gang needs whole nodes.
4Reserve whole nodes for waiting gangs
when a large job has waited beyond a threshold, stop placing small jobs on nodes that are about to become free, so the gang can start.
5Idle culling
notebooks idle beyond a limit are checkpointed and stopped (Design 03).

The code. Choosing nodes to drain to create whole nodes for a waiting gang, by fewest GPUs moved (Python).

def plan_compaction(nodes, needed_whole_nodes: int, gpus_per_node: int = 8):    """nodes: dicts with name, used_gpus, movable (all pods preemptible + checkpointable)."""    candidates = [n for n in nodes if 0 < n["used_gpus"] < gpus_per_node and n["movable"]]    candidates.sort(key=lambda n: n["used_gpus"])                  # cheapest to empty first    plan, moved = [], 0    for n in candidates:        if len(plan) == needed_whole_nodes:            break        plan.append(n["name"]); moved += n["used_gpus"]    free_elsewhere = sum(gpus_per_node - n["used_gpus"] for n in nodes if n["name"] not in plan                         and n["used_gpus"] < gpus_per_node) - moved    ok = len(plan) == needed_whole_nodes and free_elsewhere >= 0      # evicted pods must fit elsewhere    return {"drain": plan if ok else [], "gpus_moved": moved if ok else 0, "feasible": ok}
Going deeper2 points
  • Compaction costs work: evicted jobs lose progress since their last checkpoint; only move checkpointable, preemptible jobs, and only when a pending gang will use the freed nodes.
  • Partitioning changes the unit of quota: a team's quota for MIG slices is separate from its whole-GPU quota; model them as separate resources or flavors.

Quotas: nominal, borrowing and lending

Scenario. Each team had a hard limit on GPUs. The vision team's 96 GPUs sat idle on weekends while the LLM team's jobs waited, and nobody could lend them without an admin changing limits by hand.

What the picture shows. The quota model: guaranteed shares that can be lent and borrowed.

1ResourceFlavors
kinds of capacity (H100 on the fabric, H100 standalone, spot), each mapped to node labels.
2ClusterQueue per team
a nominal quota per flavor, the team's guaranteed share.
3Cohort
ClusterQueues in a cohort lend unused nominal quota to each other.
4Borrowing limit
the most a team can take beyond its nominal quota.
5Lending limit
the most of a team's unused quota others can borrow; the rest stays reserved for the team (for latency-sensitive work that must start immediately).
6Reclaim
when a team needs its nominal quota back, it can preempt borrowers (next sections).

The YAML. Two teams' ClusterQueues in one cohort, with borrowing and lending limits (v1beta2).

apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: ClusterQueuemetadata: { name: llm-team }spec:  cohortName: gpu-fleet  namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { team: llm } }  fairSharing: { weight: 2 }                     # larger share of borrowable capacity  resourceGroups:  - coveredResources: ["nvidia.com/gpu", "cpu", "memory"]    flavors:    - name: h100-fabric      resources:      - { name: nvidia.com/gpu, nominalQuota: 512, borrowingLimit: 256 }      - { name: cpu, nominalQuota: 6144 }      - { name: memory, nominalQuota: 48Ti }  preemption:    reclaimWithinCohort: Any                     # get nominal quota back from borrowers    borrowWithinCohort: { policy: LowerPriority, maxPriorityThreshold: 100 }    withinClusterQueue: LowerPriority---apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: ClusterQueuemetadata: { name: vision-team }spec:  cohortName: gpu-fleet  namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { team: vision } }  resourceGroups:  - coveredResources: ["nvidia.com/gpu", "cpu", "memory"]    flavors:    - name: h100-fabric      resources:      - { name: nvidia.com/gpu, nominalQuota: 128, lendingLimit: 96 }   # 32 always kept for vision      - { name: cpu, nominalQuota: 1536 }      - { name: memory, nominalQuota: 12Ti }  preemption:    reclaimWithinCohort: Any    withinClusterQueue: LowerPriority
Going deeper2 points
  • Nominal quotas should add up to the fleet: quotas that sum to more than the hardware promise guarantees that can't all be kept; quotas that sum to less leave capacity owned by nobody.
  • Quota counts requests, not use: a notebook holding a GPU at 8% use consumes a whole GPU of quota; idle culling and right-sizing protect the quota as much as the hardware.

Fair share: weighted shares and fairness over time

Scenario. Borrowable capacity went to whichever team submitted first after it freed up. One team with an automated sweep generator got most of it every week.

What the picture shows. Two fairness mechanisms that work at different levels.

1Fair sharing between ClusterQueues (preemption-based)
borrowable capacity in a cohort is divided by weighted share; a queue below its fair share can preempt workloads of queues above theirs, using dominant resource fairness across resources. Weights express how much each team should get of what's shared; a weight of 0 means always last.
2Admission fair sharing between LocalQueues (usage-based)
within one ClusterQueue, workloads from LocalQueues (for example, projects within a team) that used fewer resources recently are admitted first. It reorders admission and doesn't evict running work.
3Preemption strategies
Kueue's fair-sharing strategies only preempt when it moves shares toward fairness (the preemptor's share after admission must not exceed the victim's), avoiding preemption cycles.
4What fairness can't fix
if total demand inside nominal quotas exceeds the fleet, fairness only decides who waits.

The YAML. Admission fair sharing for a team's ClusterQueue with several project LocalQueues (v1beta2).

apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: ClusterQueuemetadata: { name: research-team }spec:  cohortName: gpu-fleet  namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { team: research } }  fairSharing: { weight: 1 }  admissionScope:    admissionMode: UsageBasedAdmissionFairSharing   # projects that used less go first  resourceGroups:  - coveredResources: ["nvidia.com/gpu"]    flavors:    - name: h100-fabric      resources:      - { name: nvidia.com/gpu, nominalQuota: 128, borrowingLimit: 128 }---apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: LocalQueuemetadata: { name: sweeps, namespace: research-sweeps }spec:  clusterQueue: research-team  fairSharing: { weight: 1 }                         # an automated sweep queue gets no extra weight
Going deeper2 points
  • Weights are a policy decision: write down why each team has its weight, and review weights quarterly against business priorities.
  • Show teams their share: a dashboard of each queue's share against its fair share ends most "the queue is unfair" debates with data.

Priority, preemption and backfill

Scenario. A release-candidate evaluation needed 64 GPUs immediately; all were busy with borrowed research jobs. Preempting them would discard four hours of work, because those jobs checkpointed every four hours.

What the picture shows. How urgent work gets capacity without wasting the work it displaces, and how gaps get filled.

1Workload priority classes
a small set (for example, production, release, standard, best-effort) set on workloads; Kueue orders and preempts by them, independently of pod priority.
2Preemption rules
reclaim nominal quota from borrowers, preempt lower priority within a queue, and borrow by preempting only below a priority threshold.
3Cheap preemption
preemptible work must checkpoint often (minutes, Design 14) and handle termination signals by saving state; preemption prefers victims with the most recent checkpoint.
4Backfill
while a large gang waits for whole nodes, short jobs that will finish before those nodes are needed can run in the gaps, if they declare a runtime limit (Kueue enforces a maximum execution time set on the workload).
5Guardrails
limits on how often a workload can be preempted, so best-effort jobs still finish eventually.

The YAML. Workload priority classes and a preemptible job that declares a maximum runtime for backfill (v1beta2).

apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: WorkloadPriorityClassmetadata: { name: release }value: 1000description: "Release-candidate evals and production runs"---apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: WorkloadPriorityClassmetadata: { name: best-effort }value: 10description: "Sweeps and exploration; preemptible, checkpoint every 10 minutes"---apiVersion: batch/v1kind: Jobmetadata:  name: sweep-lr-0042  namespace: research-sweeps  labels:    kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: sweeps    kueue.x-k8s.io/priority-class: best-effort    kueue.x-k8s.io/max-exec-time-seconds: "5400"      # Kueue stops it after 90 min: a known bound makes it safe to backfillspec:  parallelism: 1  completions: 1  template:    spec:      schedulerName: gpu-binpack      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120              # time to save a checkpoint on preemption      restartPolicy: Never      containers:      - name: train        image: registry.example.com/train:2026.11        resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 2 } }
Going deeper2 points
  • Preemption cost is measurable: record the work lost per preemption (time since last checkpoint × GPUs) and include it in the GPU-hour breakdown.
  • Fewer priority classes are better: every extra class is a negotiation; most fleets need four or five.

Measuring and tuning the scheduler

Scenario. A proposed change to bin-packing weights is debated for weeks. Nobody can say what it would do to queue wait times or fragmentation, because the only way to find out is to deploy it.

What the picture shows. The metrics that describe scheduling quality, and how to test changes safely.

1Efficiency
busy share of GPU-hours, the GPU-hour breakdown, fragmentation share and the largest startable gang.
2Latency
queue wait per job size class (1, 8, 64, 256+ GPUs) and per priority; time from admission to all pods ready.
3Fairness
each queue's usage against its nominal quota and fair share over time; borrowing and reclaim events.
4Disruption
preemptions per day, work lost per preemption, evictions by waitForPodsReady timeouts.
5Trace replay
record submissions (size, runtime, queue, priority) and replay them against a scheduler simulator or a small test cluster with fake nodes, to compare policies before changing production.

The code. A fairness report per queue: usage against nominal quota and fair share (Python).

def fairness(usage_gpu_h: dict, nominal: dict, weights: dict, fleet_gpu_h: float):    """usage_gpu_h: queue -> GPU-hours used; nominal: queue -> guaranteed GPU-hours; weights: queue -> weight."""    borrowable = fleet_gpu_h - sum(min(usage_gpu_h[q], nominal[q]) for q in nominal)    wsum = sum(weights.values())    rows = {}    for q in nominal:        fair = nominal[q] + borrowable * weights[q] / wsum          # nominal + weighted part of the rest        rows[q] = {"used": round(usage_gpu_h[q]), "nominal": nominal[q], "fair_share": round(fair),                   "ratio_to_fair": round(usage_gpu_h[q] / fair, 2)}   # far below 1 while waiting = unfair    return rows
Going deeper2 points
  • Report wait time by size class: a scheduler that improves average wait by starving 256-GPU jobs looks better on average and worse where it matters.
  • Change one policy at a time: packing weights, preemption rules and fair-share weights interact; replay each change separately, then together.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, measure: the GPU-hour breakdown per team and queue, fragmentation, queue wait by size class.
  • Phase 2, gangs: all workloads through Kueue; waitForPodsReady with measured timeouts; topology-aware scheduling for jobs over one node.
  • Phase 3, packing: a bin-packing profile for GPU pools, pools by job shape, GPU partitioning for small work, idle culling.
  • Phase 4, sharing: cohorts with borrowing and lending limits, fair-share weights, admission fair sharing within teams, workload priority classes, checkpoint-aware preemption, backfill and compaction.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • All-or-nothing admission can leave capacity idle while a large job waits for its whole gang; topology-aware admission and backfill reduce it.
  • Bin-packing concentrates risk on fuller nodes, in exchange for whole free nodes for large jobs.
  • Preemption discards work since the last checkpoint; frequent checkpoints are required for preemptible work.
  • Lending limits leave some capacity idle on purpose, so teams with urgent work can start immediately.

Open questions.

  • Native gang scheduling: as kube-scheduler gains workload-aware scheduling, how much of the gang logic moves from Kueue into the scheduler?
  • Elastic jobs: can training jobs grow and shrink with free capacity (Design 14's per-step recovery) so fragments become useful instead of waiting?
  • Runtime prediction: can predicted job runtimes make backfill safe without users declaring limits?
  • Cost-aware sharing: should fair share count GPU-hours equally across GPU generations, or by cost?
Design 18 · 12 sections

Design 18: A multi-cloud GPU fleet that researchers don't have to think about

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Fleet architecture
  3. Sites and capacity sources
  4. One job API for researchers
  5. Placement: choosing the site
  6. The Kubernetes execution operator
  7. The Slurm execution operator
  8. A portable environment
  9. Data and checkpoints across sites
  10. Identity, secrets and access
  11. Fleet operations: onboarding, health and cost
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we stand up a GPU fleet that spans hyperscalers, GPU-focused clouds ("neoclouds") and on-premises clusters, orchestrated through custom Kubernetes and Slurm operators, so that researchers describe what their job needs and never have to think about where it lands? Design 02 covers a hub dispatching jobs to several Kubernetes clusters, Design 05 covers the network between sites, and Design 17 covers scheduling inside one cluster. This design adds what changes when the sites are different providers with different hardware, contracts, fabrics, storage and schedulers, including Slurm.

The short version: one job API, one placement brain, many execution sites behind adapters. Researchers submit a ResearchJob (image, command, GPUs, gang shape, data, checkpoints, deadline) through one CLI. A fleet control plane keeps an inventory of every site (provider, accelerator, fabric, storage, contract and price) and a placement service picks the site that can run the job soonest at the lowest true cost, using committed capacity first. Execution operators turn the job into native work: a JobSet under Kueue on Kubernetes sites, an sbatch job through slurmrestd on Slurm sites (including Slurm running on Kubernetes via operators such as Slinky or Soperator). Portable images, per-site runtime profiles, replicated data and cross-site checkpoints make the job behave the same wherever it lands, and a conformance suite decides when a new site may join.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. A research lab's GPUs come from five places: an AWS account with capacity blocks of H100s, a Google Cloud reservation of A3 nodes, a three-year contract for 2,048 GPUs at a neocloud running managed Kubernetes, a second neocloud cluster delivered as Slurm, and an on-premises H100 cluster run by the university with Slurm. Researchers keep six sets of launch scripts, learn three schedulers and two container runtimes, and copy datasets by hand. Last quarter, the neocloud contract (paid whether used or not) averaged 61% utilization while 140 jobs queued for weeks on the on-premises cluster because "that's where the data is."

What the platform must do.

  • One way to submit: the same job definition and CLI regardless of provider or scheduler.
  • Automatic placement: the platform chooses the site; researchers state constraints (data residency, accelerator type) only when they matter.
  • Use what's paid for first: reserved and committed capacity before on-demand, without starving urgent work.
  • Same behavior everywhere: the same image, environment, data paths and checkpoint semantics on every site.
  • Move work when needed: a job interrupted at one site can resume at another from its checkpoint.
  • Onboard and retire sites safely: a new provider joins after passing tests; a contract that ends drains cleanly.
  • One view of cost, health and usage across all sites.

Out of scope: wide-area networking design (Design 05), in-cluster scheduling policy (Design 17).

Fleet architecture

Scenario. Each new provider brought its own console, scheduler and scripts. The lab needs a structure where adding a provider means adding an adapter, not teaching every researcher something new.

What the picture shows. The fleet as a control plane over heterogeneous execution sites.

1Fleet control plane
the job API and CLI, the site inventory, the placement service, policy (quotas, budgets, residency), and the execution operators. It runs in its own Kubernetes cluster, independent of any provider it schedules onto.
2Kubernetes sites
hyperscaler and neocloud managed Kubernetes clusters with Kueue; jobs arrive as JobSets (dispatched directly or through MultiKueue, Design 02).
3Slurm sites
bare-metal Slurm (on-premises) and Slurm running on Kubernetes (via Slinky or Soperator, often what neoclouds deliver); jobs arrive through slurmrestd.
4Shared services
container registry with per-site mirrors, object storage with replication, identity federation, observability and cost data.
5Adapters, not forks
everything provider-specific (instance types, fabric drivers, storage classes, auth) lives in a site profile and adapter; the job definition never changes.
Going deeper2 points
  • The control plane must not depend on one provider: if it runs only in one cloud, that cloud's outage stops the whole fleet. Keep its state replicated and a warm standby in a second location.
  • Sites keep local autonomy: each site's own scheduler (Kueue or Slurm) still decides placement inside the site; the fleet decides only which site, so a control-plane outage stops new dispatch but not running work.

Sites and capacity sources

Scenario. Nobody can answer "how many H100s do we have, at what price, until when?" The answer is spread across five contracts, three consoles and a spreadsheet.

What the picture shows. The inventory: every site described in one schema.

1Hardware
accelerator type and count, GPU memory, node shape, interconnect inside nodes and between nodes (InfiniBand, RoCE, EFA, or Ethernet only), and the largest gang that fits in one fabric domain.
2Scheduler and runtime
Kubernetes with Kueue, Slurm on Kubernetes, or bare-metal Slurm; container runtime (containerd, Enroot with Pyxis).
3Storage
parallel filesystem, object storage, local NVMe; measured throughput.
4Contract
reserved or committed (paid regardless of use), on-demand, or spot/preemptible; the price per GPU-hour, the commitment's end date and how much of it has been used.
5Constraints
region and jurisdiction, data residency classes the site may hold, export or compliance tags.
6Live state
free GPUs, queue length and estimated wait, health and recent reliability.

The YAML. A site described as a custom resource in the fleet control plane.

apiVersion: fleet.example.com/v1alpha1kind: Sitemetadata:  name: neocloud-a-us-eastspec:  provider: neocloud-a  region: us-east  jurisdiction: US  dataClasses: [public, internal]                 # may not hold restricted data  scheduler: { type: kubernetes, kueue: true, kubeconfigSecret: site-neocloud-a }  hardware:    accelerator: nvidia-h100-80gb    gpusPerNode: 8    nodes: 256    fabric: { type: infiniband, maxGangGPUsPerDomain: 1024 }  storage:    sharedFS: { type: vast, readGBps: 180 }    objectStore: { endpoint: https://s3.neocloud-a.example, region: us-east }  contract:    type: committed                              # paid whether used or not    gpuHourPrice: 2.10    committedGPUs: 2048    endsAt: "2028-06-30"  runtimeProfile: profiles/ib-mlx5-cuda12.yamlstatus:  freeGPUs: 312  estimatedWaitMinutes: { "8": 0, "64": 12, "512": 340 }  reliability30d: { jobFailureRate: 0.012, nodeMTBFHours: 1900 }
Going deeper2 points
  • Committed capacity has a "use it or lose it" value: idle committed GPU-hours cost money anyway; the placement service treats them as nearly free at the margin until the commitment is fully used.
  • Status is measured, not declared: estimated waits and reliability come from the site's own history, refreshed continuously.

One job API for researchers

Scenario. A researcher moving an experiment from the on-premises Slurm cluster to a cloud Kubernetes cluster rewrites a 60-line sbatch script into 140 lines of YAML, and gets the NCCL settings wrong.

What the picture shows. What a researcher declares, and what the platform fills in.

1The researcher declares
image, command, number of GPUs and how they're grouped (for example, 64 GPUs as 8 nodes of 8), accelerator class or minimum GPU memory, data inputs, checkpoint location, priority or deadline, and constraints only if needed (data residency, a specific accelerator).
2The platform fills in
the site, node selectors, fabric settings, mounts, credentials, queue names, the native job object and its scheduler settings.
3One CLI
submit, status, logs, attach, cancel and resume, with the same commands on every site; the CLI shows which site was chosen and why.
4Escape hatches
experts can pin a site or pass scheduler-specific options, recorded as constraints so the job remains portable by default.

The YAML. A ResearchJob: everything a researcher writes.

apiVersion: fleet.example.com/v1alpha1kind: ResearchJobmetadata:  name: rl-math-ablation-17  namespace: team-reasoningspec:  image: registry.example.com/reasoning/rl:2026.11       # mirrored to every site  command: ["python3", "-m", "rl.train", "--recipe=recipes/ablation-17.yaml"]  resources:    gpus: 64    shape: { nodes: 8, gpusPerNode: 8 }                    # gang: all 8 nodes or none    accelerator: { class: h100-class, minMemoryGB: 80 }    interconnect: high-bandwidth                           # needs IB/RoCE/EFA, not plain Ethernet  data:  - { name: prompts, uri: datasets://math-verified@v6, mount: /data/prompts }  checkpoints: { uri: ckpt://team-reasoning/rl-math-ablation-17, everyMinutes: 15 }  scheduling:    priority: standard    deadline: "2026-11-21T09:00:00Z"    preemptible: true                                      # may be moved between sites  constraints:    dataClass: internal                                    # sites allowed to hold this data
Going deeper2 points
  • The API is versioned and small: every field must have a meaning on every site type; anything that exists only on one site is a constraint, not a field.
  • "Why here?" is part of the answer: the CLI shows the placement decision (sites considered, scores, the winner) so researchers trust it instead of pinning sites by habit.

Placement: choosing the site

Scenario. Researchers pinned jobs to the on-premises cluster because their data lived there. Moving the 2 TB dataset once to the neocloud would have cost $40 in transfer and saved weeks of queueing.

What the picture shows. How the placement service picks a site.

1Feasibility filters
accelerator class and memory; a fabric domain large enough for the gang; data class and jurisdiction allowed; budget available; site healthy.
2Scores
estimated start time, true cost per GPU-hour (committed capacity costs almost nothing extra until used up), data movement cost and time, the site's recent reliability, and spreading risk across providers.
3Data gravity, measured
move the data if moving it is cheaper and faster than waiting; keep it where it is otherwise.
4Decisions are re-evaluated
a job still waiting after its estimated start can be re-placed at another site.

The code. A placement scorer over feasible sites (Python).

from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclassclass Option:    site: str    feasible: bool    wait_h: float              # estimated time to start    gpu_h_price: float         # marginal price per GPU-hour (≈0 for unused committed capacity)    data_move_usd: float       # transfer cost for inputs not already at the site    data_move_h: float    failure_rate: float        # recent job failure rate at this site def score(o: Option, gpus: int, est_runtime_h: float, deadline_h: float,          usd_per_wait_h: float = 50.0) -> float | None:    if not o.feasible:        return None    start_h = max(o.wait_h, o.data_move_h)                       # data can move while waiting    if start_h + est_runtime_h > deadline_h:        return None                                              # can't meet the deadline    compute = gpus * est_runtime_h * o.gpu_h_price    risk = o.failure_rate * gpus * est_runtime_h * 0.25 * max(o.gpu_h_price, 1.0)   # expected rework    delay = start_h * usd_per_wait_h                             # a researcher-hour of waiting has a cost    return compute + o.data_move_usd + risk + delay def place(options, **job):    scored = [(score(o, **job), o.site) for o in options]    scored = [(s, site) for s, site in scored if s is not None]    return min(scored)[1] if scored else None
Going deeper2 points
  • Price the wait: without a cost for waiting, placement always picks the cheapest site and queues there forever; the waiting cost is a policy knob per priority.
  • Burn commitments deliberately: track committed GPU-hours used against the plan; when a commitment is behind, lower its marginal price so more work flows there.

The Kubernetes execution operator

Scenario. The same JobSet worked on one cloud and failed on another: different GPU node labels, a different network device plugin, a different storage class, and NCCL needing a different transport plugin.

What the picture shows. How a ResearchJob becomes native work on a Kubernetes site.

1Render
the operator turns the ResearchJob into a JobSet (one replicated job of N pods for N nodes) with Kueue labels, topology annotations (Design 17) and the checkpoint and data mounts.
2Overlay the site profile
node selectors and tolerations, the fabric's device resources and environment (for example, EFA devices and the libfabric NCCL plugin on AWS, InfiniBand devices and RDMA settings on IB sites), storage classes, and image pull secrets or mirrors.
3Dispatch
create the JobSet in the site's cluster (directly, or through MultiKueue when the site is a MultiKueue worker), then watch it.
4Sync status back
queued, admitted, running, failed or succeeded, with the site's reason, into the ResearchJob status.

The YAML. A site runtime profile the operator merges into every pod it renders for that site.

# profiles/aws-p5-efa.yaml — overlay for AWS P5 sitesnodeSelector: { node.kubernetes.io/instance-type: p5.48xlarge }tolerations: [ { key: nvidia.com/gpu, operator: Exists, effect: NoSchedule } ]resources:  perNode: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8, vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: 32 }   # EFA interfaces per nodeenv:  FI_PROVIDER: efa  FI_EFA_USE_DEVICE_RDMA: "1"  NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME: "^lo,docker"imageOverlay: registry.example.com/runtime/aws-ofi-nccl:1.14   # adds the libfabric NCCL pluginvolumes:  sharedFS: { storageClass: fsx-lustre }  scratch: { hostPath: /opt/dlami/nvme }---# profiles/ib-mlx5-cuda12.yaml — overlay for InfiniBand neocloud sitesnodeSelector: { gpu.nvidia.com/class: h100 }resources:  perNode: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8, rdma/ib: 8 }env:  NCCL_IB_HCA: "mlx5"  NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME: "eth0"volumes:  sharedFS: { storageClass: vast-rwx }  scratch: { hostPath: /mnt/local-nvme }
Going deeper2 points
  • Profiles are tested artifacts: a profile change runs the site conformance suite (below) before it's used for real jobs.
  • Same image, different overlay: keep the researcher's image identical everywhere; fabric-specific libraries come from a thin per-site layer or from the node, never from researchers rebuilding images per site.

The Slurm execution operator

Scenario. Two sites only offer Slurm. Researchers who never used Slurm can't use them, and those who did write scripts that only work on one of the two.

What the picture shows. How the same ResearchJob runs on a Slurm site.

1Render
the operator generates a batch script from the ResearchJob: node count, GPUs per node, time limit, partition and account from the site profile, and a containerized srun (with Pyxis and Enroot) running the same image and command.
2Submit through slurmrestd
the Slurm REST API, authenticated with a short-lived token for the mapped Slurm account; the operator stores the Slurm job ID.
3Watch and map states
PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED, TIMEOUT and NODE_FAIL map to ResearchJob states; preemption and requeue map to the fleet's resume logic.
4Slurm on Kubernetes
where Slurm runs inside Kubernetes (Slinky, SchedMD's operator, or Nebius's Soperator, which also provides a shared root filesystem across nodes), the fleet still talks to Slurm through slurmrestd, so the operator doesn't care how Slurm is hosted.
5Same semantics
the job sees the same mounts, environment variables and checkpoint location as on Kubernetes sites.

The code. The rendered batch script and its submission through slurmrestd (Bash, Python).

#!/bin/bash#SBATCH --job-name=rl-math-ablation-17#SBATCH --nodes=8#SBATCH --gpus-per-node=8#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=8#SBATCH --time=36:00:00#SBATCH --partition=h100          # from the site profile#SBATCH --account=team-reasoning  # mapped from the researcher's team#SBATCH --requeue                 # fleet resumes from checkpoint on preemptionexport NCCL_IB_HCA=mlx5           # from the site profilesrun --container-image=registry.example.com#reasoning/rl:2026.11 \     --container-mounts=/fs/datasets/math-verified-v6:/data/prompts,/fs/ckpt/rl-math-ablation-17:/ckpt \     python3 -m rl.train --recipe=recipes/ablation-17.yaml --ckpt-dir=/ckpt
import httpx def submit_slurm(site, script: str, job_name: str, token: str, user: str) -> int:    """Submit through slurmrestd; use the API version your Slurm release provides."""    body = {"job": {"name": job_name, "script": script,                    "current_working_directory": site.workdir,                    "environment": ["PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin"]}}    r = httpx.post(f"{site.slurmrestd}/slurm/{site.api_version}/job/submit", json=body,                   headers={"X-SLURM-USER-NAME": user, "X-SLURM-USER-TOKEN": token}, timeout=30)    r.raise_for_status()    return r.json()["job_id"]
Going deeper2 points
  • Account mapping is policy: each team maps to a Slurm account with fair-share settings on each Slurm site, managed by the operator from the same quota data as Kueue (Design 17).
  • Don't hide Slurm from people who want it: experts can still log in to a Slurm site; the fleet just means nobody has to.

A portable environment

Scenario. A job that ran fine on one site crashed on another with a CUDA driver mismatch; on a third it ran 40% slower because NCCL fell back to TCP.

What the picture shows. The layers that make a job behave the same on every site.

1Base images
a small set of blessed base images (CUDA, NCCL, PyTorch versions) tested against every site's driver versions; researcher images build on them.
2Driver compatibility matrix
each site's GPU driver version and the CUDA versions it supports; placement rejects sites whose driver is too old for the image.
3Fabric layer
NCCL network plugins and settings per fabric, supplied by the site profile, not by researchers.
4Registry mirrors
images pushed once, replicated to a mirror or pull-through cache at each site; lazy-loading image formats for very large images.
5Runtime differences hidden
containerd on Kubernetes sites, Enroot with Pyxis on Slurm sites, both running the same OCI image.
6Startup check
every job's first seconds verify GPUs, driver, NCCL transport and mounts, and fail fast with a clear message if anything is wrong.

The code. A startup check that fails fast on environment problems (Python).

import os, sys, torch, torch.distributed as dist def startup_check(expect_transport: str | None = None):    problems = []    if not torch.cuda.is_available():        problems.append("no CUDA devices visible")    else:        need = int(os.environ.get("EXPECTED_GPUS_PER_NODE", "8"))        if torch.cuda.device_count() != need:            problems.append(f"expected {need} GPUs, found {torch.cuda.device_count()}")    for path in os.environ.get("REQUIRED_MOUNTS", "/data,/ckpt").split(","):        if not os.path.isdir(path):            problems.append(f"missing mount {path}")    # FLEET_NCCL_TRANSPORT is exported by the site's fabric layer after it loads the NCCL net plugin    if expect_transport and os.environ.get("FLEET_NCCL_TRANSPORT") != expect_transport:        problems.append(f"NCCL transport is not {expect_transport}: would fall back to TCP")    if problems:        print("STARTUP CHECK FAILED: " + "; ".join(problems), file=sys.stderr)        sys.exit(42)                    # config/environment error: fail fast, don't retry (Design 13)
Going deeper2 points
  • Measure, don't trust, the fabric: a short all-reduce bandwidth test at job start (a few seconds) catches silent TCP fallback that a configuration check can miss.
  • Keep the number of base images small: each base image multiplies the compatibility testing across sites.

Data and checkpoints across sites

Scenario. A job preempted at the neocloud should have resumed on AWS, but its checkpoints were on the neocloud's filesystem, unreachable from AWS. It waited a day to restart at the same site.

What the picture shows. Where data lives, how it moves and what it costs.

1Source of truth
datasets and checkpoints in object storage in a "home" region, with versioned snapshots (Design 13).
2Per-site caches
datasets replicated or cached at sites that run jobs on them, populated before the job starts (placement accounts for the copy time).
3Checkpoints
written locally first for speed, then copied to the site's object storage and replicated to home, so any site can resume.
4Data classes and residency
restricted data never leaves allowed jurisdictions; placement enforces it.
5Egress budgeting
transfer costs per provider and direction are part of placement and chargeback; large recurring transfers get dedicated links or are avoided.

The code. Estimating the cost and time of preparing a site for a job (Python).

EGRESS_USD_PER_GB = {("aws", "internet"): 0.09, ("gcp", "internet"): 0.12,                     ("neocloud-a", "internet"): 0.0, ("onprem", "internet"): 0.0}   # illustrative def staging_cost(inputs, site, link_gbps: float = 10.0):    """inputs: dicts with size_gb, home_provider, cached_at (set of sites)."""    usd, gb = 0.0, 0.0    for d in inputs:        if site in d["cached_at"]:            continue        gb += d["size_gb"]        usd += d["size_gb"] * EGRESS_USD_PER_GB.get((d["home_provider"], "internet"), 0.1)    hours = gb * 8 / (link_gbps * 3600)                       # GB → Gb, at the link rate    return {"gb": gb, "usd": round(usd, 2), "hours": round(hours, 2)}   # feeds placement
Going deeper2 points
  • Checkpoint replication is a recovery feature: replicate only the latest few checkpoints across sites; older ones stay at home.
  • Prefer pulling to pushing: a site fetches what its jobs need through its cache, so data movement follows placement decisions instead of predictions.

Identity, secrets and access

Scenario. Each site had its own long-lived keys in researchers' home directories. When a researcher left, it took two weeks to find and revoke them all.

What the picture shows. One identity for people and workloads across all providers.

1People
single sign-on to the fleet CLI; the fleet maps each person to their team and its accounts at each site. Nobody holds provider credentials to run jobs.
2Workloads
jobs authenticate to storage and services with short-lived tokens from workload identity federation (OIDC trust between the fleet's issuer and each provider), not static keys.
3Operators
the fleet's own credentials per site are scoped to job submission and status, rotated automatically and held in a secrets manager.
4Slurm sites
short-lived REST tokens for mapped Slurm accounts; no shared service account that can impersonate anyone.
5Offboarding
removing a person from the directory removes their access everywhere, because no site holds an independent credential for them.
Going deeper2 points
  • Audit in one place: every submission, data access and placement decision is logged in the fleet with the person and team, regardless of which site ran it.
  • Least privilege per site: a job at a neocloud gets read access to the datasets it declared and write access to its checkpoint path, nothing else.

Fleet operations: onboarding, health and cost

Scenario. A new neocloud contract started on Monday; the first real job ran on Thursday and failed because the storage was a tenth of the advertised throughput. Nobody had tested the site end to end.

What the picture shows. The lifecycle and daily operation of sites.

1Conformance suite before joining
GPU and node health (Design 14), NCCL all-reduce bandwidth at several gang sizes, storage read and write throughput, image pull time from the mirror, checkpoint write and cross-site restore, and an end-to-end ResearchJob on each scheduler path. A site joins only when results meet its profile.
2Site states
onboarding, active, degraded (no new large jobs), draining (contract ending or maintenance) and retired; placement respects the state.
3Normalized observability
the same GPU metrics (DCGM), job labels and logs from every site, so dashboards and the GPU-hour breakdown (Design 17) cover the whole fleet.
4Cost and commitments
spend per site, team and job; committed capacity burn against plan; alerts when a commitment is behind.
5Cross-site resume
jobs preempted or failed at one site, and flagged as movable, are re-placed and resume from the replicated checkpoint.

The YAML. The conformance suite run against a candidate site, as a ResearchJob pinned to it.

apiVersion: fleet.example.com/v1alpha1kind: ResearchJobmetadata:  name: conformance-neocloud-b-2026-11  namespace: fleet-opsspec:  image: registry.example.com/fleet/conformance:2026.11  command: ["python3", "-m", "conformance.run",            "--tests=gpu-health,nccl-allreduce,storage-throughput,image-pull,ckpt-roundtrip,cross-site-restore",            "--nccl-sizes=8,64,512", "--report=s3://fleet/conformance/neocloud-b/2026-11"]  resources:    gpus: 512    shape: { nodes: 64, gpusPerNode: 8 }    interconnect: high-bandwidth  constraints:    site: neocloud-b-eu-west                        # pinned: this is a test of the site itself  scheduling: { priority: fleet-ops }
Going deeper2 points
  • Re-run conformance after every site change: driver upgrades, firmware, scheduler versions and profile edits all re-run a subset; a regression puts the site in "degraded".
  • Exit plans are part of onboarding: for every contract, know how to drain it, where its data and checkpoints go, and how long that takes, before it starts.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, inventory and visibility: Site resources for every provider, normalized metrics and cost data, the GPU-hour breakdown across the fleet.
  • Phase 2, one job API on Kubernetes sites: ResearchJob, the CLI, the Kubernetes operator with site profiles, registry mirrors and placement across Kubernetes sites.
  • Phase 3, Slurm sites: the Slurm operator through slurmrestd, account mapping, Slurm-on-Kubernetes sites; startup checks and base images tested across all sites.
  • Phase 4, mobility and operations: dataset caches and checkpoint replication, cross-site resume, conformance-gated onboarding, commitment burn management.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • A lowest-common-denominator API: features only one site offers are reachable only as constraints, in exchange for jobs that run anywhere.
  • The fleet layer is another system to run, with its own availability, in exchange for researchers not learning five providers.
  • Data movement costs money, in exchange for using idle committed capacity instead of queueing next to the data.
  • Adapters lag new provider features by weeks, in exchange for stable behavior.

Open questions.

  • Gangs across sites: can large jobs span two sites (with very high staleness tolerance, as in asynchronous RL, Design 09), or must every gang fit one site?
  • Spot and preemptible capacity across providers: how much movable work can absorb interruptions without losing more than it saves?
  • Placement learning: can estimated waits, failure rates and runtimes be predicted well enough from history to make placement fully automatic?
  • Contract planning: how should next year's mix of commitments, on-demand and on-premises capacity be chosen from this year's fleet data?
Design 19 · 12 sections

Design 19: Building a scheduling layer that measurably raises accelerator utilization

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Defining utilization so it can't be argued with
  3. Baseline instrumentation
  4. Architecture of the scheduling layer
  5. Quotas as code
  6. Simulate before you ship
  7. Staged rollout with guardrails
  8. Proving the gain: separating policy from demand
  9. Idle reclamation: often the biggest lever
  10. Team scorecards that keep the gains
  11. Running the layer: SLOs and continuous tuning
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we build a scheduling layer (gang scheduling, bin-packing and fair-share quotas) and prove, with numbers that survive scrutiny, that it raised accelerator utilization across teams? Design 17 explains the mechanisms: Kueue admission, topology-aware gangs, bin-packing profiles, cohorts and fair sharing. This design is about delivering them as a program: defining the metric, instrumenting a baseline, building the layer as code, simulating changes before rollout, rolling out in stages, attributing gains to each change, and reporting per team so the improvement lasts.

The short version: define utilization precisely, measure a baseline before touching anything, and ship each change as an experiment. Utilization is measured from GPU activity (not allocation), per team and per pool, from one pipeline. Quotas live in Git and generate the Kueue objects. Every policy change is first replayed against recorded jobs in a simulator, then rolled out to one pool while a comparable pool stays unchanged, so the gain can be separated from changes in demand. A per-change attribution shows which lever moved the number, and team scorecards keep the gains from eroding.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. Leadership has approved a scheduling project with a target: raise GPU utilization across the 1,024-GPU fleet from "about 58%" to 75% within two quarters, instead of buying 300 more GPUs. Three problems appear on day one. Nobody agrees on what "58%" measured. Two previous efforts claimed improvements that disappeared when demand dropped over the holidays. And team leads worry that "utilization" means their jobs will be preempted more.

What the program must deliver.

  • One agreed metric: a definition of utilization that teams, finance and the platform team accept, measured the same way every day.
  • A trustworthy baseline: several weeks of data before any change, by team and pool.
  • The scheduling layer as code: quotas, queues and scheduler profiles generated from versioned definitions.
  • Evidence before rollout: simulated impact of each change on utilization and on wait times.
  • Causal attribution: how much of the change came from the scheduler, separated from demand changes.
  • Guardrails: utilization gains that don't come at the cost of large-job wait times, preemption losses or fairness.
  • Lasting results: team-level reporting that keeps idle allocation from creeping back.

Out of scope: the mechanics of each scheduling feature (Design 17) and multi-cluster placement (Design 02, Design 18).

Defining utilization so it can't be argued with

Scenario. The platform dashboard said 58% (GPUs allocated to pods), the finance report said 71% (nodes powered on and assigned), and a team lead's notebook showed 34% (average SM activity). All three were "GPU utilization."

What the picture shows. A metric tree from raw capacity to useful work, with one headline number and the ones under it.

1Capacity
GPU-hours of healthy, schedulable GPUs. Nodes down for repair are reported separately, not hidden in the denominator.
2Allocation rate
the share of capacity requested by running pods (what Kueue and kube-scheduler control).
3Activity rate
the share of allocated GPU-hours where the GPU is actually working, measured from DCGM's graphics-engine activity (above a small threshold), not from nvidia-smi utilization alone.
4Headline: active utilization
= allocation rate × activity rate: the share of capacity doing work.
5Efficiency below that
SM activity and tensor-core activity show how hard the GPUs work while active; MFU belongs to training benchmarks (Design 15), not to the scheduler's target.
6The scheduler's target is active utilization;
the scheduler can raise allocation directly and activity indirectly (by reclaiming idle allocations), but it can't make a slow data loader faster.

The code. Computing the metric tree for one day and one team from per-GPU minute samples (Python).

import pandas as pd def utilization(samples: pd.DataFrame, active_threshold: float = 0.05) -> pd.Series:    """samples: one row per GPU per minute with columns       healthy (bool), allocated (bool), team (str|None), gr_engine_active (0..1 from DCGM)."""    healthy = samples[samples.healthy]    capacity = len(healthy)                                            # GPU-minutes    alloc = healthy[healthy.allocated]    active = alloc[alloc.gr_engine_active >= active_threshold]    return pd.Series({        "capacity_gpu_h": capacity / 60,        "allocation_rate": len(alloc) / capacity,        "activity_rate": len(active) / max(len(alloc), 1),        "active_utilization": len(active) / capacity,                  # the headline        "mean_engine_activity_when_active": active.gr_engine_active.mean(),        "unhealthy_gpu_h": (len(samples) - capacity) / 60,             # reported, not hidden    }) def by_team(samples):    return samples.groupby("team").apply(lambda g: utilization(g)).sort_values("active_utilization")
Going deeper2 points
  • Agree on the definition in writing before the project starts: the metric, threshold, denominator and data source, signed off by platform, finance and team leads; changing it later resets the baseline.
  • Report the tree, not just the headline: "allocation went up, activity went down" (jobs grabbing GPUs they don't use) is a different story from both rising.

Baseline instrumentation

Scenario. The previous effort measured "before" for one week in December and "after" for one week in February. Demand had doubled in between. The improvement was mostly demand.

What the picture shows. The data pipeline that produces the metric, the baseline and the context needed to interpret it.

1GPU activity
DCGM exporter on every GPU node, with pod and namespace labels, scraped every 30 seconds.
2Allocation
kube-state-metrics for GPU requests of running pods; Kueue metrics for quota usage, pending workloads and admission wait times.
3Demand context
submitted GPU-hours per team per day, pending GPU-hours, and job size mix; without these, utilization changes can't be interpreted.
4Recording rules and a warehouse
per-minute aggregates by team, pool and GPU type, stored long term so the baseline can be recomputed if definitions change.
5Baseline period
at least four weeks, covering normal variation (weekdays, weekends, deadlines), with no scheduler changes during it.

The YAML. Prometheus recording rules for allocation and activity per team (Prometheus Operator).

apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1kind: PrometheusRulemetadata: { name: gpu-utilization, namespace: monitoring }spec:  groups:  - name: gpu-utilization    interval: 1m    rules:    - record: team:gpu_allocated:sum                       # GPUs requested by running pods (label_team from namespace labels)      expr: |        sum by (label_team) (          kube_pod_container_resource_requests{resource="nvidia_com_gpu"}          * on (namespace, pod) group_left() (kube_pod_status_phase{phase="Running"} == 1)          * on (namespace) group_left(team) kube_namespace_labels{label_team!=""}        )    - record: team:gpu_active:sum                          # allocated GPUs actually working      expr: |        sum by (label_team) (          (DCGM_FI_PROF_GR_ENGINE_ACTIVE > bool 0.05)          * on (namespace) group_left(team) kube_namespace_labels{label_team!=""}        )    - record: fleet:gpu_capacity_healthy:sum      expr: sum(kube_node_status_allocatable{resource="nvidia_com_gpu"} * on (node) group_left() (kube_node_spec_unschedulable == 0))    - record: fleet:gpu_active_utilization:ratio      expr: sum(team:gpu_active:sum) / fleet:gpu_capacity_healthy:sum
Going deeper2 points
  • Label hygiene matters: namespaces must carry a team label; unlabeled namespaces are a reported category, not silently dropped.
  • Recompute, don't edit: store raw per-minute aggregates, so a corrected definition can be applied to the whole history, including the baseline.

Architecture of the scheduling layer

Scenario. Previous changes were made by hand in the cluster: a ClusterQueue edited here, a scheduler flag there. Nobody could say which configuration was in effect on which date.

What the picture shows. The components the project builds, and how they connect.

1Policy source
team allocations, weights, priorities and pool definitions in Git, reviewed like code.
2Policy controller
generates ResourceFlavors, Cohorts, ClusterQueues, LocalQueues and WorkloadPriorityClasses from the policy source and applies them; reports drift.
3Admission and placement
Kueue with gang semantics and topology-aware scheduling, kube-scheduler with a bin-packing profile for GPU pools (Design 17).
4Reclaimers
an idle reclaimer for allocations that aren't used, and a compaction controller for fragmented nodes.
5Measurement
the metric pipeline above, plus a change log of every policy version and when it was applied.
6Simulator
replays recorded jobs against candidate policies before they reach the cluster.
Going deeper2 points
  • Every policy version has a timestamp: attribution later needs to know exactly which configuration was active when; the controller writes each applied version to the change log.
  • The layer is Kubernetes-native: no custom scheduler fork; customization is configuration plus small controllers, so upgrades of Kueue and Kubernetes stay routine.

Quotas as code

Scenario. Quotas lived in a spreadsheet and were copied into ClusterQueues by hand. After a reorganization, the quotas added up to 1,180 GPUs on a 1,024-GPU fleet, and two teams had no LocalQueue at all.

What the picture shows. One reviewed file for team allocations, validated and turned into Kueue objects.

1Allocations file
each team's guaranteed GPUs per pool, borrowing and lending limits, fair-share weight and namespaces.
2Validation in CI
guaranteed quotas add up to the pool's healthy capacity (within a margin), every team has a queue, weights are positive, no namespace belongs to two teams.
3Generation
a small generator renders Cohorts, ClusterQueues and LocalQueues; a GitOps tool applies them.
4Change review
quota changes are pull requests with an owner's approval; the merge time becomes the change-log entry.

The code. Validating allocations and generating ClusterQueues (Python).
